TEN ROBBER TOES. There is a story that I have been told, And it's just as old as babies are old; For sweet Mother Eve, as everyone knows, Told her babies the tale of the toes. Told to her babies how little ten toes, Each one as pink as the pinkiest pink rose, Once on &time was naughty and bad, And sorrow and trouble in consequence had. How this big toe wanted butter and bread After his mamma had put him to bed; And thiS lying next said, "S'posen we go Down to the pantry and get it, you know." And this wicked toe cried, "Come along quick; Let's sugar the butter ever so thick." And this naughty toe said "Jelly for me, Top of the butter and sugar, you see." And this little toe cried, "Goody, let's go; We'll slip down the stairs so quiet and slow." So ten robber toes, all tipped with red, Stole silently out of their snowy white bed. While this wicked toe. so jolly and fat, Helped nine naughty toes to pitty-pat-pat Along the big hall, with pillars of white, And down the back stairs devoid of light. Then this little toe got a terrible scare, For he thought in the dark of a grizzly bear. And this little toe said, "Nurse must be right 'Bout gobbles and witches living at night" And this little toe said, "A fox may be hid In the hat-rack box, right under the lid." And this little toe cried, "Dear me, oh! Lions and tigers is coming, I know." Then mamma Came out with the beautiful light, Caught ten robber toes all ready for flight; Yes, she caught and she kissed those ten robber toes, Till redder they were than any red rose. .--Leeds Weekly Mercury.

MASTER ANn MAN.—The whole relation of master and servant is to-day corrupt and vulgar. At home in Eng- land it is the master who is degraded; here in the States, by a triumph of inverted tact, the servant often so con- trives that he degrades himself. He must be his place: and it is the mark of a gentleman to be at. home. Ile thinks perpetually of his own dignity: it is the proof of a gentleman to be jealous of the dignity of others. He is ashamed of his trade, which is the essence of vul- garity. He is paid to do certain services, yet he does them so gruffly that any man of spirit would resent them if they were gratuitous favours; and this (if he will reflect upon it tenderly) is so far from the genteel as to be not even coarsely honest. Yet we must not blame the man for these mistakes; the vulgarity is in the air. There is a tone in popular literature much to be de- , plored, deprecating service, like a disgrace; honouring those who are ashamed of it: honouring even (I speak not without book) such as prefer to live by the charity of poor neighbours instead of blacking the shoes of the rich. "Slacking shoes is counted (in these works) a thing Specially disgraceful. To the philosophic mind, it will seem a less exceptionable trade than to deal in stocks, and one in which it is more easy to be honest than to write books.—Gentlemen, by Robert Louis Stevenson, in Scribner's Magazine. MAY DAY AT WHITELANDS TRAINING CeLLEG?., CHELSEA. should like to tell you about the queen who is chosen here, in the very middle of smoky London, every May Day. At nine o'clock in the morning of the first of May, if you were to go to Whitelands Training College, Chel- sea, von would find the whole place decorated with - lovely flowers. Before you had time to wonder where they all came from you would bear from a distance the Sweet strains of a triumphal hymn. Nearer and nearer ' they come, and then we see the scholars approaching in *procession, all dressed in purest white, and wearing no ornaments but the sweet May -flowers. They walk to the chapel, and, after an appropriate service, they go into the general class-room, whidh is also beautifully decorated. Then comes the business of the day, each girl recording her vote as to whiSh of her fellows she finds " likeablest, loveablest. and cleyerest;" for these are the qualities that Mr. Ruskin considers most worthy of the crown. Music beguiles the time until the name of the queen is proclaimed amid hearty cheers. The happy scholar is led off to be robed, and presently returns, passing through an avenue of thirty girls, each bearing a basket of flowers and a long silver Mar-pole decked with ribbons and flowers. She kneels to receive the golden cross which Mr. Ruskin sends to each Queen of the May, and then takes her seat on the throne. Behind her are three maidens in attendance, and at her side is the late queen, whose simple wreath of forget-me- nots appeals silently to those who were once her sub- jesqs.—Little Folks Kigazine. GENERAL HARNEY'S DIGNITY.—The following story is told of General Harney when he was in command at Camp Verde, Texas. He was an intenselysdignieed offi- cer, and if there was one thing he detested more than another it was undignified haste. One evening, just as he was about to hold dress parade, he perceived that he had forgotten hi a handkerchief. and as the weather was very hot, he said to his orderly, "Go to my quarters, quick, and bring my handkerchief." The orderly touched his cap and started for the quarters, several hundred yards distant. After he had proceeded a short distance, remembering that there was no time to lose, he broke into a trot." "See that scoun- drel running as if the Indians were after him. If there is anything I hate it is to see a soldier run- ning instead of marching properly." "Here, my man," continued Barney to another soldier, "go after that man and tell him to walk, —him !" The second Soldier started after the first, but as the first kept on running, the second one saw his only chance to deliver the message was to hurry up, so he, too, broke into a run. To say that Harney swore is to use a mild expres- sion. "Here, sergeant. go after that man and tell him if he don't stop running I'll hang him up by the thumbs." 'The sergeant started out on a brisk walk, but as his pre- decessor had a good start he, too, began to run as hard as he could. "If all the three scoundrels ain't running like jack-rabbits r, ejaculated Barney. "I'll show 'em." and tucking his sword under his arm, he started in pur- suit SA fast as he could run, but suddenly remembering his dignity, he came to a halt, and walked stiffly back to the place where the dress parade was to come off. DATES AND COCOA-NUTS.—The contrast between the date and the cocoa-nut, both exactly analogous fruits, produced by closely allied and similar trees, marks ad- mirably the way in which purely human and culinary distinctions are allowed to mask for us the actual facts and analogies of nature. For a date and a cocoa-nut are built on precisely the same plan, and answer layer for layer to one-another; only the part that we eat in the date is the part that we throw away in the cocoa- nut, and the part that we eat in the cocoa-nut is the part that we throw away in the date. First of all comes an outside fleshy layer, which in the date becomes at last soft and pulpy, while in the cocoa-nut it grows stringier and more fibrous as the fruit ripens; next comes a hard stone or nutshell, alike in both; and inside all lies the kernel, or seed, intended in either case to germinate or grow, but eaten in the nut, and thrown away, shell and all, in the date-fruit. Moreover, as the cocoa-nut usually has its outer fibrous layer strip- ped off before being exposed for sale, most people forget about it altogether; and so the real analogy between the two cases is still more easily overlooked. But why should the date-palm produce an edible fruit with a pulpy outer covering, while its congener the cocoa-palm produces a hard-shelled nut with a tough and fibrous outer layer? Simply because the cocoa-palm grows in oceanic islands, while the date-palm grows in desert oases. Cocoas flourish best by the sea shore, on coral reefs and atolls, within easy reach of the salt-laden breezes. The seeds are wafted hither and thither by winds and waves from island to island; and in no other way, as Darwin and Wallace have shown, could any plant succeed in peopling the widely dispersed archi- pelagos of the South Pacific and the Malay region. Hence the cocoa-nut requires great fieatirm power, pro- tection from salt water, a hard shell, and an immense stock of nutriment for its tender early years upon the beaches and sandbanks where it is finally tumbled. These requirements are amply met by nature in its fibrous matting, its smooth outer rind, its solid covering, and its rich store of copious albumen. The date-palm, on the other hand, asks for dispersion from oasis to oasis across the open desert, and it lives in regions thickly peopled by baboons and other monkeys. What more natural than to develop a pulpy outer fruit, to entice these unconscious friends, enclosing a 'very tough and hard shell, which no monkey's teeth can possibly penetrate? For this reason the date has now a sweet and fleshy outer coat, where the cocoa-nut has a light and fibrous external covering; and the well-dis- posed monkey, climbing the tall stem, and appropriating the fruit, frequently throws away the stone and seed by the water's edge, where it may best take root and grow and flourish. Of course, he throws away millions un- needed on the bare expanse of desert too; but that does not count; Nature always provides against these little accidents. Of a thousand seeds, says the poet with some modesty of statement, she often brings hut one to bear. Very well, then, the'date-palm will at all costs be even with her. A single tree produces as many as 20,000 dates in one season. Since the object of all these seeds is merely to keep up the usual number of date trees in the world, and since each date tree lives about 200 rears, men average of one date well placed out of four millions will be quite sufficient to effect her purpose. As a mat- ter of fact, wherever you find a tiny spring or stream in the desert, there also You find a date-palm. The stones germinate wherever the playful baboon throws them down in wet soil near the source of a river, or even in a damp fissure of the rock. The date-palm uses the mon- key to transport its seeds in just the same way as it uses the bee to transfer pollen from blossom to blossom. —From Of Dates, in the Cornhill Magazine for May. THE COON AND THE OYSTER.—SOMetiHMS, as you are aware, the biter gets bit. One night an old Racoon went to catch oysters at Cat Island, near New Orleans. Spying a big one with its shell open, the coon crawled up to it and put in his paw to scoop out the meat. No sooner had he done this than the shell came to with a snap, and the would-be captor was caught. In spite of all his efforts he could neither remove the oyster from the mud nor set his paw free from its clutches. Presently the tide turned, and the coon soon found the water about his feet. He had now to choose between death by drowning and the loss of a foot; so without more ado he actually gnawed his paw off and limped away on three legs. He won't go oyster fishing again in a hurry, that coon won't.—Littte Folks Maaazt.pe. GOOD MANNERS IN THE STEERAGE.—I once sailed On the emigrant side from the Clyde to New York; among- my fellow-passengers I passed generally as a mason, for i the excellent reason that there was a mason on board who happened to know; and this fortunate event enabled me to mix with these working people on a footing of equality. I thus saw them at their best, using their own civility; .while I, on the other hand, stood naked to their criticism. The workmen were at home, I was abroad, I ' was the shoeblack in the drawing-room, the Huron at -Versailles; and I used to have hot and cold fits, lest per- chance I made a beast of myself in this new environ- ment. I had no allowances to hope for; I could not plead that I was "only a gentleman after all," for I was known to be a mason; and I must stand and fall by my transplanted manners on their own intrinsic decency. It chanced there was a Welsh blacksmith on board, who was not only well-mannered himself and a judge of man- ners, but a fellow besides of an original mind. He had early diagnosed me as a masquerader and a person out of place; and as we had grown intimate upon the voyage I carried him my troubles. How did I behave? Was!. upon this crucial test, at all a gentleman? I might have asked eight hundred thousand blacksmiths (if Wales or I the world contain so many) and they would have held my question for a mockery; but Jones was a man of ' genuine perception, thought a long time before- he answered, looking at me comically and reviewing (I could see) the events of the voyage, and then told me that "on the whole" I did "pretty well."—Robert Louis Stevenson, in Scribner's Magazine. In some parts of Africa the natives compound a kind of fermented beer, and have learned that monkeys are exceedingly fond of it. So they fill calabashes with this beer and place it on the ground in those parts of the forests where they know the monkeys most frequent. They hide to watch the result. As soon as one of these I animals comes in sight of these calabashes his curiosity' tempts him to examine and filen, test what the dish , contains. No sooner does the 'over-curious monkey taste of the liquor contained in the calabashes than— finding it very good and amply sufficient for ninny—he utters loud cries of joy to attract his comrades and call of them to partake with him of the feast. Once assembled, a wild scene of bacchanalian revelry and riot begins. Learning no prudence from any for- mer experience of a similar indulgence any more than human beings do, they are all soon in a state of intoxication, that when the negroes come forward they feel no distrust, and, looking on them as a larger species of their own kind, they accept the hand of their captors as that of a friend to help them off the ground. The nearest monkey lays hold of the captive one for support also, no longer able to guide himself to a place of repose. Then another catches hold of the second, and so on, till the negro, without any resistance on the part of his pri- soners, leads a staggering band of a dozen or more tipsy monkeys into close quarters, where they sleep off their drunken folly, and wake, like many a poor mortal, to find that they have sold their freedom for a very un- satisfactory mess of pottage. ON GROWN-HP BABIES AND OTHER HOMAN PHENOMENA. —True children are simple. We once heard of a little girl, an earl's granddaughter too, who had been carefully kept ignorant of all distinctions between poor and rich, and who would say, "Mother, this old lady has asked me for a penny," and "Why does not or new nurse have her dinner with you? She is grown up, and she tells nice stories." To which my lady would answer, "Nurse would not like that; she has a particular liking for dining with the cook." Now the very opposite to this type is the grown-up baby who looks like a little figure cut out of a fashion-plate. She is a society baby, and she has been so much with older people that she has grown up too, and the basis of her happiness is the fact that she is very pretty, and so are her dresses. This child detects beggars with a sagacity that leaves the house-dog nowhere. She shrinks from ara e-ged coat; she dislikes a shabby one. No old sailor will-ever show her a boat and give her a finger to shake when she goes to the seaside. No gardener will ever play at pretending that she helm; him to drag the garden roller. There is a broad division between this dainty little drawing-room lady and the common world; and in all gay folk and showy things she is prodigiously interested—not in kindly, poorer folk. There is no use in giving her toys unless they have cost money; she is proud to possess a great deal of riches of her own in a money-box, and finer nursery treasures than any of her friends can show her. If the little Jenkynses (with a p, mind, always) had a larger china tea-set than hers, she would weep aloud—and very much aloud—till she gets one at least twice as large as the Jenkynses'—which is exactly, in miniature, what happens with all her grown-up acquain- tances, who have no happiness in this world and worry everybody else unless their china dolls, of a grown-up sort, are twice as tine as those of the friends they love and play with—in their own way. Altogether, the little lady is a miniature woman of the world; she left off being a child a long time ago, and is considered at home to be perfection in embryo. She will look down on her teachers by-and-by. "Learn Mozart!" she will say in placid ignorance—" Is Mozart nice grown-up music?" "Yes, every one likes Mozart." "Ah ! then I would rather not; Mozart must be common." She will be lame at eleven, and despise everything—trom chocolate to Christmas-tune. At twelve she will no the victim of ennui. "It is an empty world; let me buy a new hat!" —(lagseirs Fanki:u Magazine. CHRISTIE'S ATLI' Sett ROOM.—The story runs that once in the early days cf the.firm, Mr. Christie was descanting on the beauties of a landscape by Wilson. ",Look at the tone, gentlemen," lie cried; "look at the colour and the beauty of the composition. Just observe the wonderful luminosity. It's a masterpiece—a perfect masterpiece! It was painted by Mr. Wilson, gentlemen, a good many years ago: he can paint nothing like that now." "You're a liar !" cried a little bottle-nosed man near the door, "he can paint ever so much better!" A roar of laughter greeted the interruption, for the spec- tators, turning round, recognised poor Wilson himself, who had come to try and forget the empty stomach he had brought with him from the Tottenham Court-road. . . Again, as an illustration of the effects of rivalry, I may remind the reader of the duel between a member of the Rothschild family and the late L-rd Dudley, when the latter ran a Sevres vase up to £6,000. On another occasion the last-named nobleman is said to have forgotten that he had already left a limit on a certain lot, and actually ran himself up to his own prohibitive limit. The late Mr. Beckett-Denison. too, was a very reckless buyer. The incident of his Purchase of Ruben's " Daniel in the Lion's Den." at the Hamilton sale, will not readily be forgotten. He bid up to four thousand ana nine guineas for it, and at his death, three years later, the Dnke bought it back for two thousand having thus practically hired it out for a thousand a year. . . . .Measrs. Christie, whose sales have for some years averaged £300,000. may be said to have reached their apogee- in 1882, when the Hamilton Collection (which realised the unprecedented amount of £397,562) brought their total of art sales for the eight months of the year to the enormous sum of £600,000. To what greater commercial heights the concern may still attain it passes the wit of man to guess. But it is pretty certain that, however much its turn-over may grow, its influence as a great art-centre and decentraliser can scarcely increase. All that can be fairly hoped for (and the expectation is hardly likely to be falsified) is that, by sustaining its extraordinary prestige, it may continue to retain the confidence of the art-patrons of England. and, so to speak, popularise still further the love and practical encouragement of art in all its de. velopments.—The Magazine of Art for May. div.head: OUR LONDON LETIER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETIER.

LONDON. THURSDAY The good fortune which has attached itself to the Government since the session opened still clings to their flag. The process by which they carry on their business is not, perhaps, very dignified or per- sonally distinguished. But it serves. They hold their places, pass their bills. and, best of all, keep out Mr. Gladstone. This week business has marched along at an exhilarating pace. The Budget Bill has left the House of Commons and passed the formal supervision of the House of Lords. It is still called the Budget Bill, though it differs considerably from the measure brought in by Mr. Goschen some weeks ago. By ,;iving way here and there whenever seri- ous opposition was threatened, Mr. Goschen has got through a Budget Bill, though it can scarcely be called his. It was upon an issue much less serious than one or two raised on Mr. Goschen's Budget that in 1885 Mr, Gladstone was tamed out. But the condition of affairs was then entirely different. Facing, ministers were an unscrupulous Oppoeition, who harried the Government at! every- step, made what they themselves c illed "a shameful alliance," at any cost, eager only to taste, for whatever brief time, the sweets•of office. Now obstruction is not only dead, kut buried. The Government make pro- gress with their measures with a rapidity that, as happened, on Monday night, really embarasses them, and if the promise of these opening months of the session be fulfilled, they will, before the proroga- tion, be able to boast the largest measure of accom- plished work since the Parliament of 1868 was set free from the incubus of obstruction. Of course, whilst the men responsible for the measures are Conservatives, the measures themselves are Liberal. That is not a model arrangement; but it does very well for the time.

Next to the phenomenal progress of public business in the House of Commons the Thief talk is about the juvenility of Mr. Gladstone. He seems to have been more suc- cessful than Mr. Rider Haggard's acquaintance "She" in his bathing in the magic flame that re- news youth. It is no unusual thing for him to astonish the House of Commons by sudden, more or less prolonged, manifestations of almost juvenils vigour. J3ut just now he has succeeded in surpris- ing an appetite grown familiar by usage. He has not yet presented himself in that suit ot light clothes, blue necktie, and white hat, with which at the earliest approach of summer he is accustomed to compete with " Bobby" Spencer and other beaus of the House. That will come by anu bye; meanwhile he is in constant attendance at the House, watches over the questions, and is pretty certain to take part in whatever debate is going on. In addition to this he gaily fulfil§ all the duties of a socal character which press upon popular persons at this time of the year.

London is now in the very height of the season. The young leaves and the spring flowers have all come out in the park togaze at fashion, old and young, in the Row. Picture Galleries are in full swing. there is the inevitable dinner party at night, with one or two "crushes" to follow. Mr. Gladstone takes his full share with the youngest votary. He has not missed any one of the three private picture views. Last Friday night he delivered two impor- tant speeches in the House of Commons, attended to his vast correspondence on Saturday morning, paid a series of social and political visits in the after- noon, dined at Sir Arthur Hayter's in the 'evening, stayed till nearly midnight at Lady Haytees recep- tion, and then drove off to Doll's Bill to spend a quiet Sunday-to-Monday with Lord Aberdeen. His great speech at the Memorial Hall yesterday after- noon, where he appeared as the centre and object of enthusiastic admiration of one of the most impor- tant representative public meetings of recent years. was merely an item in his week's programme, though for an ordinary man it would be sufficient public work for three moriths. According to his own testimony, he was Dever better in his life, and his appearance bears witness to his assertion. Amiable gentlemen who long ago had convinced themselves that he really could not last much longer, and that with him would go all hope of ex- tending Home Rule to Ireland, are beginning them- selves to take on a look of added age and hopeless weariness. I gather that some gentlemen who heard• Mr. Parnell for the first time at the Eighty Club were a little disappointed. They themselves attended full of enthusiasm. The room surged with welcome to the mysterious recluse whom Lord Salisbury once hailed as "the Irish Chief." Mr. Parnell, standing up haggard, tired looking, and apparently a little bored, betrayed no sign of pleasure or satisfaction. , He was, one tells me, "as cold as an icicle," his speech dripping forth with chilling regularity and precision. • This is Mr. Parnell 's later manner, one he has so , completely grown into that most people forget the possibilities of his reaching boiling pitch. I remember Mr. Parnell when he first entered the House of Commons, avowedly in the train of Mr. Butt. He was as little known to Ireland as he was to the House of Commons. His boon companion in the politics of those days was Mr. Biggar. The two were inseparable on the bench below the gang- way, one always ready to fol:ow the other in speech denunciatory of the Saxon. In those days. Mr. Parnell used to stand with clenched hands held straight down at his side, his eyes blazing with wrath, his face ashy pale, and the words of uncon- trollable hatred of everything Saxon hissed between his teeth. 'A very different man from the cool, collected, aristocratic man hi evening dress who on Tuesday night chilled a hearty English audience with unresponsive speech.: ' It is pretty to see Lord Randolph Churchill seated on the corner bench behind Ministers, playing with his moustache, while Mr. Balfour stands at the table the exponent of the views of the cabinet which Lord Randolph left in a moment of .pety anger. It is one of Lord Randolph's peculiarities that he cannot stand any competition for the first place. He must he everything or he will be nothing: - At one time he seemed to have comple- ted his dominion over Lord Salisbury, and it was the discovery that the Prime Minister would not backhim up in his peremptory efforts at snubbing Lord George Hamilton and Mr. Stanhope that caused him to quit the Ministry. Still, that Lord Salisbury should assume a position of personal supremecy is a matter for which some excuse may be made. He is well up in years, he is the head of a patrician hciuse, and he has earned the confidence of the party. What- vexes Lord Randolph is that Mr. Balfour, who a few years ago was quite a junior member of the Fourth Party, should now, without assistance from him, and even in opposition to his wishes, have reached a foremost place in the esti- mation of the Conservative party and of the House of Commons. Lord Randolph remembers the time when Mr. Balfour used to fetch and carry for him, and felt distinguished by a. nod of approval. Now he lords it on the Treasury Bench, confident in the assurance that with the Conservative party both in the House and the 'Country, he is absolutely the most popular minister. Lord Randolph, it is noted, never tries a fall with Mr. Balfour. Other members of the Ministry whom he holds are indebted to him for their personal ad- vancemeht suffer occssionally from his resentful lash. He has openly expressed his contempt for Mr. Henry Matthews, whom he made Home Secre- tary, and never misses an opportunity of giving him a little prod in debate. Sir John Gorst, who was the most active half of the party of which Mr. Arthur Balfour was really only an outsider, Lord Randolph does not even speak to. That he should be Under Secret ary of State for India, with a comfortable salary, whilst Lord Randolph haunts the cold shades •of the Opposition, is more than an amiable spirit can bear. Accordingly Lord Randolph cuts Sir John Gorst in private and in public, as happened the other day, when a question was put on the Hydera- bad Deccan business, he gave him a back-handed

slap. He would take even more delight in striking at Mr. Balfour, if that were possible. His absten- tion from active hostility is one of the highest tri- butes to the position Mr. Balfour has gained. At college Mr. Balfour used to be known as "Clara," in recognition of his graceful posturing and that laca— ilaisical manner which to-day drives the Irish mem- bers mad. But beneath the silken glove Mr. Balfour has shown the steel clad lian;., and is strong enough even to withstand the onslaught of his old friend and sometime,chief.

The New Gallery was opened for the private view on Tuesday, and before it closed at seven o'clock there was no doubt that there had been secured one of the completest and biggest successes of the kiiid ever achieved in London or elsewhere. People who care about pictures owe so much to the Grosvenor Gallery that, I think, there has been throughout the controversy an undercurrent of sympathy with the old institution. If it had been possible to stand by the Grosvenor that stand would have to be taken. But the New Gallery, has been opened, people have come, have seen, and the New Gallery has con- quered. The Academy has got Alma Tadema's big six thousand pounder, 'The Roses of Heliogabalus.' But the New Gallery shows the sketch of the pic- ture, which many simple people will think a greater delight. It has in addition some charming little things from the Master's brush. The Borne- Jones pictures are, of course, a thing apart, and be- sides these there are at least three hundred pictures that one would like to have for a private possession. Unquestionably the place to spend a happy after- noon in is the New Gallery. The celebration of the eighty-first birthday of Mr. Holden, which took place at Keighley the other day, was a very pleasant event. No one, to look upon the member for the Keighley division of Yorkshire, would guess his age. I have not of late noticed him so frequently in the House of Commons as was, his wont. I fancy the work is getting ridiculously light for him, and the hours of -labour are too short. In the golden days (or rather nights) when business used to be carried on till dawn flooded the chamber. it was quite a common thing to see the slight, erect figure of Mr. Holden walking to and from the divi- Sion lobby. Like Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Holden was blessed at his birth with a 'powerful constitution. But in his present state of blooming health and unimpaired strength, he is an example of what may be done by a man who orders his daily life upon scientific principles. Mr. Holden has done much substantial good through his long and honourable' life. There is one thing he might yet do, which would not fall short of the high average. That is to write a book that might be entitled " How I lived to be Eighty one," telling less favoured brethren what he eats, drinks, and avoids, what he thiaks,about the Turkish bath, and what are his views of the pre- cise temperature at which one's living rooms should be maintained.

div.head: 4'p
div.p: HUGH BETTE'S FIRST NOVEL.

There is something in the cutting out, and grinding up, and polishing of a novel that puzzles me. Of course it is easy enough to read a novel and to understand it; but the question is, how did the author manage to spin it out to such length. This is no doubt one of the secrets of the novel-writing profession. I have read a good many novels in my time. I have stood breatklessly behind the young midshipman and watched him mow down twenty or thirty armed pirates with his single cutlass. I have trembled for the brigand hero who dauntlessly kept a whole company of the king's soldiers out of his cave by his own unaided efforts; yet I am sure that I couldn't write either of their biographies to occupy more than ten pages at the outside, even if I were given the license of a "three- penny dreadful." Now a friend of mine, who said he had great influence with ol certain firm of publishers, one day, when con- versing with me, asked me if I didn't think I could write a novel. He remarked, "You know, Bette, there is a good thing to be made out of a well-written novel, and I don't see why you shouldn't write one; that is if you have time." Time! Certainly I had time; and I told him so. I wrote that novel immediately. I got so interested in it, in fact, that I couldn't go to bed and leave the thing "to be continued," so I finished it the same night. _ .

When I showed it to my friend he said it was "just about long enough for an introduction." He asked me if I was serious. I told him to read it through, and he would see how serious I was; but he wouldn't. I don't think I shall ever write another. The following is the novel, if you care to read it. It is sensational.
CHAPTER I.—THE KNELL. bie honriing blasts drive devious, Tempest tossed. Sails ripped, seams opening wide, And compass lost.

The elements were in a fury; the starm-spirit howled and shrieked in the air as if tortured by some giant demon; the lightning hurled its lurid flashes to the earth; the deafening crash of thunder rattled overhead ,almost without intermission; the rain poured down in torrents; and when there was a momentary lull in the mad rage of the storm, even the heavy splash of huge rain-drops appeared to the overcharged senses a solemn stillness. It was a fearful night; sure a night upon which the bravest of human beings might cower by the fireside and tremblingly listen to weird stories of the spirit world. Yet amid the raging storm; when the lightning cleft the iuky blackness, the figure of a man might have been see it emerging cautiously from the plantation close to Major Griffin's house, and to button his drenched coat nearer to his shivering form. It was Jabez. Bvery flash of the electric fluid identified him. He had a wart on his nose that would have done splendid duty as a public-house sign, and he couldn't have hidden those knock-a-knees anywhere but in the bowels, of the earth. (The reader will naturally say, "What the deuce did he want there at such a time ?" Quite right!) Let us follow his movements. He looked cautiously to the right and left, and nearing the fence of the Major'S garden, he climbed over it with the grace of a hedge- hog climbing a greasy pole. and with thelexception of tearing a small piece out of his pants, he got over easily, and floundered over the other side., Almost simul- taneously thire was a sharp ringing snap and a yell of agony, and Jabez found one of his legs clutchea in a man trap with a force sufficient to straighten that limb for life. . . (By the way, Jabez was the fourth son of old Peggy the village charwoman.) CHAPTE 12 If. Of all sad words by tongue or pen, The saddest are "it might have been."

The inside of the Major's house bore traces of quiet sadness. The blaze of a large fire in the drawing-robin roared up the chimney as though essaying to rival the storm without; and as the bright light diffused through the room, its-ruddy glow was cast upon a man who sat apparently buried in deep gr,ef, his chin resting upon-his broad massive chest. It was the Major. He moved not, save for the heaving of his manly breast; and the choking sounds that appeared to be-torn from his bosom, when properly analysed, proved to be the snores of an inebriate. Briefly, the Major was quite bottled. A female figure glided softly to the sleeping form,. and after stooping over him in breathless anxiety, it winked at the counterpart of itself in the large mirror over the mantelpiece and silently withdrew. For what dark pur- pose is this stealth? Let us follow. Arrived in the kitchen, the figure cast a hasty glance over a large rabbit-pie, and knives and forks for two, and then exclaimed with bitter vehemence. "If he thinks he'll make a fool of me I'll let him see—but no! Oh I Jabez ! Jabez !" t,he then looked at the clock, took "six hasty strides" to the back door, reached out an empty sixteen-gallon barrel, stove one end in with a fervour that could only be prompted by passionate love (and a coal hammer), placed the barrel upside down over her beauteous form and, taking her bearings throughthe bunghole, strode forth into the wild night. (I for- got to state that the female's name was Mary Ann.— Ammon.) .

div.head: CHAPTER 111.
div.p: CHAPTER 111.

There's nothlnehalf so sweet In life as love's young dream. The billiard balls rattled gaily at the Vagrant's fashionable club, and several rollicking young officers were conversing on their love exploits. Said young Tom Cassidy, "That Julia Mc.Closkte is a stunning girl. I've half a mind to begin coarting her." The son of Major Griffin here stepped forward, and, with a frown on his well-cut features, said as he raised himself to his full height, "Base villain ! are you aware that Julia is my betrothed ? You shall wipe out the dastardly insult with your heart's blood." Cassidy however dexterously shot out his left, and while young Griffin lay senseless with his nose in a spittoon. Cassidy went out and engaged a ruffian with a pair of iron clogs, who came in and kicked Griffin to death, at the same time making the remark, "Love is a queer thing."

CHAPTER IV. But at intervals there gushed, Accompanied with a convulsive splash, The solitary shsielc, the bubbling cry Of some strong swimmer in his agony. It was a cairn delicious evening; the birds poured forth their joyous feelings in glad song; only the gentle zephyrs fa.ined the woodland leaves; the shouts of merry children at play mingled with the lark's thrilling notes ; all nature seemed hushed in quiet beauty. But hark! there comes the measured tramp of horse, and shouts of cavalry advancing. Major Griffin rushed to the canal bank just in time to see two boatmen fish up a beer barrel with two limp feet dangling out of one end. The Major Identified both the barrel and the feet on account of their respective sizes, and after shedding two large tears, and taking one pinch of snuff, he ordered the barrel, containing the remains of his once blythe and lovely cook Mary Ann to be removed to the hall, and followed in its wake, weeping, and wailing, and gnashing his gums. CHAPTER V.

Soft eyes looked love to eyes that spoke again. In a sweet little cottage, with a picturesque garden full of beautiful flowers, the odoriferous scent of which floated upon the passing breeze, and filled the air around with fragrance, with the ivy intertwined in luxuriant festoons upon its walls, and over its humble porch In this cottage (at the rent of 2s. 9d. per week clear, with the understanding that the tenant whitewashed all through, annually), at the half-open window, sat Julia Mc.Closkie, weeping as only a tender maiden, newly aware of her lover's death, can weep. "Julia, my love,' said her mother, "stay this passionate grief. You can- not recall him." Julia gulped down a choking sob, and remarked, "It isn't that, mother. I cannot now wear my new spring dress. I shall have to go in mourning." As she spoke a gentleman raised his hat and walked up to the window exclaiming, "Dearest! forgive this sudden introduction; I have long loved you from afar; be mine !" The speaker was none other than Thomas Cassidy. She rooked at him for one moment as though she would fathom his very soul, and then with a hysteric sob she sprang through the window into the loving arms open to receive her. At that moment, Mrs. Mc.Closkie (who had been taking gin several days for the back- ache), in a state of frenzy, took down the duck gun from the wall, and discharged both barrels through the open window with such deadly effect as to put Cassidy's light out for ever, and Julia, who had long suffered from heart disease, fell lifeless on her lover's corpse, and weltered in his gore. Mrs. Mc.Closkie. stung with remorse; then took a mouse powder, and retired into the cellar to watch its effects.
Cue.Prait 'VI.
Stop! for thy tread is on an empire's dust, An earthquake's spoil is sepulchred below. _

A few days after the events narrated, a niourning coach might have been seen slowly moving from Major Griffin's house; containing one solitary living occupant. The rest of the seats were occupied with coffins, ends upward. The sulitary occupant was the Major‘ (I for- got to say that old Peggy, and several oth..: villagers who had played very important parts not narrated, but of the first importance, had met with untimely deaths.) As the coach rounded the Major's plantation, the driver happened to look over the fence, and pulled up to call the Major's attention to a ghastly form laid in the grass. They dismounted to examine it. It was Jabez ; cold and stark. They loosed his leg from the trap and exchanged looks of deep pity. "Chuck him in with the rest," said the Major kindly, and this being done, the sorrowful procession moved on. But ere it had proceeded many yards, a flash of lightning struck the whole concern (for description of the sort of lightning required for this purpose see chapter I), killing the Major and the driver instantly, and scattering the contents of the coach all over the highway. . . . People who live in that village e'en now pass that dreaded spot after dusk with feelings of awe; and so they ought.
THE E.

The foregoing is the first novel I have written. and it has made me so Miserable that, in order to prevent any- body who reads it from committing suicide, I feel bound to acknowledge that it is nothing but a pack of lies from beginning to end. My conscience is now clear. Ae

div.head: WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB.

A special meeting of the members of this club was held on Wed3,esday evening, at the Farmers Stores. The chair was occupied by Mr. G. Percival, the president of the club, and there was a moderate attendance.

div.head: SALE OF FOREIGN MEAT.
div.p: THE SALE OF FOREIGN MEAT.

Mr. Jonx L. STELFOX (Lyrnm), read a short 1 paper regarding the sale of foreign killed meat, and I described the evil effects to the public and to far- mers of its present mode of sale. Recently, he said, I principally owing to the action taken by the club, ' the subject he was dealing with had created con- siderable attention, and had been mentioned several times in Parliament, but it had not yet been handled in a satisfactory manner. More than half of our butchers, he asserted, regularly sold foreign-killed meat, but only in a few cases was that fact known to the purchasing public. So great, indeed, was the ignorance of the public on this point that, under the impression that they were buying fresh meat, they were parting with six millions a year more money than they had occasion to part with, solely for the benefit of foreign farmers, and butchers who were unscrupulous. English farmers also materially suf- fered by such sale, by reason of a depreciation in repute of English fresh meat, by the foreign article being so extensively substituted for it It 'was said that the public were fools to be imposed upon in this Way, but he believed it to be as necessary to protect the public nurse against systematic robbery of this kind, as it had been found necessary to pro- tect it against thieves and fraudulent debtors. ' Another phase of the question was the sale of horse- , flesh, which was some w h at'extensively carried on, the purchasing public often being under the impression that it was beef. A butcher might let a person buy it under the impression that it was beef, without having made any distinct fraudulent representation. In his opinion it would 131 reasonable to call on the Legislature for a measure dealing with this question. He then pro- posed that the following resolution should be adopted, and forwarded to various members of Parliament, viz.: —"The members of the Warrington Farmers' Club desire to draw your attention to the discussions which have recently taken place in the Houses of Parliament on the sale of foreign-kilted meat. when Government finally de- clared their intention of not interfering until farmers had first tried prosecutions and found them to fail. We wish to point out to you our difficulty in prosecuting under the present Act for the prevention of fraud, be- cause of the manner in which the sale of meat is carried on. The public, being blind to the fact that foreign- killed meat is now sold at most butchers' establishments without any distinguishing feature, only ask, as they have been long acenstomed to do, for a certain quantity of beef or mutton; and inferior foreign-killed beef and mutton, bought at 20 to 4d per lb., is often supplied to them at prices which the public would only pay for home-killed fresh meat if the fact was made known to them. We do not ask, as a remedy for this, that every piece of foreign-killed meat should be branded, but only ' that the fact of such sale should The plainly indicated on the usual signboard—just in the same manner as was done when its sale first commenced in this country. In addition to this, we would suggest that the Government ask every district authority throughout the country to placard such notices calling the attention of the public Ito the extensive sale of foreign-killed meat in such a man- ner that the public are robbed of £6,000,000 annually, and our farmers are injured to an even greater extent. We also desire to draw your attention to the fact that America does not send us the best beef at Bid to 4d per lb. The price of fresh beef is much higher in their own country, and the meat sent here' is very inferior and often diseased, as has been lately shown by an inquiry conducted by Congress."— Mr. Joirs MARSH (Grappenhall) seconded the resolution and remarked that horseflesh was only in consumption in the larger towns. in places like Manchester and Liverpool, he believed, it was dealt in on a large scale.— Mr.W. DARBYSHIRE (Grappenhall) supported the proposi- tion. Thousands of carcasses of beef and mutton, he said, came to this country and found purchasers. Bad and inferior meat that could not-be sold in America was sent to England to be disposed of.—Mr. JOHN DARBY-, SHIRE (Stretton) agreed with the proposition, but wished it to be known that the action of the club was in no way,directed against honest traders ;it was aimed entirely at the people who were practising imposition upon the farmers of England, and upon the public at large.—The resolution, which was also supported by Mr. T. DUTTON (Newton-by-Daresbury), was then adopted.

THE MILK SUPPLY. The question of fresh outlets for milk was introduced by the CHAIRMAN, Who, in a short paper, described the cost of working and starting a cheese and butter factors, that he had visited, which, he pointed out, yielded to farmers a much higher price for their milk than they ob- tained by sending it to Manchester or Liverpool. Con- sidering the times, the factory was paying a good per- centage for the money laid out on it.—Mr. Join; MARSH (Grappenhall) advocated the establishment of such factories. It would be a very good thing if the surplus milk in inland places could be converted into butter and cheese, but he scarcely thought that Warrington, situa- ted as it was, would be a suitable place in which to establish a factory.—Mr. DUTTON (Newton-by-Dares- bury) also advocated the factory system.—After a little further discussion, the subject dropped. This was all the business.

LORD SPENCER AT GunnFoul:l.—Earl Spencer, speak- ing at Guildford on Wednesday night, said Mr. Parnell's speech at the Eighty, Club was a memorable event. Mr. Parnell had done more than anybody else to increase the force of constitutional agitation by a blow at those who in past times had endeavoured to carry Irish reform by outrage and violence. He did not know who could take exception to Mr. ParnelPs programme of Tuesday night. The only course open was to subscribe to its sentiments, by the adoption of which, he trusted, the Irish party might always within the law obtain redress.

GLASGOW EXHIBITION.—The Prince of Wales, accom- panied by the ;Princess, on Tuesday, opened the inter- national Exhibition at Glasgow. Their Royal High- nesses were received with great enthusiasm by the populace, and, weather and other circumstances being favourable, the proceedings passed off successfully. The Royal party left for England in the evening. After the Royal party had passed Sauchiehall-et., on their way to the Exhibition, a rail, on which was seated a number of people. fell, and two persons had their limbs fractured. while several others sustained bruises. Another serious accident is reported in connection with the opening of the Exhibition.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT
HOUSE OF LORDS.—Moamm

The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after 4 p.m. Earl CLDOGAN gave notice that soon after the Whit- suntide recess he would move for the appointment of a Select Committee to consider the Standing Orders of the House. The Customs and Inland Revenue Bill was read a first time. The Merchant Shipping Life-saving Appliances Bill passed through Committee. The House adjourned at 70 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Moimar. _ _
--- The Speaker was in the chair shortly after 3 0 p.m., having recovered from his recent attack of lumbago.

There were 80 questions on the paper. Mr. GOSCHEN said that ploughs and, thrashing machines will not b 3 taxed under the Budget Bill, nor would horses or other vehicles used exclusively within the boundaries of docks for transferring timber from steamers to railway trucks. canal barges, or stackingyards within the docks. Trac- tion engines and machines which used the roads would be. taxed. Replying to Sir E. Birkbeck, Mr. GOSCHEN said he could not grant any further concessions to cultivators of tobacco in the United Kingdom this year than were allowed last year. In reply 3to Sir G. Baden-Powell, Mr. GOSCHEN said that at present the persons liable for payment of income tax were only those who received their income in this country. Whether that would be the ultimate settle- ment would depend on the ruling of the judges on a point of law submitted to them. Mr. W. H. SMITH, being asked what arrangements the Government were making in reference to the Whitsun- tide holidays, said he hoped the Local Government Electors' Bill would pass its third reading before the HouSe rose. It was hoped that the House might bt. enabled to adjourn on Friday, the 18th, and resume on Thursday. the Ist. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT ELECTORS BILL.
The House went into Committee on the Local Govern- ment Electors Bill. _ •

On Clause 2, which creates one register for all pur- poses in the county districts, Mr. Hositousr, for Mr. Rathbone, moved an addition; but Mr. Rrrentn said the only difference. between it and the bill, so far a, simplicity of register was concerned, was that it would substitute two lists for three. He held that the Govern- ment were right in adopting the municipal franchise. There was, in his opinion, a strong argument for making owners of property in the county, whether they were ratepayers or not, admissible as members of the &linty Council, and if a proposal to that effect were made in connection with the larger bill he would give it favour- able consideration. After some debate Mr. Hobhouse withdrew his amendment, taking Mr. Ritchie's Utter- ances as a pledge that the Government would introduce a second bill to enable those who had a substantial in- terest and stake in a county or district to be 'qualified to sit on a County Council. -- •

Mr. AMBROSE moved an addition to the 'same clause to the effect that a person really ought to be registered as a county elector in the parish in which his qualifying property was situated.—Mr. Rrrcuia WAS not prepared to accept the amendment. —Lord Onatmonwa urged hon. members to maintain the ownership vote, and an inferesting discussion followed.-,---Mr. SMITH asserted that the representation of property would be secured by the residential vote, and that it would be impossible to introduce the plural vote into the maniciptil franchise. —Mr. AMBROSE said his amendment as he now pro- posed it did not include the plural vote, and he must press it to a division.—The Committee afterwards divided, and the votes were—For the amendment, 52r: against, 259; majority against, 207. The announcement was received with 'laughter, and ironical cheers from the Opposition. Mr. STANLEY LEIGHTON moved an .amendment to the same clause that only persons who paid rates should be entitled to be registered as electors for the county autlio- ritim but it was negatived withont'a division. Mr. Hannouss moved an amendment giving Boards of' Guardians power to annually appoint a 'fit person to act as registration officer within the 'Union .for which an assistant overseer had not 'been appointed.—The Government accepted the amendment, as it was a per- missive one.

Several clauses were agreed lo without discussion, and a number of new clauses were added. There was a narrow escape from a count•out,lbut the'billwas passed through Committee. CBIMINAL EVIDENCE 'BILL.' • _

In Committee on tho Criminal Evidence 'Bill, Mr. CALDwELL moved to insert in Clause 1 the words "This Act shall apply to England orily:"—Mr. J. R. div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

Mr. John Aird, M.P., has bought Mr. Alma Tadema's "Feast of Helio,gabalus" for £6,000, Mr. Tadoma throw- ing a small picture in. During the voyage of the steamer Massilia, from Bom- bay to Plymouth, Mrs. Jacobs, a passenger, jumped from tim cabin and was drowned.

It is officially announced that the Duke of Cambridge willvisit Crewe on the 9th of June to open a public park and review a newly-formed battalion of Volunteers. Efforts are being made in Dublin society to bring about a visit of the Queen to Ireland this year. It is pointed out that her Majesty has now reigned some 18,700 days, and out of that extended period the total time she has resided in Ireland has been only 18 days. At an adjourned meeting of the Hull and Barnsley Railway Co., at Hull, on Monday, Col. Smith announced the result of the recent voting on his motion to proceed with a bill incorporating the working agreement with the Midland Company. The motion was declared lost by 3,991 votes. The other night a fire broke out on a farm at Milsted, near Sittingbouree, resulting in the destruction of two stacks and farm materials. Since then, however, human remains have been found among the ruins, though who the unfortunate victim may have been it is impossible to ascertain, the fragments being charred almost to cinders.

--- On Monday, an inquest was held by Mr. T. Taylor, coroner, at the Railway Hotel, Huddersfield, on the body of Robert Farringdon, mill-hand, aged 18, who le ommitted suicide on Saturday by throwing himself in front of the 453 train from Clayton West 'when it wasiapproaehing Shepley station. A verdict was returned in accordance with the facts. ' An inquest was held at Holborn Town Hall. on Monday, on the body of Louisa Mary Blake, wife of Charles Carter Blake, D.Sce, New North-street, Theobald's-road, who died while under the influence of chloroform. Dr. Gould said the deceased was the greatest chloroform taker in the world, and took as much as a pint a day. A verdict of "Death from misadventure" was returned. A CHILD flux= nv A Fraurr.--Edwin Wild, aged five months, died at Sheffield Hospital, on Monday, from injuries inflicted by a tame ferret. The animal was kept for worrying rats. The child was left in its cradle, and in the absence of its mother the ferret got in and bit its forehead over the left eye., The child's7cries attracted the mother, who, however, was too late in rescuing her infant. A young servant named James visited her home at Hereford. When alone she had a fit, and tumbled into the kitchen fire. On recovering her senses she was in flames, and in excrutiating agony. She dashed to the front door. Xt was locked. The flames from her dress set the kitchen things on fire. At last the poor girl went screaming into the yard, and a neighbour there found her "dying with all liet clothes burnt to cinders. The salt boring operations which have been proceeding for sometime at Seaton Carew have led to the discovery of a suiphur spring which may have an important influence on the future of this popular watering place. Salt brine was found months ago, and the operations , which have led to the present discovery were pursued in the hope of tracing coal. The boring will be continued. The depth already reached is about 1,300 feet.

A WOMAN linarr TO Devrir..—A shocking occurrence took place, on Saturday night, at Marlin-street, Bristol. A woman, named Hunt, was preparing some clothing for her children to wear on Sunday, when she unfortunately overturned the petroleum lamp on the table, and it fell on the floor between her infant child, which was lying in cradle, and herself. The woman, fearing the flames would reach the child, removed it from the cradle, but in doing so caught her own clothes on fire. She rushed outside and placed the child in safety, but becoming overcome by flames, she fell down, and was burnt to death before assistance arrived. THE WORKINGTON DISASTER: A PONY FOUND ALIVE.— A party from the Whitehaven Colliery have been engaged in clearing the workings of the Workington. Colliery, of gas, and putting in stoppings and doors which were blown out by the explosion with the object of restoring ventilatidn. In the last district examined, the missing pony Tip, which had been in the pit since the 19th ot April without food or water, was found alive, although a skeleton, and was brought out to the stables and fed. /go trace was found of any of the men's bodies.' The water will be partially drawn off from the pit, but it will be months before it will be safe to take it all out. If the bodies are not found in the dip. they will have to remain. .To draw all the water off at. once now, and allow a full current of air to go through the pit, might result in a more serious explosion than the lamentable Otte on the 19th of April.. A Vic. n SUMMONED Fon POOR RATES. - At Bearsted Petty Sessions, on Monday, the Rev. F. Allen, vicar of East Farleigh, was summoned for the nal- payment of £4O poor rates. The defendant asked the magistrate to postpone the case until that of the Rev. Mr. Lamplaugn, vicar of Yolding, was settled. He had an award of Commissioners under Extraordinary Tithe Redemption Bill, and he believed it would cover this case. lie had LES owing him for tithe, and he was absolutely unable to pay this rate at the present time unless he distmined for his tithe, which he did not feel disposed to do in the present state of things. Therefore, unless the case was adjourned the collector would have to re- cover by distraint on his goods. The collector said it, would be unfair to other ratepayers to consent to :in adjournment, and the Court ordered a distraint to be issued, as they had no option but to administer the law. AFFAIRS IN THE ISLAND OF LEWIS.—Lady Matheson, Proprietress of the Island of Lewis, having resolved to eive up her residence in the island, owing to the crofter and eottar agitation and disturbances, left Stornoway on Monday. A considerable 'Crowd collected-to witness , her ladyst tip's departure, but there was DO demonstration, mud not even a cheer was raised as the steamer left the harbour. Lewis Castle. which is the only m build- g of any architectural pretension in theisland, -a advertised to be let. Most of the servants, many

of whom have been in Lady Matheson's employ for twenty years, have been dismissed. Since the crofters' agitation commenced little or no re", has been paid to Lady Matheson. The poor law and board aulehinery is hi a disorganised state owing t the non- imyrnent of rates. About £4.000 of rates are at present et arrear. The pecple in the Lochs district are hopeful of making some 'money out of the new industry of col- lecting grouse eggs. 'Many cottars and crofters have ' taken to the moors and are said to be very successful in obtaining the eggs. A 'LIVERPOOL SHIP BURNT AT SEA.—The Spirit,, of the Dawn, of Liverpool, has arrived in the Tyne • from 'Plaque, South America, and reports sighting the • iron ship .Galgate, of Liverpool. totally dismtisted. Capt. Judd put off in a boat with provisions, and boarded the Galgate. On examination it was found she had been on tire, and the woodwork was destroyed. She had ap- parently been laden with jute, but the cargo was burnt to ashes. There beim,. no 'signs of the crew, Capt. Judd . returned, the Galgate being lost sight of. Subsequently the Spirit of the Dawn sighted the iron sailing ship Iron Queen, of Newport, with her foremast gone. Signals of distress were hoisted, and a boat from the Spirit of the Dawn boarded her. The captain stated that he was from 'Bull River, and had experienced fearful weather., During .the gale the foremast was carried away, .and three •teen working on the jibboorn narrowly escaped neing killed. The crew were exhausted and short of provisions, which were supplied. The Iron Queen had experienced gales for 51 days. THE 'ROYAL ACADEMY BANQUET—The annual ban- quet ,of the -Royal Academy was held at Burling- ton Rouse ,on Saturday evening, Sir Frederick 'Leigh- ton presiding. The Prince of Wales, Prince Albert Victor,•and the 'Duke of Cambridge were among -the dis- tinguished guests.—The Prince of Wales, responding for the Queen, thanked the president for his kind reference to the Emperor and Empress of Germany, and wished it, were possible to give greater hopes Of the life of one so near and dear to him. Recent news had been rather more favourable.—The Marquis of Salisbury, respond- ing for the Ministers, said that last year he invoked their powerfnl .sympathy •for hisS colleagues in the House of ! 4 'ominous exposed to party influeemes fatal to any but the mostathletic constitution. He was able now to render a more encouraging tale. By cultivating regular boars all , dangerous symptoms had been removed. Order had Succeeded chaos, and peace had succeeded confusion. Hererring to public affairs, he observed that Europe was standing hushed by the bedside of its most powerful and mast admired potentate. They earnestly followed the .!orerse•of sufferingaof the Emperor with hope such as the Prince of Wales had expressed, and with a deep sense .of the tragic import of the . present crisis,—Pro- fesewl"ridall, Mr. tecky, the Lord Mayor, and the Lord 4:}tancOlar afterwards spoke. ttoYAL ACADEMY OF ATVS IC. —Oa Saturday after- . . . .

;oon.,the new principal,of the ItO7Val Academy olMusic, it. A. C. Mackenzie, delivered his inaugural address to he students in the hall of t‘lio institution, Tenterden- street. flanaver-square. Ile paid a warm tribute to the late principal. Professor-Sir George Maciarren, much of whose life work was done within the walls of the Aca- demy, with which he was connected for the long period of 59 years. If it ,could be said of any man that he had fulfilled the destiny for which nature had intended him, that truly might he said of the late Sir Geo. Macfarren. very feeling reference was also made to the late Mr. Walter Bache. Coining, then, to the future; the'princi- pal said that. when he found among the students those who were sufficiently advanced to be entrusted with the baton, and to whom a knowledge of conducting was - likely to be of service later, ho would let them try their "'prentice" hand as often as possible. Some might be placed as organists, and he proposed systematically and regularly to turn the attention of the choir to the works of the English Church writers; while through the already organised operatic class same helpigi t perhaps be given to the neglected cause of. English opera. The library would be extended, end with the help of those associated with him in the privilege of sharing the work of the Academy, it was hoped that the students might be pointed to as. a body of hiriflg examples o f earnest. labour. By unceasing application to general studies and the development of particular gifts, some of them might be- come exceptional specimens of that musical talent, the possession of which some nationswere disposed to deny to this country at the present day. In conclusion, Dr. Mackenzie inculcated habits of punctuality, order, and diligence, and spoke of the i in porta nee of doing well,whatp ever was taken in. hand. The address was received with frequent applai3se,

TERRIBLE CATASTROPHE: A GERMAN EXPEDITION LOST. Information which has been received by main from Sydney, and dated March 31st, points to the belief that the members of a German expedition to the Island of New Britain have perished through a volcanic eruption and a great tidal wave visiting the island. From the intelligence which is to hand it appears that on the 6th March the Germamsteamer Otillie, with his Excellency Governor Baron von Schlenitz, Mr. von Below, coffee planter, Mr. Heinstein, naturalist, 16 Kanekas, and four Malays, arrived at Lioko, and left all the party there excepting the governor. On the 15th the steamer re- turned, and nobody coming off, the captain went or. shore to see how the expedition had got on. To his sur- prise he found the place in ruins, all the trees having be uprooted and floating about in the harbour. He could see nothing of the expedition, but while he was looking about five of the Kanakas came up. They said they bad been up trees, and had had nothing to eat for three days. They could give no information as to what had become of the remainder of the expedition, number- ing 17. The captain, however, learned that the place had been visited by a volcanic eruption and also a tidal wave. which, by the marks on th,e shore, had risen about 40 feet. The remainder of the expedition were supposed to have perished. All the building material and stores had disappeared. The Otillie left on the next day and re- ported the terrible disaster to the Governor at Finschaven. An expedition was organised at once, and proceeded its the Otillie to Lioko. There the OtMe left them searching for the missing people. Up to the time the steamer left they had only found a suit of clothes belonging to Mr. von Below, and a pair of boots and a single boot belong- ing to Mr. leinstein. It was the belief that all of the 17 persons had perished.
EXECUTION IN IRELA.ND.-A DYING

PROTEST. At eight a.m. on Monday, James Kirby, known by the nickname of "Fox," was hanged at Tralee Gaol. for the murder of Patrick Quirke, at Liscahane, near Ardferk, Kerry, on the morning of the Bth of November last. Patrick Cournane, a youth, who was also con- demned to death for complicity in the same crime, had had his sentence commuted to penal servitude for life. A memorial was sent to the Lord Lieu- tenant on Kirby's behalf, and on Saturday a reply was received stating that after careful consider- ation his Excellency had decided that the law must take its course. Kirby was about 35 years of age, married, and had two ehildren. and was a fairly comfortable tenant farmer. His victim, Quirke, was nearly 80 years old. Quirke's daughter was married to Kirby's first cousin who occupied part of the adjoining farm. The latter was evicted for non-payment of rent, and went to America. The farm was vacant for a long time until last April, when Quirke redeemed the place for his grandchildren, who entered into pos- session. Quirke , was immedititely boycotted on the date mentioned. He was called out of bed by a party of armed men who fired the contents of a double- liarrelled breechloader into his thighs, and he died before either priest or doctor arrived. Cournane, Kirby's servant, was arrested the same day, and when in gaol he asked Why ' Fox Kirby had not been arrested. This was afterwards done, and Garrett Kirby, Quirkc's grandson, aged nine years, identified him as the man who, fired the shot. F'urther identification was obtained, and Kirby was sentenced to death at Wicklow Assizes. The culprit was calm on -Monday, and, while being pinioned by Berry, said, "I am going before my sod, and as sure as there is a God in heaven, I never handled a firearm or shot you, Patrick- Quirke." He then ascended the scaffold steps deliberately, and made no further statement. He received a drop of 6ft., and death was instantaneous. Cournane, who was taken to Dublin after his reprieve, stated, when leaving Tralee in the train, that he was content to serve penal servitude for the part he had taken, and further, said KirbY was not innocent. The condemned man slept well on Sunday night, and rose at five o'clock. He was engaged in prayer until seven when the Rev. Father O'Callagan, the assistant chaplain, celebrated mass in the prison chapel, 'rho condemned man recanted the Holy Communion, and took no breakfast or stimulant.

An inquest was held at twelve o'clock.—The Governor gave formal evidence of the execution.—in reply to a Surer, the Governor stated that Kirby, when about being pinioned, declared that he was innocent of the murder. Ile left no written statement after him.—The Sub-Sheriff gave formal evidence.--The Prison Surgeon deposed thal leath was caused by the dislocating of the upper portion of the spine.—The usual verdict was returned.

TEMPERANCE REFORM IN IRELAND. In moving the second reading ,ef the Public-houses klreland) Saturday Closing Bill, Mr. T. W. RUSSELL said the opinion prevailed that such a change would be a blessing to the country. The only opposition to it. he contended, was from a certain section of the liquor trade, and theclergy and the policewereentirely in favour of the bill. He explained that by its principal provision public-houses in towns of over 10,000 inhabitants would be closed at nine o'clock on Saturday night.—M. Rem O'Coexon moved the rejection of the bill, maintaining that the settlement of the question should wait until Ireland had a parliament of its own. Such a restriction as that proposed would lead to illicit drinking and the establishment of bogus clubs.—Mr. PETER IPDONALD protested against the bill as a piece of class legislation; but Colonel WATLING thought it a most beneficial mea- sure.—Mr FLYNN. though an advocate of temperance, opposed the bill, regarding the speech of Mr Russell as a declaration that the Irish were dirty boys. and that the bill was an attempt to wash them by force.—The LORD ADVOCATE, having experience of similar legislation in Scotland, remarked that Sunday closing in that country had had a salutary effect, reducing the evils of intern-, perance.—Mr. Maurice 'Healy supported the bind so did Mr. Mahony, though he thought it did not go far enough—The debate '•• was continue by Mr. E. Harrington, Mr. Tomkinson, Mr. Fen- wick, and Mr. M. Harris. Mr. Parnell also took cart in it, feeling that the interests of temperance were not likely to be promoted by the measured What he sug- gested was that they •lihmild watt until they were in 'a position to pass the Irish Local Government Bill, and then assign to the bodies constituted under that bill the same powers with reference to the questiOn that it was proposed to give to the County and District Councils in the case of England. The passing of the present bill would grievously hamper social reformers in Ireland, and he declined to support the second reading .—ln order to bring the matter to a. decision, Mr. RUSSELL ninved that the question be ,put.—The resolution was carried, and the House divided, when there were—for the bill, 178: against, 102; majority for, 76.—1 t was then read a second time, and referred to the Select Cominitteeon the Sunday Closing (Ireland) Act.—The House adjourned at 25 minutes to six o'clock. TILE LOCAL GOVERNMENT AND THE POLICE..--111 reply to Mr. Trotter, Mr. RITCHIE stated that under the Local Government Billthe town councils of boroughs, of be- tween 10,000 and 30,000 inhabitants, would continue to exercise exclusive control over their police. PUBLIC-HOUSE RETUR/SS.—Mr. HANDEL COSSHAIL asked whether the Government could obtain and give the House a return of the number of public-houses owned by brewers in half a dozen typical towns in England and Wales ?—The Home' SECRETARY said he was making in- quiries as to the possibility of presenting such a return, but he could give no pledge upon the subject. TRADE MAens.—Sir MICHEAL HICKS-BEACH told Mr. F. Hardca.stle that a'bill on the subject of trade marks and designs was in course of preparation, but the possibility of introducing it this session must depend on the progress of business. NEW BILL.—AibiR to prevent the disclosure of Govern- ment secrets either by spies or by officials betraying their trust WAS introduced by the ATTORNEY GENERAL and read a first time.--The Electors Bill as amended was con- sidered, reported to the House, and read a third time. RAILWAY asei CANAL TRAFFIC BILL. Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACIE moved the second reading of the Railway and Canal Traffic Bill, which had come down from the House of Lords. He explained that it was identical in principle and similar in detail to that introduced by Mr. Mundella in 1886, and its object was to secure publicity and fairness in the tonduct of our railway and canal traffic, to let the public know what they were charged and why they were charged, and to give them better means of getting unfair charges remedied. It was pro- posed to render ,permanent the Railway Commission Court and enlarge its powers, to provide for a revision of charges and the amendment of the law relating to undue preference, and to bring canals under proper con- trol, prohibiting their acquisition by railway companies. —Mr. MUNDELLA, criticising the bill, said the clause deal- ing with theclassification of rates had suffered consider- ably in its passage • through another place. The old maximum clause was replaced by a new minimum clause which would-work adversely in the interests of trade. The Post-office, he said, amid amusement, had discovered that they could carry parcels cheaper than the railways, and were ripening an old stage-coach down to Brighton at a saving of £1,500 a year, and would probably run one from Manchester to Liverpool, or between Leedsand Manchester.—Sir E. BIRKBECK trusted the House would be firm about 'the question of preferential rates.—The debate was continued by Sir B. SAMUELSON and other members.—The bill was read a second time, and re- ferred to the Standing Committee on Trade and Agricul- ture. The second reading of the National Defence Bill was agreed to, and after other business the House adjourned at a quarter-past twelve o'clock.

- TIIE LATE MR. DAVID DAVIDSON. The late Mr. David Davidson, of Laurel Bank, Newton-le-Willows, who died on the 22nd February last, appointed by his will as executors Mr. Joseph Langskaw Wood, Mr. Charles Culshaw, his brother- in-law, Mr. William Goldsworth, and his nephew, Mr. Wikiam GoLdsworth, junr. He bequeathed to i his sister, Miss Christina Davidson, £1,000; to his. brother, Mr. John Davidson, £i000; to his sister, Mrs Marion Goldsiworth, £7150; to his niece, Miss Annie Groldsworth, 2500; to his nephews, Mr. Mari and Mr. William Gnrdner,Xl,ooo each ; to his house- keeper, Ann Appleton, £5OO, and to her daughter, Mary Appleton, £5OO. All the remainder of his pro- perty (including his shares in McCorquodale and Co., Limited, in the North Wales Paper Company, kl'arr's Banking Company, and the Maryport and Car- lisle Railway Company), the personalty being valued at .£9,460,- the testator leaves in equal shares to his nephews, Adam and William Gardner.
