div.head: CURRENT, POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT, POLITICS.
Mr. Yarburgh, M.P. for Chester, has resigned the post private secretary to Mr. W. H. Smith, si hich he has hal for some months. . .

--- Mr. Akers-Douglas, chief Government Whip, had an interview, on Monday, with Lord ,Salisbury, Mr. Smith, and Mr. Ritchie, regarding the Government busi- ness in the House of Commons. THE BUDGET TAXES. Sir John Gorst writing to a constituent, says :—The proposed addition of 20 per cent io the publicans' licenses will only be imposed when a license is taken away in a district Sir Frederick 'Milner, Bart., was presenton Monday evening at a Primrose League gathering' at Ringley. He delivered an address, in which he referred to the Budget proposals, and contended that it was unfair to speak of the Budgets a rich man's Budget. At a meeting of Liverpool teamowners, on Monday, in the Common Hall, flackiLs-hey, a resolution was passed objecting on principle to the proposed tax on trade vehicles, as placing heavy and invidious bur- dens on certain classes, from which the agricultural and other large classes of cart and van owners were to be entirely exempted. Under the auspices of the "Van and Wheel Tax League," a great demonstration and parade of vans, waggons, carts, and other vehicles took place in London on Saturday, with the object of protesting against the imposition of the proposed new van and wheel tax. Soon after two o'clock a number of vehicles began to arrive at the eastern end of the Victoria Embanirment at Blackfriars Bridge. and the number was rapidly augmented by carts and vans from various districts of the metropolis, and as they took up their position in line along the Embankment presented a strange mixture of two and four-wheeled carts, vans, and waggons which would, be sub- ject to the new tax. A number of them were de- corated with banners and flags of different nationalities kmong the inscriptions were the following: —" Why :sting the wheels of British industry ? " "No one-sided exemptions," "Our home industries shall not be taxed," "The people are greater than Parliament," "Taxation on industry is starvation and death." Contingents kept arriving until nearly four o'clock. Some time elapsed before a movement was made, and some of the vehicles ci arted towards Hyde Park, where, by permission of her Majesty's Office of Works, platforms were erected near. the ' Reformer's Tree." The route of procession, which was attended by several bands, was by the way of St. Bride-street, along Holborn-bars, New Oxford-street, to the Marble Arch into the park. The speakers addressed themselves to a resolution protesting against the tax as being likely not only to injure British industry, but to add to the number of unemployed workmen. THE NATIONAL DEFENCE BILL'

Mr. Stanhope's National Defences Bill was issued, on Saturday. A memorandum attached states that the ()b- -in& of the bill is to facilitate, in case of emergency, first the coffin. out of the yeomanry and volunteers; second, the royal' naval artillery; third, the use of rail- ways for naval and military purposes; and, fourth, the provision of horses and carriages. As regards the first, the object of the bill is to authorise the .I.,,eotnanry and volunteers to be called out for actual military service, whenever 'the military is embodied; out it is not proposed to impose any additional liability on men without their consent. As re- gards the second, it authorises the Royal Naval Artillery Volunteers to be called out for actual service whenever the naval reserve is called out with the 03n5ent of the existing men. As respects the railways and horses, the object is to enable the Queen, whenever the militia is ordered to be embodied, to order that the naval volunteers or militia shall have prece- dence without the Secretary of State being obliged to have recourse to the extreme step of taking possession of the railway, and to provide for the purchase of horses. ATTEMPTED MEETING IN TRAFALGAR-SQUARE. On Saturday afternoon Mr. Ouninghame Graham, M.P., Mr. Conybeare, M.P., Mr. William Saunders, and others, went to Trafalgar-square. with the apparent intention of holding a meeting there. A strong body of police was, however, soon in attendance, and kept the crowd which had assembled in circulation. Some resistance VMS offered to the action by Mr. E. D. Lewis, a solicitor, but whether for the purpose of testing the right of the police to move persons on or not could not be ascertained. Attempts were made by a Socialist named Walker and others to address the people, but they were speedily in- terrupted by'the police. After remaining in the Square for about a quarter of an hour, Mr. Ouninghame Graham drove away in a cab, and his example was followed a little later by others. A number of persons continued, however, to loiter about the Square, and later on the police found it necessary to arrest two young men for disorderly conduct. It is stated to be the intention of Mr. Graham and his friends to visit the Square next Saturday afternoon, and upon subsequent Saturdays.

A man, horse, and cart, were run into' by an express I rain, near Middlesbrough, on Tuesday, and smashed to pieces. THE DEATH Or MR. WALTER SHIRLEY. -- In an interview, on Saturday, with an official of St. Thomas's Hospital, London, as to the allegation that the late Mr. Shirley was refused admission to that hospital a few days before he died, it. was stated that on Mr. Shirley's arrival at the hospital, there were unmistakable signs of mental derangement; and Dr. Hawkins (resident physician) eonsetriently considered that the case was not one for admission. This opinion was confirmed by Dr. Edmunds, who appears to have considered that Mr. Shirley's condition to be such that had he been taken. into St. Thomas's Home the other patients would pro- bably not have remained. Had even Mr. Shirley's case been, in Dr. Hawkins' opinion, a proper one for admis- sion, there was no bed vacant in which to place him.
LIBERAL MEETING 4T HOLLINFARE.

On Monday evening a meeting was held in the Na- tional Schools, Hollinfare, to consider the Land Question and Mr. aladstone's Irish Palley. Notwithstanding the outdoor attractions of a beautiful evening, a goodly number of petsons assembled, amongst whom were— Messrs. W. Crossley, J. Arstall, J. Hayes, Robert Parr, A. Brooks, and P. Foxroft. The chair was taken at 7-30 by Mr. James Davies, and on the platform were Messrs. F. A. Roberts and Vivian Evans, of Warrington; Mr. G. W. Rawlins, of Rainhill ; and the Secretary of the Newton Division Liberal Association. Mr. Rawlins moved the first resolution, "That this meeting protests against the cruel Irish policy of the Government, which as an institution is unjust, and dangerous to the true unity of the empire ; and records its unabated confidence in Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues." (Applause.) Mr. H. Vivian Evans seconded the resolution. Mr. F. A. Roberts, who was cordially received, rose to support the resolution. In regard to the land question, he referred to the fact that in travelling from Warrington that day he passed through a tract of country which was to a great extent reclaimed land, and it struck him that some of that land was getting into a nice state of cultivation, and that a number of the leases would be running out, and the land be very valuable to the landowners. He was wondering whether the latter would consider the tenants, who had had so much trouble with the land, or whether they would want the full improved value of it. (A Voice: "Ys, and more too.") It struck him the owners would want their land, and a good rent for it as well. He thought that a crying shame. Speaking , of the Irish question, he said many of them had been Home Rulers for a number of years. During the Par- liament of 1880-85 they rejoiced in Warrington in hav- ing a Liberal member, and, owing, to the special circum- stances of Ireland, caused by the assassination of Lord , Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke; he had supported Mr. Forst,er's Coercion Bill. When the time came for this measure to run out, it was thought that the Liberal Goyernment intended to re-enact it, wholly, or partly, and their member wrote to him (Mr. Roberts) to say that he could not be a party any more to such an enact- ment, and desired the Liberal party of Warrington to be called together, so that he could explain his views upon that subject. What was the result; They unani- mously endorsed Mr. McMinnies's opinion. So he (the speaker) distinctly said the Liberal party in Warrington declined to go any further with coercion. (Applause.) The Chairman then put the resolution to the meeting, and it was carried unanimously.

div.head: DAY SCHOOL TEACHERS ON THE WALKING DAY QUESTION.
div.p: DAY SCHOOL TEACHERS ON THE WALKING DAY QUESTION.

A meeting of the Warrington and District Teachers' Association was held in the Trinity School- room, Museum-st., on Monday evening, for the pur- pose of considering the question of the postpone- ment of " Walking Day" to the 3rd Friday in June, or such other date as may be deemed more conve- nient. The president of the association, Mr. Corney, occupied the chair.—Mr. DzwiniusT said there were many reasons why Walking Day should be held on the third Friday in June. as in former years. That seemed to be the proper time for the breaking up of the schools for the half-year, and it would be a great drawback if they had a week's holiday at Whitsun- tide. Another reason why such an alteration would be better was that the weather, as a rule, was much more settled in June than it was, in May. He be- lieved that the manufacturers in the town wished to change the Walking Day cuiginally, but now they had found the present date inconvenient, and would willingly go back to the old state of things. Since he had been in Warrington he had taken part in all the Walking Day processions except one, and he could assure the meeting that the proceedings had never been interfered with by bad weather except on one occasion. He thought that this showed the weather wali more settled in June. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN remarked that the feeling of the meeting seemed to be that the holidays happened at an unfortu- nate time. The best way to settle the matter would be by a resolution.—Mr. FINNEY said that he had spoken to the Mayor about the matter, and he had intimated that if a requisition was signed by a number of influen- tial people, and presented to him in the usual way, he would call a public meeting. He (Mr. Finney) thought it would be better to ask the Mayor to convene a public meeting to consider the matter. He himself was quite convinced that the third Fridayin June was the best time for the holidays for many reasons. The Manchester Walking Day took place on the Friday in Whit-week, and he was told that there were many of the children who were ill owing to having caught cold. Mr. Dew- hurst had brought up the question of the weather. Whit-week was too early for Walking Day. He was sorry that this meeting had not been called earlier. He proposed that a requisition be signed and for- warded, to the Mayor asking him to convene a, pub- lic meeting to consider the question. The sooner the meeting was held the better. (Hear, hear.)— Mr. C. Twos seconded the motion.—Mr. BRIMELOW moved as an amendment that no action be taken in the matter at all. He knew one Sunday school which had arranged for a trip to'Frodsham on Whit-Friday. When the meeting, during the Mayoralty of Alderman Harri- son, was called to settle the date of Walking Day he was I surprised that more day school teachers did.not attend. All teachers were invited to attend. If a quarter of those now present had put in an appearance the motion for the third Friday in June would have been carried.— The amendment was not seconded, and it fell to the ground.—Miss SHAW said that when she had been col- lecting subscriptions for Walking Day many people had objected to its being held in Whit week.on account of the coolness of the weather.—Mr. Finney's resolution was then put to the meeting, and was carried unanimously. —The meeting then concluded.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE AT THE MEMORIAL HALL.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE AT THE MEMORIAL HALL.

Mr. Gladstone was on Wednesday morning pre- sented at the Memorial Hall, London, with an ad- dress sighed by thousands of Nonconformist minis- ters who support his policy with regard to Ireland. Dr. Clifford, President of the Baptist Union, took the chair, and the'hall was crowded to excess. The address was presented by the Rev. Gainess Rogers, and Mr. Gladstone delivered a lengthy and anima- ted reply. He pointed out that it was an inflexible rule in current pdlitics that whether the House of Commons was discussing Irish affairs or not, Ire- land was the key to the whole scheme of legislation. Englishmen were• subjected to in- justice in regard to the death duties, and they saw their commercial relations with their nearest neigh- bour imperilled by the new wine duty, because there was a determination on the part of the com- posite majority in the House of Commons to do nothing that would admit of the possibility of a Government doming in that wouldi grant Home Rule to Ireland. Moreover, they saw the same , majority supporting, and for the same reason, a 1 Local Government Bill which was in some important respects objectionable. The right hon. gentleman indicated that he should oppose the licensing clauses, and he specially condemned the attempt to create by statute the hitherto undreamt of right on the part of. a publican to a vested in- terest in his license. Turning then to the Irish question, hischarged the majority in the House of Commois with having violated the pledges on which they had been returned by the English constituen- cies. He reviewed the history of Mr. Balfour's ad- ministration in Ireland, and took credit to the op- position for having prevented by their denuncia- tions any repetition bf the scenes at Ennis or Mitchelstown, or the scandal of " doubling " sentences on appeal. He accused the Government of being the real authors of the Plan of Campaign because of their refusal to accept measures which .they afterwards passed when "out of time." What, he asked, did they want in Ireland ? They wan- ted not only law but legality; not a forced obedience maintained at an enormous cost of trea- sure and infinite ill-feeling. They wanted willing obedience to the law—that spirit of obedience to the law which they called legality, that spirit of obedience to the law which never could be generated by coercion, that spirit of obedience which was the child of freedom, the mainstay of order. Coercion had been superseded in Englfind, greatly owing to the efforts of the Nonconformists, by a respect for law, and by freedom. Coercion had been substi- tuted by liberal and generous government, and the reward had been the establishment of order upon foundations as firm and strong as ever were laid in any age or in any country. In Ireland the opposite course had been pursued; but be was sanguine that when they had brought home to the upright, honest Englishman the full knowledge of the great wrong, justice would be done to Ireland, and that Op future, it it could not cancel would at least confess and in some degree redress the sad and terrible errors of the past. The right hon. gentleman, to whom a vote of thanks was passed, left the hall amid prolonged cheering.

MURDERS IN IRELAND.—What is supposed to be an agrarian murder of a shocking character is reported from the neighbourhood of Maghera, in county Derry. A man named Francis Bradley and his uncle, Patrick Bradley, 70 years of age, had a dispute about the owner- ship of a field. The.younger man was shot dead in the 'field on Wednesday morning, and the uncle having been seen walking away from the spot with a gun under his arm, he was arrested. Another murder in connection with land troubles is reported by a Cork correspondent. A" bog ranger" named Quinn had, in disregard of warnings, let portions of a boycotted bog, and on Tues- day evening he was found dead, with three bullet wounds in his body.
PROPOSAL TO MAKE ST. HELENS A COUNTY.

At the last meeting of the St. Helens Town Council, it was decided to present a petition to Par- liament asking that under the pr posed new Local Governroent Bill, all towns havin,..4 a population of 50,000 and upwards should be made into separato • county districts. The petition was forwarded to Mr. Henry Seton-Karr, M.P., and that gentleman presented it to the House of Commons on Thursday week. The "Daily News" has since stated that the list of boroughs which it is proposed to add to Schedule 4 of the Local Government Bill, thereby creating them counties, is daily increasing, among the latest editions being" Swansea, Rochdale, Croy- don, St. Helens, Huddersfield, and Bath. The "Standard" understands that Sir Henry James will propose in Committee on the Local Government Bill that every borough with 50,000 inhabitants.shall be of itself a county.

THREE INQUESTS AT RUNCORN. Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner for the Honour and Fee of Halton, was engaged at Runcorn on Monday morning inquiring into the circumstances of the death of several persons who had come to a violent • or sudden end. A. TRADESMAN DROWNED. The first inquest wits on the body of William Blythe, aged 35 years, outfitter and hatter, of Bridge-st.—Fred Blythe, of 15, Bold-st., said the deceased was his brother. On Thursday night, about ten o'clock, he was going to Widnes with hitn with the intention of escorting home their wives. Opposite to the Parish Church at Runcorn they had to shelter from the rain, and the deceased promised to wait whilst he (witness) returned home for their overcoats and the ladies' mackintoshes. When he got back in about ten minutes the de- ceased was not there, and he called at the West . Bank Hotel and the Bridge Inn, -but the deceased was not there. He then went across the bridge alone. After bringing home the ladies he starched about the town until half-past two, %tut he could not hear any tidings of the deceased, and the ladies then went out, but were equally unsuccessful. The de- ceased was not sober when he (witness) left him.—John Owen watennan, of Massey's Court, Brunswick-street, deposed to finding the body of the deceased on the grid at the end of the gut near the Bonded Stores.--P.C. Gibson said there were no marks of violence on the body. In the pockets was a watch and 2s id in money. The watch had stopped exactly at half-past ten.—A verdict of "Found dead" was returned.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH,
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH,

An inquest was htld on the body. of John Whitfield, 68 years of age, a lock tenter, who had lived in English- row. It appeared that he went home at noon on Satur- day, and having had a hearty meal and a smoke, he went to bed. As he complained of being cold his wife made a fire in the room. When she Went to rouse him in order to get his tea at five o'clock she discovered that he was dead. He had suffered from chronic rheumatism for years, and had lately complained of a pain in his side.—The jury brought in a verdict of" Natural causes, probably heart disease." s DRIVEN TO SUICIDE BY A HUSBAND.

An inquiry was held into the , death of Mary Wilson, wife of Thomas Wilson, painter and decorator, 43. Heath- road.—Thomas Wilson said the deceased was his wife and was 33 years of age. On Sunday morning, about ten o'clock, he went out for a walk, and returned home about a quarter past one. He found her in a sitting posture between two chairs, quite dead, and above sus- pended to a hook in the ceiling was a roller towel. He knew no reason why she should commit suicide except that he had seen her at dinner times and frequently on other occasions kneeling down and praying, with a Bible before her. She would say to him "I have had a good time." They had been happy together for more than seven years, and he could bring preachers and witnesses to prove it. He had no quarrel with her on Sunday morning.—Alice Palmer, wife of Thomas Palmer, butcher, 45, Heath-road, said she had :known deceased eight years. For anything that she knew the deceased and her husband lived comfortably together. She was very religious, and went to Halton-road Chapel. She (witness) did not think her religion affected her mind. On Sunday morning the deceased appeared just as usual. —Jas. Bowyer, shipwright, of 41, Heath-road, said he had known the deceased and her husband for six years. He could not say that they had • lived comfortably to- gether. Her husband was addicted to having drinking bouts, and his conduct caused his wife great grief, and disagreements arose. He -was drinking last week, and on Friday the deceased fetched him home. He was not violent towards her; and she tried to screen him as much as she could. Inspector Millington deposed that he went to the house about two o'clock on Sunday. The woman's neck was dislo- cated, and was also discoloured. The towel was very much twisted, and there were evidences that she had hung herself with it. The end of the towel was four feet four inches from the ground.—The coroner said the de- ceased had been a very good, religious wife—her house, he was told, was a model of cleanliness—and she was a Woman of strong religious feeling. She had the misfor- tune to have a bad husband, and his frequent fits of in- temperance had a strong effect upon her. If the jury I thought they were sufficient to unhinge her mind and to render her at the time she committed this rash act insane, they would return a verdict accordingljL—The jury re- turned a verdict to the effect that the ddbeased commit- ted suicide whilst temporarily insane, and requested the coroner to censure the husband for his intemperate habits.—Wilson was thereupon summoned into the room and the coroner told him that the knowledge of the fact that his repeated acts of intemperance had driven Ids poor wife to do the rash act which had caused that in- quest,ought, if he had feeling left, to have greater weight than any words that a coroner or a judge, or any- body could address to him.—Wilson, who appeared to be under the influence of drink at the time, received the coroner's remarks with apparent indifference.

MR. Join DittoN, M.P., was ptesented, on Von' day, with the freedom of the city of Drogheda; and, in acknowledging the honour conferred upe'' him, he took occasion to refer to the Papal decree against boycotting and the Plan of Campaign' With characteristic frankness, Mr. DILLoN ad' mitted that he was one of the authors of the PIO of Campaign; and added that he had nelref, hesitated to justify and recommend the policy °: ' boycotting to the people of Ireland as an evil, 10' the lesser of two evils. This, as it seems to us is straightforward and sensible way of dealing Witi. the question; and disposes of a good deft! of Ole nonsense that is talked on the subject. Lau SALISBURY has himself admitted that the law CO not grapple effectually with boycotting. He knoWS that it has been the custom of Tory magnates fron/ generation to generation to boycott Liberal trades; men, and that the practice has by no means die° out. It is an evil thing to put pressure upon po°' ple in this way—just as it is an evil thing in Ire- land to apply "the screw"; but there is this to b° said for the Irish, that in their case it is tbe struggle of the Weak against the strong—the eoor bination of the oppressed many against the oppres" sion of the few. There are worse things than bol cotting ;itis a worse thing for a landlord to , rent tenants, and when, through misfortuneor boo seasons, the whole of the rent cannot be paid, 10 come forward, in the name of the law, and take from the tenants not only the value of the rent owing, but something in the shape of improve' ments which may be worth twenty times the rent' Itnbbery of this kind is not less robbery when it i 5 done under the sanction of the law; and it is rob' bery of this kind which, in the eyes of men 114'8 Mr. JOHN DILLoN and Mr. W. O'BRIEN, justifiee boycotting and the Plan of Campaign. "Nothing succeeds like success," and there is no denying that the Plan of Campaign has been successful. It little less than marvellous that a scheme of tine hind, irregular, illegal, and depending so entireli on the firmness and loyalty of comparatively put'r men, should have broken the backs of the rack; renters of Ireland. It is not sufficient to say thav the tenants were actuated solely by greed of gaj They felt, no doubt, that they had their homes an hearths to defend; but they felt, too, they wore fighting a national battle; and, further, that the were being led. by patriots whom they could iiO plicitly trust. It is to the enduring credit of tle3 authors of the Plan of Campaign that the mane- tions in rent which they proposed to make we° not, in the main, in excess of the reductions made by the Land Courts. They did quickly that whicb the law was doing slowly, and they rendered, 10 the end, a vast service by putting landlord an tenant on a right footing as to a possible rent' As to the evil of boycotting, that of course i 5 question of degree. We have in mind the case ° a teacher in a Church of England Day School, 141° ventured to object to teaching as a regular thiug on Sundays. She had to go, and the Vicar of the parish followed up hig Plan of Campaign so sharPlit that the young lady found it impossible to ge another place in a Church School; she was b°Y; cotted, and she had lio remedy at law. Her rail came in getting a better place at a better seh,°°o outside the pale of the Church. We think 14i

. Vicar Wu wrong; and boycotting is always wrong When carried to extreme. But desperate diseases require desperate remedies; and in view of all that the people of Ireland have suffered and are till suffering, we hesitate to say that they are not instified in using the Vfeapons of defence which are being condemned by the Catholic Church. The l'Aders of the Irish people are better judges of the situation in Ireland than any number of men can

Possibly be who reside in Italy, and have to rely on 4/econd-hand information. That, at any rate, is What Mr. DILLON thinks, and he is considered a true son of the Church. ,He knows who are pull- ing the strings, and the end for which they atm being pulled. It is the Tory way of seeking to gain a Tory advantage. Referring on Monday to 'the rescript, Mr. Dtmort said : It was impossible for politicians who were respon- lINe to the people for leading them into danger to °de lit their eyes to the politicial significance of this r,Qcilrnent. It was a humiliating thing for Irish l'atholics at this time of day, and after the long `ievotion of the Irish people to the Church of Rome he thought, would compare favourably tll the record of English Catholics—to see that iii he hour of struggle and difficulty the voice of the rtholics of England (a miserable crew) prevails at tome over the voice of their rwn Bishops, and to 'e told by the papers that they were to show ilia- Plieit obedience to the head of their Church. Their Obey had been examined into by men who were „sPonsible before the judgment seat of God for tiae true guidance of their people, and whoought to :aye the confidence of the Court of Rome more Lord Emly 'and Mr. Ross, of Bladensburg; and thf3Y had stated that in their policy there was no- immoral. n :-- • They owed a duty to their friends; they °Wed a duty to the ancient traditions of their .."entry—tp the fathers who left them that iuntry ; they owed a duty to their Protestant vrtl°W - countrymen who expected that they _ere about t share with them a free Ireland—that ould not be an Ireland conducting its affairs at e bidding of any Cardinal—and they owed a duty *° their English friends. He took his stand upon • thst principle, and he would stand or fall by that Principle. :'8 do not doubt that the Catholics in Ireland will Illare Mr. DILLON'S views. Whatever they may do ' to matters of faith and morals, pure and aim-
tle, they will not take their politics from Rome. tide of Nationalism in Ireland is advancing, 4141 it is not to be stayed at the bidding of any .%lute—whether English or Roman.
Ma. PARNELL was tie guest of the Eighty Club Tuesday evening; and in the presence of the aders of advanced Liberalism in this country he

stained the high reputation he has attained as leader of the Irish people. It is interesting to °te that Mr. PARNELI:S speeches are, if we may °e Pardoned the phrase, purely English in their characteristics. There is nothing about them of Ilihernian heat, Hibernian eloquence, or Hiber- humour. But what Mr. PARNELL lacks as an , orator, he makes up in force of character. He gives the impression of a man who knows exactly What he wants; who is firm in purpose, and who 11,,ever spoils a point by talking for talking's sake. ,4'lll CARNARVON showed good judgment when he wecalne Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, in 1885, in linterviewing Mr. PALL; and, despite his °rdship's loss of memory as to some things which .t,**(3k place at that interview, he still shows good ' Judgment in declining to contradict. the statements Which ,Mr. PARNELL has to make on the subject: As far as I am concerned," says the Irish "lie has never contradicted from first to \‘:4111,...„ any statement I have made. He has sought 'wge in evasions, in the raising of other issues, in assertions with reference_ to the intentions „liers, which have no bearing on the case." Mr. _,lter.r. has all along stated that the interview .o'weh he held with Lord CARNAAVON was at Lord k't.tavoN's request; and that his lordship when said he wished to speak about a consti- ,-"Qon for Ireland. Mr. PARNELL pointed out that • Mere local government scheme, such as that 141:glIT,.e8ted by Mr. CLIAXBERLAIN would settle the h,.."4414 question; it must be a Parliament, and not ▪ erelY be called a Parliament. thxben (says Mr. Parnell) we went on to talk about Powers of this Irish Parliament, and I said that 'l7 Order to create manufacturing industries in Ire- Zrid it was absolutely necessary that that Parlia •e - ,7 lit should have the power of protecting those in- . "aptries. Lord Caniarvon said he quite agreed with fist. and he has n.,t contradicted that. Finally, he ..lted me, if this concession were to he made, 4"..4!ther the National League would be dislodged, 1,73 I said that certainly it wbuld be dislodged; it .„e.uld dislodge itself, because its progress and the Oect for which it had been formed would hays '4711 completed. Now he tells us he doesn't contra- ,;,t any of these statements. " grant that Lord CARNARVON himself has been ftr.lful not to give a specific contradiction to these ,115ecific statements; but the Tory Press, since'l "ues' "rounded" on the Parnellites, have given similar 1 lltateraents the lie a thousand times. At first it :as point blank denied that any member of the °tY Cabinet had held an interview with Mr.PAR- Its!" ; and when Lord SALLsnonv's name came ,he mixed up with the subject there was some- like a chorus of delight as to a statement a, made, that not only had he had no interview ith the Irish leader, but he could not Y that he had ever seen him. This evasion .°1 the issue served but for a short time. r_rd CARNARVON was constrained to admit having 'l4l communications with Mr. PAB.NELL and the 1)114 int then raised by the Tories was that his lord- tilfP had acted on his own responsibility as an in- uidual member of the Cabinet. At this stage • gj't_. GLADSTONE intervened, and raised the question and again whether Lord CARNARVON had 17 the interview with Mr. PARNELL without the iawleclge of Lord SALISBURY as Prime Minister. )3:t a time Mr. GLADSTONE could get no answer; tist lime, the revealer, has disclosed the fact that o'r chief of the Tory party was perfectly cognisant eh. the negotiations that were going on with the isLef of the Irish party. Lord CARNARVON has at admitted that he wrote to Lord SALISBURY otea4 accurate a statement as possible of what had • iirred within twenty-four hours after the inter- ow" As to this statement, we agree with Mr. go ELL that it would, be satisfactory to the ptit'beral public if Lord SALISBURY were to make it par.:,io• It would settle a good many points—more plcularly how far Lord CARNARVON'S memory beailed him since he committed to paper, for the rineat ef Lord SALISBURY, the results of his inter- ell with the Nationalist leader. c1,°39 like Lord SALISBURY it is, with this precious of't nient in his possession, denying all knowledge Home Rule proposals, and practically assur- -4'lB deluded followers that Mr. PARNELL was 41 lit the last man in his thoughts ! It smacks of 4,\VaY in which he had prepared to go into the th:n Congress with the secret treaty in his pocket re_ he had executed with Russia as to the sur- 4tnver c'f Bessarabia. But reverting to Lord CAR- A., 151• I's memory, it would be interesting to certain . ja'l4e T with certainty where it has played him etspu,. he memories of men do play them tricks, • Q.p.:lally when they are growing old. Did not Sir It GREENALL solemnly assure a Warrington ee that he had never once voted in favour of '°ggilag n the army, although there were the prov-` Porte of Parliamentary proceedings to a tli4t he had voted for it several times?

And so it would seem to be with Lord CARNARVON ; he is an old man with a bad memory. Correspondence has been published this week which took place between his lordship and the late Mr. E. DwvEn GRAY, which shows that Mr. PARNELL is not the only Irish member of Par- liament who has had interviews with Lord CAR- NAEVON at Lord CARNARVON'S request. It shows, ' UK>, how little the memory of his lordship is to be depended on; for, when closely pressed, he is compelled to admit that a certain conversation as to the release of Irish prisoners took place at a totally different time and at a totally different place to the time and place named by the late Lord Lieutenant. We are not blaming Lord CARNARVON ; lint we wish it to be seen that he is not infallible. He is entitled to respect as a Lord Lieutenant who was amongst the first among the leaders of the Tory party to see that some form of Home Rule for Ireland was inevitable. It is to his credit, too, that he resigned office when: he found that the Government of which he was a member were disposed to fall foul of the Parnel- lites as soon as they thought they could hold office without them. Mr. PARNELL did well, on Tues- day, to unbosom himself as to these matters before the members of the Eighty Club. He cannot but feel that he and his friends have been belied in a cowardly and villainous fashion since the memorable day in 1885, when they made it pos- sible for the Tories to take office. Happily, there is little talk to-day about the 'Parnellites being the associates of assassins ; for the Tories,stupid as they are, have begun to see, in view of these awkward revelations, that in bedaubing the , Nationalists, they bedaub themselves. Home , Rule was in the air when Lord CARNAIt- voN requested an interview with Mr. PAR- NELL ; it is in the air to-day; and we are perhaps a little nearer its achievement from the fact that Lord SALISBURY is at last challenged to produce the written report which was given him as to what took place at the interview, in 1885, be- tween the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland and the leader of the Irish party.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

/smother use has been found for the dress-im- prover. This time it was utilised in a case of poaching, at Lincoln, for disposing of two hares. That dress must have been very much improved; but perhaps the hares were very young ones. Anyhow, it is no worse than improving the improver by means of a quart bottle full of beer.

Wales is not the only place wherethere is trouble about tithes. Owing to the refusal of the inhabi- tants of Lagos, a small town in Crete, to pay the tithes falling due from them, the place has been surrounded by a cordon of gendarmes. It is a suggestive sign of the times that the demands in support of a gospel of peace should so often lead to civil war.

An American, named Davidson, has just been refusedthe divorce, which he applied for, on the ground that his wife had not spoken to him for three years. Byron describes "wordless woman" as " silent thunder." There are husbands it need hardly be said, who would profer the silent to the sounding thunder. Mrs. Davidson, in their eyes, would be a jewel of a wife, say, very early in the morning, after "making a night of it.'!

The other night the house of a Liverpool Police Inspector was broken into and robbed; and on Wednesday morning it was found that the private offices of the Hull Police Inspector were broken open, the thieves getting away with £l7. It would seem as if the light-fingered gentry have been showing how they can play off their jokes upon police inspectors. Let us hope that it will be the turn of the inspectors before long.

The demonstration against the wheel tax, on Saturday, was a most imposing one. If Mr. Goschen does not mind what he is about, he may find the tax an Ixion's wheel to him, or, to put it another way, if the agitation continues to grow, it will be "as if a wheel had been in the midst of it wheel," His proposal deserves the worst fate, for, as one of the inscriptions had it on Saturday, it is "a tax on labour to relieve the rich."

The Rev. Wright Williams and Mrs. Williams carry with them to their new sphere of labour, at Rainford, the warmest wishes for their welfare of the people of Widnes. From the speeches made at the presentation gathering, on Tuesday, it was obvious that the late vicar of Widnes has won the hearts of the parishioners. It is to be hoped that change of air and of scene, and lighter labours, will be the means of obtaining that health which, as Emerson puts it, is the first wealth.

The following good story is just now on the move, so we help it forward:—" Why do you draw all our ladies in Greek and Roman costume ?" asked a sweet young thing recently of a well known R. A. " Because, said he, "modern fashions change too rapidly for me to meddle with them. One year it is bangs, and the next year bustles. As the father of a family, I cannot afford to have my works dependent on the caprices of woman's taste."

Now that Lady Walker has been presented at Court, the curious are wondering if as the next move she will .turn to temperance reform. It is understood that she has a taste in this direction. What an audience there would be if Sir A. B. Walker was announced to take the chair at a temperance meeting, with Lady Walker as a patron of the movement!

That quarter of million ficom Sir A. B. Walker to build a cathedral for Liverpool seems to have been a castle in the air. The wish was, in all liklehood, father to the thought on the part of some inventive genius. If the brewery had been converted into a Limited Company, Sir Andrew might perhaps have been willing to shell out. "Conversion " has always been a factor in the erec- tion of cathedrals.

Perhaps the great brewer is waiting to see how it goes in Parliament with the question of com- pensation. There is small hope however, of a cathedral for Liverpool, if it has to depend on the Government carrying tho compensation clauses of the Local Government Bill. The tide of public feeling is rising steadily but surely against them. According to the London correspondent of a con- temporary the Government "cannot count on the unanimous support even of their own party in this matter. It it stated that from 30 to 35 Unionists have intimated their intention to vote against the clauses unless they are modified." A little more time, a little more pressure' and these Icompensation clauses will have gone to the wall.

As Councillor H. and Mrs Roberts were walking through Warrington Park the other evening, they espied a bird hanging by the legs and tied to a tree. It was alive, poor thing, and proved to be a thrush. The bleeding bird was placed in the aviary, and every care was taken of it, but it died within two hours. It is supposed that this piece of brutality has been executed in defiance of the notice which has been issued with the object of protecting birds' nests. The miscreant who could tie up a throstle in this way deserves to be tarred and feathered.
Betl

At a meeting of the Newton Improvement Commissioners, on Monday, it transpired that , at a recent committee meeting, it was re- solved that the contract for the erection of , market shops and offices be proceeded with the Law' Clerk having reported that the erection would not be in contravention of the lease. Mr. Forster thought the point at issue should have been decided by the Board as a whole before any- thing was done • but it was explained that in this particular instance it was not necessary.

Mr. Fairclough retorted upon Mr. Forster that he ought to have been present at the committee meeting, and discussed the matter then. But pub- lic business should be discussed publicly as well as in committee. It is not sufficient that a committee satisfy themselves as to taking the right course. They ought never to forget that they are the repre- sentatives of the ratepayers, and that it is their oluty to make matters clear to those who elect them. It is the weak point of Town Councils. and other authorities, that, after transacting business in committee, they treat inquiries as to the busi- ness as impertinent. The impertinence is to lose sight of the fact that ' they are merely representa- tives of the public.

Mr. Yerbergh, the member for Chester, is about to do better than dance attendance bn Mr. W. H. Smith as his private secretary. He is engaged to be married to Miss Thwaites, the only child of Mr. , Daniel Thwaites, chief brewer of Blackburn, anti for a time one of its representatives in Parliament. As Mr. Thwaites is over seventy and a• there is every prospect of Mr. Yerbergh being put in a position to pay his own election expenses for the future. Wealth, if not greatness, will be thrust upon him.

In the House of Commons; on Monday, Mr. Smith, replying to a question, said "they might look forward to a general revival of trade by a renewal of the confidence reposed in the institu- tions of the country." But he did not say what institutions. Does he mean the Church, the House of Lords, or the Brewery? Imagine Mr. Gladstone, or even Lord' R. Churchill, uttering political cant of this kind as leaders of the House of Commons! Mr. Smith is very "small beer," and if he would keep still, it would be less noticed that the beer is stale and without head.

St. Helens is shooting ahead. Four years since, it had no Parliamentary status; it was a part of South-West Lancashire. Now it has not only a member of its own, but there is a fair prospect of its becoming a county in itself under the Local Government Bill. Sir Henry James intends to propose that every borough with 50,000 inhabi- tants shall be of itself a‘county. it is hardly likely that the member for Bury would take this course without consulting Lord Hartington, and if Lord Hartington sap "aye" we may say that it will be done.

This is, of course, good news for St. Helens, and other towns with a population above the magic hue; but what of Warrington and like places that are just below the line? They will be not only shut out, but mill be called upon, as the bill stands, to bear an extra burden consequent upon the large towns ceasing to contribute, for certain purposes, to the rates of the county of Lancaster. This will never do. The smaller places must be up in ‘rms against being further handicapped. We are glad to observe that steps are being taken to ascertain the present population of Warrington. .ter miss the Local Government Bill for this ses- sipn than allow it, by passing it in a haste, to be- Ane an engine of oppression.

The International Trades Congress is to meet in London in November to discuss the following, amongst other topics:—" (1) The most efficacious means for removing the obstacles to free combina- tion in foreign countries; (2) the best methods of combination among the workers in various coun- tries; (3) the limitation of production by means of the reduction of the hours of labour; (4) the desirability or otherwise of state regulation of the hours of labour." There is nothing " wild " in such a programme. There is hope for the Con- gress when it takes a stand on firm ground.

The Prince and Princess of Wales had fine weather at the opening of the Glasgow exhibition on Tuesday, and on Wednesday at Blackburn, at the laying of the foundation stone of a new Tech- nical School. Blackburn has never before in its history been favoured with a royal visit, and there has been a good deal of official and other rejoicing. The Corporation had set aside £3,000 for vlecora- tions, grand stands, 65c., and it is probable that the inhabitants would spend another £2,000. Would it not have been better, instead of all this flummery, if the £5,000 had been added to the fund which is being raised for the new building P But "Tommy loves a lord," and dotes on a prince.
They had a good time of it in crowning the May Queen at Golborne, on Saturday. For once the goddess Maia was obliOng. As Mr. H. D. Trail has it in the current issue of the English Maga-

zine : Merrily Joan a-Maying goes, Sing hey! such a day! 0 the buds of May! In her kirtle short, and her blue, blue hose, Merrily goes she a-Maying An' its 0 but her heart is as gay as a jest, And the Spring is a tiptoe within her breast. She laughs at the hawthorn, dim with bloom, And the litter of gold at the root of the broom, And she hears what the brooks are saying,

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 12, 1888.
TILE.WEELEYAN SALE OF WOltE AT WIDNE6.--o•ThetOtal

receipts of the sale of work in aid of the fund for renova- ting and beautifying Victoria-rdad Chapel and lancey-st. Schools was £53. WIDNES Smoot. BOARD.—Mr. G. H. Danby, clerk to the,Widnes School Board, on• Thursday probecuted a number of parents for not sending, their children regu- larly to school. The magistrates imposed a fine of 5s in each case. ROSE KELLY ONCE MOUE.—R.ise Kelly was stunmoned to appear at Widnes Court on ThursdaY, to answer a charge of being drunk and disorderly in Warrington-rd. She failed to obey the summons, and ,in her absence the Bench sentenced her to a month's hard labour. This is the woman's 62nd conviction. LieEriszso MArrEirs AT RuNconx.—The Runcorn mag- istrates, ort Monday, granted the transfer of the follow- ing license.; :--The Darwell Vaults, Dukes Field, from Joseph Bradburn to Samuel Spann; the Swan Inn, , Shaw-st., from W. Hayward to Allred Baker.; theßoyal Oak, St. John-st., from Samuel Spann to John Duna; and the Friendship Tavern, Fryer,st., from Geo. Leach to Thomas Philips. SUDDEN DEATH OF A CHILD AT Rusconx.—The sud- den death of an infant occurred at Runcorn on Sunday night under strange circumstances. Mrs. Hartley, wit's. of Joseph Hartley, of Wellington-st., had been visiting some relatives, and when she was returning the infant appeared to be sleeping on her arm,but on arriving. home it•was in a dying condition. Dr. Robinson was Imme- diately summoned, but death had occurred before his arrival. ' As Dr. Robinson gave a certificate as to the cause of death, the coroner deemed aninquest unneces- sary.

FRODSHAM PAROCHIAL COMMITTEES.—The first meeting of the newly-appointed Parochial Committees for Frod- sham and Frodsham Lordship Was held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, the Other evening. Mr. A. Thomas pre- sided, having been re-elected chairman- for the current year. The Inspector of Nuisances produced plans of several wooden houses proposed to be built on Frodsham Marsh by the contractor to the Manchester Ship Canal Company, but on examination several objections were made thereto, and it was resolved that the inspector have the plan amended previous to its again being submitted for approval. DEFRAUDING THE REVENUE AT WIDNES. Lewis R. 'en, of Victoria-road, Widnes, was brought before the magistrate S on Thursday, to answer 'a charge of having sold two boxes of cigars without having a license thus making himself liable to a penalty of £so.—Mr. Heal, supervisor of Inland Revenue, prosecuted, and called Ed- ward Ranks, landlord of the Vine Motel, Waterloo-road, who proved that the defendant sold him two boxes of cigars on the 28th December.—The defendant said he had only recently entered the business, add was rather dilatory in taking out a license. He had, however, ob- tained one before he knew this matter was in hand. He was fined lOs and costs, 16s. A VIOLENT WOMAN AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Ellen Goodall, a married woman, of Witt-road, was Charged with assaulting Jane Ramsey, of Victoria-road.—Mr. Knowles was for the plaintiff, and Mr. T. /. Peters for the detendant.—lt was alleged that on the 4th May Mrs. Goodall accused Mrs. Ramsey of deceiving her husband. Afterwards the latter went to a house where Mrss Goodall was in order to obtain a retraction of the statement, Iput the defendant ejected her from the place, and gave her a good thrashing, a black eye, and a bruised body being the result.—For the defence it was contended that Mrs. Ramsey entered the house in a towering passion and strucic the defendant a blow on the face.—A fine of ss, and costs 15s, was im- posed. • AN IRISIr FARMER A WIDNES PAUPER.—Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Pre.scot Guardians, on Thursday brought Patrick Murty.before the Widnes magistrates to prove his settlement, in order that he might be removed from the workhouse.—Murty, a good-looking Irishman, with iron-grey hair, said he was seventy years of age, and was born at Fermanagh, in county Longford. He only came to England three months ago, and hact no settlement in this country.—Mr. Hartle); said Murty had a small farm in Ireland, but whether he was in arrears with his rent and had been evioted he could not say. He had two sons at work in Widnes', but he desired to return to Ireland, and the Guardians had decide/ to gratify his wish.—Thl old man having signed the neces- sary papers, then left the court. ---•-

. . ASSAULTING A SWEETHEART AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Thomas lliesn'and John Dean, father and son, of 55, Nelson-g., were Charged with assaulting Mary Ann McKeown a single young woman, who lived in the same neighbourhood. It was alleged that on the 24th ultimo the prosecutrix was walking down Nelson-st., when John Dean ran after her and at- tempted to strike her. In avoiding the blow she fell to the ground, and then both prisoners kicked her, in- flicting such injuries that, on the advice of Dr: Hutchin- son, she was removed to the Union Hospital. Mr. Knowles explained that the younger prisoner had courted the woman, but a dispute having arisen he com- mitted the assault. The prisoners had agreed to par costs, and give the prosecutrix a sovereign, and she wished to withdraw the charge. The prosecutrix con- firmed this statement, and the prisoners were accord- ingly discharged. A DIAMOND ROBBERY AT RI7NCORN.-At Runcorn Pollee Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. John Brundrit and Major C. W. Hazlehurst, Joseph Blackburn and Samuel Thomp- son, young men, were charged with having on or about the 27th April feloniously stolen a glazier's diamond, worth 255, the property of James Kirkham, builder, Greenway-road. The prisoners we also charged with having received the diamond knowing A to have been stolen. It appeared that both prisoners had worked for Mr. Kirkham. On Monday the diamond was taken to the pawnshop of Mr. E. Imison, Church-st., by a woman, who was told to fetch the owner. Blackburn then turned up and said a young man named Sam Thompson had given the diamond to him to pledge. P.S. Gosling thereupon apprehended Blackburn, and afterwards he arrested Thompson in the news-room of the Free Library. Thompson pleaded guilty. Blackburn said he was In- duced to pawn the diamond, because Thompson §aid he would pay him off a debt if he did so.—Mr. Kirkham asked the Bench to deal leniently with Thompson, as he had very respectable parents, and they were almost broken-hearted about him. He had always foood Black- burn strictly honest. Blackburn was discharged, and Thompson was fined 20s, and costs 22s.—Mr. Kirkhata paid the fine. PAWNBROKERS AND CRIME AT RT/NCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. J. Brundrit and Mr. H. Reynolds, Hannah Jordan and Elizabeth Jordan (aged 13 years) mother and daughter, were charged with having, on the 4th May, stolen two pairs of boots' value 5s 10d, the property of George Tyler and Sons of Bridge- et. supt. Hollingworth said the evidence against the mother was so small that he withdrew the charge against her.—The daughter pleaded guilty.--John Hill, manager of the shop, said the boots were missed from the shop door on Friday last, and evidence was given that a pair was pledged at the shop of Mr. Crad- dock, and a pair at the shoprpf Mr Imison.—The pr;soner also pleaded guilty to stealing two frocks, the property of Wm. Marsh, pawnbroker, Church-st.—lnspector Mil- lington said the girl had pawned one frock with Mr. Imi- son and had thrown the other away because Mr. Crad- dock would not receive it.—Mr. Lake, on behalf of the parents, asked that the• girl should be sent to an Indus- trial School .—Supt. Hollingworth 'Wished the Bench to say something to the tradesmen about hanging their goods outside their shops. It was a great inducement to people to steal.—Mr. Brundrit was of the same opinion and he added that these people would not steal if they could not so readily dispose of the article aat the pawn- brokers. The pawnbrokers ought to exercise more care and make inquines. WESTON SONS OF TEMPERANCE.—At a meeting of the Weston Sons of Temperance, held on Wednesday even- ing, in the Wesleyan Day School, Weston, under the presidency of Mr. Wm. Dunbabin, it was resolved, on the motion of Mr. Wm. Norman, seconded by Mr. John Cotteral. "That the Nil Desperandum division of the Sons of Temperance, located at Weston, near Runcorn, protests most emphatically against the proposals in the Local Government Bill relating to licenses for the sale of intoxicating liquors, believing that the placing of the revenue derived from such licenses in the the hands of municipal bodies will give those bodies a direct interest in maintaining the present inordinate number of licenses, and tend to prevent their diminution, almost universally , considered desirable, unless provision is made for a direct vote of the inhabitants, ' license or no license.' This division also denounces the attempt to create a vested in- terest not hitherto recognised by law in licenses granted for one year and no longer ; tonsidering that if any com- pensation is to be awarded, itis due from the liquor- sellers to the widows and orphans created by their trade, and to the ratepayers and taxpayers mulcted in the cost of workhouses, prisons, and lunatic asylums directly and indirectly resulting from this traffic.' It was also re- solved that a petition, duly signed by the officers of the division, together with a letter, be forwarded through J. T. Brunner, Esq., M.P. for this division, to the House of Commons, and praying that the House will be pleased to reject the compensation clauses of the Local Government Bill. The resolutions were ably supported by Mr. Thos. Pickering, Mr. Samuel Leach, Mr. J. Ward, and Mr. Thomas Ford, of Weston; also by Mr. Thomas Heesom and Mr. Thomas Cooke, of Runcorn. The resolutions were carried unanimously. It was also unanimously resolved that copies of the resolution should be forwarded to C. T. Ritchie, Esq., M.P., President of the Local Government Board. • RUNCORN UNION SANITARY AUTHORITY.—The fortnightly meeting of the Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. There were pre- sent Lieut.-Col. Ashton (chairman), Revs. J., Lock- wood and J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs Mclntyre, W. Hewitt, Hadfield, Aaron, Stokes. Weir, Brandreth, Whitlow, Knowles, Lewis, H. Linaker (clerk), W. II Linalcer (assistant clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer), and Farrington (inspector.)—The Clerk sub- mitted a copy of model bye-laws for the regulation of common lodging houses, and after some altera- tions had been made in them, they were adopted and the Clerk was directed to have them printed, andposted to the overseers in th% Authority's district. —There was some discussion As to the occupation fd navvies huts at Acton Grange, a report of which will be found along with our other Ship Canal news.— This was the principal business.

- - - - - *** A REPLY AND A CIIALLENGE.—OR Saturday, April 14th the Warrington Guardian said as to its circulation that it was "many times greater than ,1 that of all our local contemporaries combined." As we have good reason to doubt so extraordinary a statement, we are willing to put this trumpet- blowing to a practical test. We, therefote, offer to submit our books to any firm of accountants agreed upon, on the understanding that the pro- prietors of the Warrington Guardian do the same; and we undertake to subscribe £lO to the War- rington Infirmary if, as the result of the investiga- tion, it is not shown that the Warrington and Mid- Cheshire Examiner has a LARGER SALE in the borough of Warrington than our boastful contem- porary. We mention tke borough of Warringt3n because it is a distinct and definite area, the cen- tre of local population, and the head quarters of both newspapers. The further condition stipula- ted is that the proprietors of the Warrington Guardian shall engage to subscribe £lO to the Infirmary if they, on their side, fail to make good a similar claim. By SALE, we mean the total number of papers for which payment can be shown to have been received; the time covered to be the first three months of the present year. As the Warrington Guardian is a bi-weekly journal, either the Wednesday's or the Saturday's issue can be taken for comparison. It is time the public ascertained, beyond cavil, what there is behind this bounce on the part of our local con- temporary, and whether it will be able to boast when it has been brought to book. We have only to add that this challenge will be open for ac- ceptance for four weeks from the date of its issue (April 21). AMATEUR PROTOGRIPTIT.—What a wonderful thing photo- graphy is coming to. A. Franks, of 95, and 97, Deansate, Manchester, has just invented and registered a complete quarter-plate Camera outfit, which he offers at the marvellous- ly low price of 6s 64. He will guarantee that it is not equalled In the trade. It consists of camera. lens, dark slide and port- able stand strongly made, and will be found a perfect instru- ment for landscapes, lantern transparencies, groups. Ac. A novelty of this camera is that by a slight movement it can be made to take either vertical or horizontal pictures. To be had only of A. Franks, of 95, and 97. Deansgate, Manchester. 143, Lord-st.. Southport, and 60, Whitefriargate, Hull. Carriage 6d extra.--ildrt. RuNcons BUUIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was called for Wednesday, but only Mr. W. H. Rogerson and Mr. H. Coleburn, with the secretary, Mr. W. F. Salkeld, put in an appearance, and the business had to be ad- journed. The interments during April numbered 19, last year 20. The fees received during the same period amounted to £2l is, last year £22 15s 6d ; decrease £l. 14s ed. RUNCORN INDUSTRIAL BUILDING SOCIETY.—The third annual meeting of this society was held on Tuesday night in the National schoolroom, Mr. A. Jordan. the chairman, presiding. The report and balance sheet which showed a profit of £57 4s 10d. together with a sum of £271 lOs Od aggregate premiums were fully dis- cussed, and were adopted on the motion of Mr. J. K. Digges, seconded by Mr. T. J. Mitchell. The following gentlemen, Messrs. Joseph Itaynor. George Burrows, T. J. Mitchell, and W. H. Rogerson, were elected directors in place of those who retired. Messrs. Edward Ridge and D. S. Garner were appointed auditors. The direc- tors thought that when the ballot and sale principle was more fully understood there would be increased eager- ness on the part of the public to join the society. The hearty co-operation of the members was requested.

BRANCH LINE FROM LANCASTER TO MORECAMBE. —Up to a very recent date the London and North- Western Railway Co were not in a position to claim an adequate share of the passenger traffic with More- cambe. The station was incommodious and the line from the south was circuitous and inconvenient.
These hindrances to the development of the traffic now, however. no longer block the way. A hand- some row of bull ings providing _excellent &MOM-

modation for passengers and goods have been erec- ted in Euston-road in close proximity to the most thickly populated parts of the town, and the loop branch line which will bring Morecambe into direct connection with the main line from the south, and

obviate.the ntcessity of tithing the return by way of Hest Bank will be opened for traffic by Whitsun- tide. The Company appear determined to make the best possible use of their improved tacilities. They have hitherto hen handicapped in the competition . • . . .

for ordinary and eicursiot. traffic to. Moiecarabe,' but now they will be able to offer the best possible facilities to the public. They propose to run 1 or 14 trains daily between.Landaster and Morecambe and there is little doubt the undertaking will prtwe successful.—Lancader Gazette. ACCIDENT AT DAILESIDTRY.—On Saturday even- ing Mr. Stokes, farmer, of Halton, near Runcorn. was driving in his trap near Darqmry, when the horse stumbled, and the occupant of the trap was. thrown'tmt on to the road. He alighted on his head

and received injuries which ne'cessitated his re- moval to the Warrington Infirmary. It s stated that Mr. Stokes had been to Warrington with Mr. Knowles, of Norton Lodge, each driving in separate vehicles. On the return, when near to the bridge over the railway at Daresbury. Mr. Stakee's horse shied at something. and ran off at a mad pace The vehicle came in contact with a corner stone of the bridge, and the unfortunate gentleman was thrown with great violence on to,the r.ad, and alighted on _ .

his bead: Ur., Knowles immediately went to the assistance of Mr. Stokes, who was insensible at the time, and had him removed to- the station, and thence to Warrington. Mr. Stokes, who was suffer- ing from concussion of the brain, was still uncon- scious on arriving at, the Infirmary, and remained in that condition till Monday afternoon, when a slight improvement was noticeable. On inquiry at the In- firmary yesterday, it was ascertained that the in- jured gentleman is progressing favourably. The news of the accident was received with nsu.gh regret in Halton and district, where Mr. Stokes is much esteemed. COLLIERY EXPLOSION NEAR Sr. Iliturss Six MEN BURNED.—On Friday afternoon an explosion of gas occurred in the Potato Delph Mine of the Lea Green Colliery, three mites from St. Helens. whereby six men, named Thomas Lunt (father). William bunt and John Lunt (sons), of Prescot Francis Osborne, of Duke-st.. St. Helens Matthew Mercer, of Parr; and Christopher Sherrott, of Thatto Heath, were injured, The most serions case being that of William Lunt. It Is stated that the mine has always been considered a safe one, so much so that naked lights were used A level had been driven, and working back operations were going on, the men leaving a large vacant space be- hind them. It is supposed that gas accumulated in this space, and a fall of roof occuring, the gas was driven forward on to the naked lights used by the men. An explosion followed with serious results. As soon as possible assistance was rendered, and the six persons taken out of the pit. It was then found that William Lunt was shockingly burned ' about the face, arms, neck, and body; that Mercer was injured in similar _Places, but not to such an I extent as Lunt; that Thomas Lunt, Osborne, and Sherratt were badly burned about the hands, arms, and neck, the latter being also bruised from the effects of being blown down; and that John Lunt was slightly burned about the hands. The first live men were taken home, and a messenger des- patched to the surgery of Dr. Gaskell, Church-st., St. Helens. As 'quickly as possible Mr. 0. G. Williams, assistant, was in attendance and dressed the injured parts, and the men were afterwards seen by Dr. Gaskell." All the *men are progressing favourably with the exception of William Lunt, whose conditions is regarded as critical. The colliery belongs to the executors of the late Alder- man Hadley, J.P:

CALIFORNIA AS A FIELD FOR B3IIGRANTEL—Under the auspices of the Yorkshire Ladies' Council of I Education, Mrs. M. E. Parker, of Penketh, delivered I a lecture on Monday evening, in the Philosophical Hall, Leeds, entitled. "A tour in California." Alder- ' man Tatham presided. Mrs. Parker stated that she considered the State of California to be the poor 1 man' paradise. It had boundless resources. Meat I was sold at from aid to 441 per pound. Bread was about the same price as at home. A cooking stove with all necessary utensils costs about .23. There was no need for people to take out furniture, as it cost about the same there as in England. She ad- vised people, however, to take blankets and bed and table linen, as they were mainly imported from this country, and had a heavy duty placed on them. House rents were exceedingly dear, but strange to say a house might be ,built cheaply. She could not advise anybody to go to San Francisco. Labour there was very cheap, and the temperature rather cool. Los Angeles was also over-populated. She could, however, advise persons to go to San Diego or Frasno. In all the newer towns there was scope for everybody. In a great many households Chinese labour was objected to, and consequently the lady of the house had to do the housework. There was thus a boundless field in California. for the sensible women of this' country who were not ashamed of doing housework, and who would make themselves real helps to the over-taxed wives there. House- hold helps—they were not called servants—could earn from £36 to £6O and £7O a year. Cooks were the best paid, and it often happened that the cook was the owner of the house she was working in. A seamstress earned 6s a day, and laundresses from £5 to £6 a month.—On the motion of Mr. Jos. Latch- more, votes of thanks were accorded to Mrs. Parker for her lecture, and to Alderman Tatham for pre- siding.
It is announced from Tangier that the dispute be- tween the United States and Morocco has been finally settled.

The present strength of the brigade is three officers and twelve men. Three members have resigned during the year and threekothers have been appointed to , their tobices. The condition of the brigade, lboth as re- ' gards discipline and efficiency', is good. The police force have on several occasions rendered excellent ,a.%fistance to the brigade.
