div.head: PRESENTATION TO THE. REV. WRIGHT
div.p: PRESENTATION TO THE. REV. WRIGHT

WILLIAMS. An interesting gathering took piece in the boys' schoolroom of the Widnes National School, on Tues- day evening. The room was crowded with an audi- ence gathered to witness the presentation to the former Vicar of Whines, the Rev. J. Wright Wil- liams, of a handsome and valuable token of their respect and esteem. and to say good-bye to him be- fore he departed for the,Vicarage of Rainford near St. Helens, which he had been offered and accepted. In the absence of Mr. T. Sutton, Tlminis, J.P., the chair was ocenpied by Mr I. Brock, J.P., and on the platform were the honoured guest of the evening. the Rev. J. Wright Williams, the Rev. I. P. Hamilton- Wilson, and the Rev. 1 Jones,.and Mr. 11. Wade Deacon, J.P. A letter was read. from Mr. Timmis, who explained that his absence was caused by illness. Nothing but dire necessity, he said; kept him from taking part in the farewell ' to their good friends, Mr. and Mrs. Williams. • The Chairman said he was sure they all regretted that Mr. and Mrs. Williams were leaving-this parish, in which they had worked so assiduously during the last eight years. (Hear, hear.) Eight years' experience had proved to the 7 trustees that in appointing( alts Williams to the living they made a good choice:. (Appllause.) That period had been a time of great activay in church mat- ters in Widne.s. The parish had been thoroughly orga- nised, two new churches had been built, and a great deal of other work accomplished' by Mr: Williams, and the result was Feel in troops of- friends and a record as a faithful minister of Christ. (Applauee.) Mr. Williams was now going to a parish where lie would have the rest which lie thoroughly needed, and which was tho- roughly due to him,and hi departed withthe goodwishes of all. Mr. Fred Neil then made the pmeentatioh to Mr. Wil- liams. The gift consisted of an expensive and beauti- ful illuminated address antra purse. containing £BO in gold. The address was a charming work of art, and was adorned With a skytch of: the old parish church and St. Paul's Church, an' with. art admirable portrait of the vicar. It read as follows Rev. and Dear Sir. The parishioners of St. Mary's, Widnes, gladly avail them- selvt s of the opportunity offered by your acceptance of the living of Itainford to.offer theit heartiest good wishes for your future welfare in that new sphere of labour. During your ministry here, extending over a period of nearly nine years, we have recognised in you the talents necessary for a successful ministerial career. Your zeal in various branches of church work has been most con- spicuous, while the tact displayed in furthering such work has tended to bring the same to a successful issue We regret that the state of your health makes it desir- able you should be moved to a more congenial atmos- phere, and we trust the change may result in that im- provement which you, as-well as ourselves, so much de- sire. We beg your acceptance of the accompanying, purse of gold in token of the high esteem in which you are held by us, and trust you may have a happy and useful future, and ' that while re- taining our heartiest good wishes you may gain in your new parish. a repetition of the good feeling which has prompted this expression. Signed by the trustees, churchwardens, and Church council on behalf of the parishioners. Trustees : John Brock, Hy. Brun- tier, Hy. Wade Deacon, Goo. ?Airington, T. Sutton Tim- mis ; churchwardens ; Fred Neil, H. N. Wharton. Widnes, May Bth,lBB3.—Mr. Neil spoke of the great ad- vance that had been made in church work since Mr. Williams became vicar. As a preacher Mr. Williams was known as an exceedingly able man, both inside and out- side the church, and as a man who had allowed the laity to take their proper part in church work. (Applause.) They would have to go a long way before they found Mr. Williams equal in tact and ability. (Applause.) He felt more than he could express at Mr Williams departure, and he could only hope that the trustees would find a good successor. (Applause.) Mr. H. N. Wharton delivered a brief speech on Mr. Williams' bonnection with temperance works Mr. J. Dickson also spoke in high terms of praise of the labours of Mr. and Mrs. Williams. The Rev. J. Wright Williams said he could hardly put into words the feelitgs of his heart. That address would remind him in future days of those hearts and those hands which had so kindly, constantly, and power- fully- helped the work of God- forward in the parish of Widnes. He recognised in the words of the address one fact only. They were the measure of the parishioners!. kindly thoughts, and not the measure of his merits. While it was his privilege and pleasure to be vicar of Widnes he had found so many bright spots, so many kind actions, and so many warm hearts, even amongst men who were labouring all day in a chemical works; that it was worth the experience to come to Widnes. Then those manufacturers, who were trustees of the parish, had been strong buttresses in carrying on the work of the church inWidnes. (Applause.) Alluding to the descriptions given of the aspect of Widnes and of its atmosphere, he said they in Widnes had to make the best of it • it was improving every year; and now, when he walked through the streets, he almost thought that it was a pity he was going away. But the reason in the address was nothing but true. It had been painfully evident to him for 18 months that his•throat was failing him, and when the offer of Rainford was made to him by the patron, who was an entire stranger to him—he had never sought a living since he had worked in the minis- try—he began to think was it not time for him to re- move, as in two or three years he might be thrown a pensioher upon Widnes. In conclusion Mr. Williams thanked the audience in most feeling terms for their gifts. On behalf of the ladies of the 'parish Mr. J. C. Craw- ford then presented Mrs Williams with a handsome and

(valuable travelling bag, together rah: a purse of gold. Mrs Williams, he said,- had done gre.t things in the parish, and had in many ways urged her hUSband on te fresh and more earnest exertions. (Applanke). Mr. L. Kiiicross alluded to Mrs Williams stork in the school, and_, .

Mr. 'H. Wade Deacori, in an appropriate speech said that farewell to Mr. and Mrs Williams was a combina- tion of sorrow and gladness. The sorrow. was forthem- 'selves and the gladness was for Mr. and Mrs Williams. They hoped, that Mr. Williams might be long spared to carry on flit-good work upon which he had set hisiteart. (Applause). • The Rev. Wright lrribiants responded* on behalf of his wife, and a vote of thanks having bean; accorded to the- chairman the proceedings terminated. Additional in- terest was lent tothe gathering by a programme of music arranged by Mr...t. B. /liaison. A glee party rendered several part songsi•and sacred songs were. given by Misr? Broad, Mr. J. B. /imison, and Master C. Bate:.

div.head: DOG OWNERS' IN. COURT.-A.MUSINZS CASE.
div.p: DOG OWNERS' IN. COURT.-A.MUSINZS CASE.

At Widnes Petty. Sessions on Thursday+, before' Mr. G. Pilkington and; Mr„.; Brock, John nay, of Dugsdalle-road, was charged' with having', on the 29th April, allowed his'dog t 0 be at large and not under proper control, in' contravention of an'order duly made by the Exectitive• Cbancil on the: 10th February.—P.S. Strickland, stared that about' ten minutes tcr twelve he was in Lugsdale-road, when the defendant's dog, a large black retriever, "set him," and foir five minutes he.coulds not move. As he was af-aid thedog would fPy at hirii.rhe drew his staff to prevent the animal doing so:- At this. time Mrs. Clky opened the doop of the house, and the dog went in. Afterwards he again met thetlog, whichdiew at him: and he struck it with his staff. The .dog was: very ferocious. and was not muzzled.—The defendant said he thought the dogs were to be at liberty after the 331st March, and' he called his wife and son, who deposed ths.t the dog was, muzzled on the night in question.—A fine of 5s and costs was imposed.--rohn Lecomberovatchmaker, Victoria- road, also appeared to answer a: similar charge.—Mr. Lecomber contended that the summons was: bad, as in the order issued by the ExecutiverCotnicil thepelice were to detain stray dogs and charge the owners with the expense. There was nothing said about summoning, or that the magistrates had the power to fine—Mr. Lewin said the summons wae under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, and the Rabies Order of 1557.—Mr. Lecomber said he would not wilfullk disobey an order, but the prevailing feeling in the town' was that dogs could be at liberty after the 31st March.—A fine of 5s and costs was imposed:—Mr. Leeomber gavemotice of appeal on the objection to the summons.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS:.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS:.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton workhouse, on Tuesday. There were pre- t-ent Lieut. Col. Ashton (chairman), Revs. J. Lock- wood, .T. W. Tanner, Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron, Weir, Lewis, Stokes, Hadfield, W. Hewitt, Brandmth, Whitlow, Knowles, Taylor, Grice, Lightburn,. H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (assistant clerk).
RETURNING THANKS.
Mr. Mclntyre thanked the Board for having re-elected him to the Ace of the vice-chair at the previous. meet- ing.
TEE EXEMPTION or MACHINERY
It was agreed on the motion- of Mr. Aaron, secondedl by Mr. Grice, to sign a petition to Parliament against the proposed exemption of machinery, other than motive. power, from rating.

MR. BRUNNER AND THE WEAVER TRUST. The Assistant Clerk referred to. the question recently asked by Mr. Brunner, M.P. in the House of Commons, with regard to the Weaver M.P., . and having, given a brief account of the Acts under which the glast was founded and has been carried on, he went on to, point out that under the last amendment Act, the' Weaver Trustees were under an obligation, to pay over to the County treasurer, to the relief of the county rateran.an- nual sum of £15,000. He failed to see upon what rea- sonable or just grounds, in face of the above facts, M. Brunner could suggest that the salt trade of Northwich —the-area of which covered so small a proportion of the county of Chester—should be directly benefited at the expense of the whole county. The present constitution of the:Weaver Trust and its present mode of election might be questions upon which might be, and, in fact, was some divergence of opinion, but, as the president of the-Boned of Trade said in his reply to Mr. Brunner, that Board "had no power to alter the management of this _ Trust

; any proliosal for the constnictiod of the Trust must come from those interested." _ The parties most in- terestad in that Trust were the ratepayers of the county of Chester generally, and he scarcely thought that Mr. Brunner would find much assistance to support him in thefurtberance of the object he sought. He (the clerk) had considered it his duty to shortly call the attention of the Board of Guardians to the matter, and would sug- gest that he be directed to forward a copy of that re- ort, together with any resolution the Guardians might pass thereon, to the clerk to the several Boards of Guar- dians and other local authorities in the county.. (Hear„, hear.).—Mr. Brandreth proposed "That the Guardians of the Runcorn Union protest against any scheme affect- ing the River Weaver Trust that would tend to divert from the County fund any payment fromsthe Trustees of the. Wearer to the relief of the County fund, and that the Guardians of other Unions, and the Urban Authorities in the county, be furnished with a copy of the clerk'are- port this day made to theßoard, and that such,Guardians and Urban Authorites be requested by resolution to pro- test against any such scheme to the president of the Beard of Trade."—Mr. Hadfield in seconding this pro- posal said that as a matter of fact Mr. Brunner, for the sake of benefiting a few salt proprietors. wanted to make each ratepayer in the countypayan increased rate_ He thought a great mistake had been made by Mr. Brunner in bringing the matter before Parliament.—The proposal was then agreed to unanimously.

_ _ THE CONSTITUTION OF THE WE&TER TRUST. Mr. Aaron remarked that he thought many thousanda of pounds were wasted in connection with the Weaver Trust,.and that he thought if the trustees were electedas Guardians were from each township in the county there would be a great deal more money given in aid of the county rates, and perhaps even something towards the poor rate. He moved the following proposition, "-That the ateention of the Government be called to the consti- * hides and mode of election of Trustees for the manage- men t of the River Weaver Trust in the county of Ches- ter, and that the president of the Board of Trade or of some other Government department be requested to in- troduce clauses in the new county Government bill now before Parliament for handing over the management of such Trust to the County Council or to a committee directly responsible to such Council."—The Chairman thought that notice should have been given of a motion like that.—Mr. Hadfield also thought that notice should have been given, and remarked that they had better let well alone and not do anything which might prevent them from getting as much as they at present did from the Trust.—Mr. Mclntyre said it seemed to him that Mr. Aaron's motion was a condemnation of the present con- stitution of the Trust.—Mr. Ha,dfield : Practically it is backing up Brunner. (No, no.)—The Assistant Clerk said that Mr. Brunner proposed-to abolish toll, but Mr. Aaron's resolution did not say that.-Mr..Ta.ylor seconded Mr. Aaron's proposal.—lt was, however, agreed after some conversation, that Mr. Aaron should give notice that he would move his motion at the next meeting. 'the relief cases were then taken.

div.head: DAMAGES AGAINST A RUNCORN CAR PROPRIETOR:
div.p: DAMAGES AGAINST A RUNCORN CAR PROPRIETOR:

Before his Honour Judge Wynn Ffoulkes at the Runcorn County Court, on. Tuesday; an action was brought against James. Peck, cab.proprietor, Run- corn, to recover £5O damages, for-injuries sustained by Alfred Woods, 5 years of age..tbrough being run over by one of the defendant's cabs. The action was brought by Ann Harrison the boy's "next friend."—Mr. Fred Smith, barrister, of Birkenhead. (instructed by Mr. T. J. Peters, Widnes), appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. A. Fletcher. ot Northwich, de- fended.—The case for the plahitiff was that the boy is the son of Sarah Ann WOod,.a. single woman, who resides with her parents in Lowlands-road. On the 20th Octo- ber last year, about half-past fLvain tlaaevaning, the boy according to his usual practice, was. going to meet his grandfather coming from, his work. As he was crossing Greenway-roadi a little above Savage's Bridge, a hansom cab, driven by the defen- dant's son came along at a speed of about twelve miles an hoer. Persons in the street shouted to him warning him of the risk he, tan, but he slackened not the speed, with the result that the boy was knocked down by the horse and run over. Apparently oblivious of the I accident, the 'driver went on until a man named Alf Capper, of Egerton-st.' stopped him. Dr. Mangan, who, accompanied by Dr. Neator, was a passenger in the cab, attended to the bers injuries. There was a contusion on the inner side of the knee, and the fingers of the left hand were crushed, He attended the boy for two months. The hand had now got back to its usual form, and he had recovered his grasping power. Dr. Mangan infornied his Honour that the cab was not be- ing driven at more than five mite.s an hour —Mr. Fletcher said Mr. Peck, like a humane man, had instructed Dr. Mangan to attend to the boy, and had made himself responsible for the payment of the doctor's bill, but by so doing he did not admit any liability. The. facts of the defence were that the plaintiff and ' another child were trying to pass in front of a lurry, and seeing the cab and hearing the shouts they appeared to have doubled back, and attempted to return to th; par- apet. Evidence would be given that the horse was not travelling at more than 4i miles per hour, but tho driver was unable to pull up in time, and the child W3B run over. Mr. Fletcher spoke of the manner in which chit- dren would rush before horses and the absurdity of the claim. He contended that his client was not liable in the least for what was a pure accident.—Mr. Peek in consideration admitted that he had offered £5 without prejudice to settle the claim.—A number of witnesses were called, and His Honour gave judgment for £5 and costs. He complimented Mr. Peck upon his huir.anity in sending the doctor to attend to tho child.

NORTHERN COUNTIES CHALLENGE CUP COMPE- TITIONS AT WARRINGTON.

On Saturday afternoon the football teams of the South Lancashire district who had entered for the Northern Counties Challenge Cup met on the ground of the War- rangton Football Club to decide which one of the teams should proceed to Barrow to take part in the final con- tests for the cup. In former years all the teams engaged in this competition have journeyed to Barrow, but this year the managing committee decided that in the earlier rounds only the North Lancashire teams should meet at Barrow, the South Lancashire teams meeting at War- rington and the Yorkshire entrants at Manningham. There were seven teams down to meet at Warrington, each team being composed of nine players. So far as attendance of spectators was concerned, the selection of Warrington as a centre proved a success, for the num- bers present were very large, but a strong wind which blew from end to end of the field was rather prejudicial to good play. The time ef each game was half an hour— fifteen minutes each way.

FIT& noI7ND. WARRINGTON (LISIIMAN'S) TEAM v. BENCORNecrAIN- IVRIGET).—Lishman's contingent was consider to be decidedly the weaker of the two Warrington teams, and Evans, one of its best members, wasgreatly incapacitated by an injured hand, but nevertheless they managed to make a very good stand against their strong opponents. Until within a few minutes of the call of time Runcorn scored nothing but minors, but Gayter eventually suc- ceeded in notching a try, which made the final result eight points to nil in favour of Runcorn. TYLDESLEY (SITAW) Y. WIGAN (SLEVIN.) Owing to their being engaged in the final for the Wigan Charity Cup;Slevin's team was unable to meet this engagement, but they found fairly good substitutes in a contingent of Woodman Rovers, the holders of the West Lancashire Junior Challenge Cup, as their opponents of Tyldesley are of the seitior cup. Though the Rovers made a brave defence they were decidedly overpowered by Shaw's lot. who in the end won by one goal, one try, three minors to nil-17 points to nothing. BYES.—Warren's Warrington team had been drawn against Aspull, but as the latter did not put in an ap- pearance, the former were awarded a bye. In the origi- nal draw Widnes had also secured a bye. SECOND IiOCND RUNCoRN v. Wilmits.--Ttie meetin.„ or these .old rivals was regarded with WWI illt4"ns't, but the "wearers of the green" turUed. tu't to be far and away the best lot. Tiouf,k Wainwright's followers in the first half had the 'wind strongly against them they still, by their fine run- ning and high-class passing, "made tracks" around the chemicals, and both Davies and Hollingsworth scored tries. In the second half the Runcorruans had it still more their own way, and in the end won easily by three tries and six minors to a, feria. WARRINGTON (WARREN'S) v. TVIZAStkk. This en- counter was a disappointing one for the spectators, as the local representatives played in anything but the style that had been expected. Their organisation was very deficient, and the passing poor and ill-judged. Tyldesley, who played strongly, consequently had the better of the ,game, but only managed to win by the bare majority of six points to three. FINAL ROUND.

RUNCORN V. TYLDESLRY.—These being the two last teams left in they were expected to meet far the final de- cision but for some reason or other the Tyldesley men left the field directly after their victory over Warrington and declined to return. The Barrow committee there- fore awarded the tie to Runcorn. who will thus be amongst the survivors of the "weeding-out" process who meet at Barrow. It should be mentioned that Messrs. Mawson (Barrow) and McNeil (Broughton Rangers) officiated as referees_ WARRDIGTON (DAVIES) V. RUNCORN (WAINWRIGHT.) On Thursday evening a Warrington team, captained by T. Davies and a Runcorn team, under the leadership of Wainwright, met on the Warrington ground in bene- fit of J. Rigby, one of the Warrington forwards who has. been seriously ill for some months past. Neither the visiting nor the local team was fully representative of the strength of their respective clubs, though, as will be seen from the list of names, in each case there was a fair proportion of first team players. The attendance of spectators was not particularly large, (here having re- cently been quite a plethora of football in Warrington. A start was not made till about seven o'clock, when Dillon kicked off for Warrington. A good return was made, but Evans, getting hold, consigned the ball well into Runcorn territory, where some well-contested scrimmages were formed. The visitors soon relieved, and, Daniels making a miss, operations for a time took place upon the Warrington lines. Appleton getting hold of a pass intended for the Runcorn back, smartly relieved, and some give-and-take play next took place near the centre. The visitors, however, gained ground, and though momentarily checked by some good passing on the part of the home half-backs and Evans, Daniels again bungled, and the visitors notihed their first minor. The feature of the next few minutes was a capital catch and run by Booth, who was deservedly applauded, but this WaS responded to by Davies (Warrington)., who made a nice ran and pale, the result being a minor for the home players. Evans (Warrington) and Davies (Runcorn) were next pro- minent with good runs,the latter nearly getting in. Run- corn again pressed,and having missed a. favourable opening for a try, another minor was obtained. The half-time score was accordingly two minors for Runcorn to one minor. From the kick-off Appleton made a capital re- turn into touch, and soon after Evans (Runcorn) getting hold from a scrimmage, threatened danger. A third minor was secured by the visitors, and afterwards Mas- sey, Bate, and Daniels made a good display, but the visitors were not to be denied, and in rapid succession gained two more minors. For the rest of the game War- nngton had the advantge, and within the last minute Massey made a drop at goal, bu-. only a minor resulted. Final score, Runcorn five minors ; Warrington, two minors. Teams :—Warrington : Full back, Appleton; three-quarters, Massey, Evans. and Daniels; half backs, Whittle and Bate; forwards, Ashton, Fair. Turner,

Davies (captain), Povey, W. Dillon, Hayes, Unsworth, Bate and Holmes. Runcorn: Full back, S. Booth, three- quarters, W. A. Riley, Crompton, and Davies; half backs, Antrobus and Evans; forwards, Wainwright (captain), Clarke, Faulkner, Hancock, Gayle?, Dolan, Stubs, P. Riley, and Hampson. Referee, Mr. T. Barnes.

A FAMILY POISONED AT SUTTOI4.—A singular case of suspected poisoning has occurred near St. Helens, where Mrs. Agnes HonthoM, wife of a working-man, named George Henthorn, of Moss Nook, Sutton, and their two children, Emma and Jane, were suddenly taken ill. It is stated that on kSaturday Mrs. Henthorn went to St. Helens and purchased some cheap beef and mutton, which was cooked on Sunday morning, and the family partook of it for dinner. On Morlday, Mr. Henthorn also ate some more, but felt no bad effects, and on Tues- day morning Mrs. Henthorn and her children had the remainder for breakfast. Shortly afterwards the mother was seized with internal pain, vomiting and cramp, and the children became convulsed and frothed at the mouth. Dr. Gaskell at once went to the house, and seeing that the patients were evidently suffering from some form of poisoning, he administered etnetics. For several hours mother and children were in a serious condition, but under medical skill they progressed favourably. Mrs. Henthorn and her relations think the illness must have been caused by the meat.

div.head: . THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 12, 1888, THE SHIP CANAL WORKS,
div.p: . THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 12, 1888, THE SHIP CANAL WORKS,

"We have inspected this establishment, which is situate in Ellesmere-at., five cottages having been appropriated. By taking out the middle wall above and below a cottage represents two sleeping rooms, Upstairs there is a pas- sage fromend to end, the wards containing six, seven, or eight single beds, some of them being supplied with spring mattresses. The rooms are cleanly, the walls newly limewashed, and special pains had been taken to ventilate in accordance with the requirements of the medical officer and the Barton Local Boasd, so that each sleeper shall have the needful breathing space. In the centre apartment there is a door communicating with an iron staircase at the outside, this being int6ded as a precaution in case of fire. There are also a number of beds on the ground floor. At the back of the premises Mr. Cordingley, who has conducted model lodging-houses in the town ofßury, is building a'three-storek extension of his establishment in which the rooms will be loftier than those in the converted cottages. An intending lodger pays fourpence, and is supposed to bespeak his bed, and secure his tin check before seven o'clock, or the 1 bed may be let for the night to any other applicant. The regulations, which are posted in the kitchen, common to all, say the house is closed at eleven o'clock—ten on Sun- days, that no drinking is allowed in the house, that per- sons smoking in the bedroom will be expelled, that wash- ing clothes on a Sunday and gambling at any time is strictly prohibited. Females are not yet accommodated. A, number of the Ship Canal men have lodged here. Some, on finding a prospect of a permanency, have left and sent for their wives. The lodger provides and, as a rule, cooks for himself, the proprietor having fitted up a large stove, and as we passed through, several men were evidently enjoying their howl of broth in a rough and ready fashion. Mr. Cordingley's lodging-house may be said to supply a want felt by tile footsore wayfarer in search of work, and those who have se :ured a job may here find at least a`temporary resting place as. good or better than they can get in any house of the kind in the kingdom.''

AN ANCIENT HOSTELRY. The headquarters of the canal engineers when on the Weston Pointsection is the Bear's Paw andßailway Hotel, atFrodsham, an ancient inn where every modern conveni- ence is now to be had. The date on it gives the year 1832 as the time it was built. Frodsham, which is much pat- ronised by summer "trippers," is an old market town, and at one time, before the railway became an =corn- plishod fact, a stage coach passed through each day from Chester to Preston Brook. The Bear's Paw was the place at which horses were changed, and the inn at that time also did service as a post office. It is recorded that in 1820 the mail, when nearing Frodsham from Chester, was attacked by a robber, who, having almost blinded the driver with a handful of pepper, plundered the coach. He, however, met with his deserts, for he was caught and gibbeted on the neighbouring hill at Helsby. His body was afterwards thrown into a pit. THE NAVVIES' HOMES. . . _

_ At Warburton the lodging difficulty is being met in some degree by Mr. Walker, who has caused to be erected, close to the river side, a row of four navvy huts. They are built of wood, and good airy rooms are provide), including a spacious dining-room fitted with two tables, for the accommodation of a dozen lodgers, who are slept upstairs in six beds. The huts are each put in the care of a navvy well known to the firm, and his wife cooks for and looks after the lodgers. Each tenant has his own washhouse distinct from the main building and provided with all requisites, and a patch of garden land 20 or 25 yards long stretching up to the river side. At this point the latter has become the Mer- sey, being known as the Irwell up to somewhere in the locality of the Cheshire Lines Irlam and Cadishead Sta- tion. It is intended to put up a number of other huts. The contractor provides coal and fittings for the tenants, who are responsible to him for tie rent charged. The advantage is mutual. A home is found for the men handy for the works, and though it may not be a primary object the contractor is assured of a return, be the same more or less, on his outlay. Due attention is paid to sanitary requirements, the necessary drains, &c., being provided. The huts are, in fact, as good, if not superior, to any ordinary cottages to be found in Hollins Green. FATAL RESULT OF AN ACCIDENT. • Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, has held an inquest at Sale regarding the death of James Ashton, (27), a single max, who lived at Victoria-road, Sale. From the evidence ad- ktuced it appeared that deceased was a joiner, and had been employed on the Ship Canal works at Thelwall. On Thursday, the 29th of March, deceased went heme in the afternoon, and told his mother that he had been working on'a ladder which had slipped, and he had hurt his thumb. He said he had been to a doctor at his work. He stayed at home a week, and thinking that his hand was better he then returned to his work. About a fort- night ago he left home on the Monday morning as usual, but returned in the afternoon complaining that he was unwell. He died on Tuesday in last week. Joseph Hinde, carpenter, gave evidence to the effect that on the day of the accident he and deceased were together en- gaged felting the roof of a smithy. There was a lalder from the ground to the roof, and another on the roof. The roof ladder was fastened on the top. Both witness and deceased were to mount the roof for the purpose of measuring; but Asbton ascended first. As he was get- ting off the ladder it gave way, and he fell to the ground, a distance of about 20 feet. When picked up he was in- sensible. Witness accompanied him to doctor. Con- siderable delay occurred, as they had to go, to Warring- ton. The accident took place at 7.30 in the morning, but it was ten o'clock before the injury could be attended to by the doctor. Deceased afterwards informed witness that he had observed that the fastening e of the ladder had become loose, 'Probably with the constant wear. Sometime after Ashton returned to his work he acciden- tally struck his thumb with his hammer. Witness before the accident had considered the ladder perfectly safe. Dr. Herbert Renshaw said the injured man was brought under his notice on the 24th of April. He then com- plained of stiffness-in the jaws and a jerky feeling in the arches of the back. He informed witness that he had hurt his thumb, which was very much swollen. He evinced symptoms of lock-jaw, which was frequently 'caused by injuries similar to those he had received. Wit- ness could not say whether the symptoms of lock-jaw were manifest from the first. It was possible that it had been caused by the stroke with the hammer which the thumb had since received. He was of opinion that death was due to lock-jaw, aggravated by bronchitis: After a short deliberation, the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death.'?

He thought the man who accosted him was not responsible for his actions.—Thomas Ran- dlas; labaurer, 64, Bostock-st., said that on Tuesday, the 24th ult., between 845 and 9 p.m. he was in Sankey-st. When wit- ness was near the General Post-office the prisoner and the tall man were near to Dr. Spinks's house. He saw the tall man strike prisoner, who returned the blow. The tall man then walked away towards Bank Quay. He heard prisoner say, "I will have it in for that man." Prisoner went after the tall man. When witness and his friend got as far as the circus they saw the prisoner turn into Crosfield-st. That would be about nine o'clock. Mr. Whittle then asked Alderman Harrison, who was atone on the bench at the conclusion of the case, whether in his opinion a prima facie ease had been made out.—Ald- erman Harrison: If you appeal to me, I have no 'hesita- tion in saying 1 do not think that there is a particle of direct testimony td connect the prisoner with the out- rage; I do not know whether Mr. White agrees with me. —Mr. White :1 think so too.—The prisoner was then discharged.

div.head: AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT ' WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.
div.p: AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT ' WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.
NO. 17.-HALTON.

No doubt many a one who has within the last few months stood on the northern summit a the rock on which stand the remains of the ancient castle of Halton, and who has viewed in front of him and away to his right the constantly advanc- ing works of the intended Ship Canal, has endeav- oured to conjure up before his mental vision the scene in front of him as it will be when all this work has been completed, and the new canal is an accomplished thing. At the present time he has before him, almogt at the foot of the steep ascent which leads up to Halton village, the.waters—which are neither pellucid nor rippling—of the Bridge- water Canal, and further away still, and nearer the Mersey, is the channel of the Runcorn and Latch- ford canal—two watcerways which, in the w3rds of the venerable historian of Halton, helped to make the " system of artificial water communication more complete in the valley of the Mersey than almost any other in the world." We assume that in time to come the Bridgewater Canal will remain much as it is, but in place of the Runcorn and Latchford Canal we will have the greater waterway of the Ship Canal. It has already been pointed out that in Norton the new canal will absorb part of the channel of the old Runcorn Canal, but at a point near the junction of the boundaries of Norton and Halton townships this latter canal takes a rather sharp bend to the north which carries it out of the Ship Canal limits, but opposite Astmoor Salt Marsh it takes as sharp a turn to the south again, and this once more brings it into the very course of the new-canal just on the south of Messrs Wigg Brothers and Steele's Old Quay Works, which lie a little to the left —that is on the, Runcorn side of a spectator on the Halton eminence. THE OLD QUAY WORKS.

It may at this point- be convenient, iii a brief digression, to glance at the " protection" of the owners of the Old Quay Works. It is one of the conditions imposed by Parliament that unless the Canal Company purchase the works of Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele, which they are authorised to do, they shall, during the execution of any works which will interfere with the access, by means of the Runcorn and Latchford Canal,. to the Old Quay Works, maintain an access to the works by other means to the reasonable satisfaction of Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele, so as to enable them to carry on their business as efficiently as they pould have done but tor the execution of the canal works. Again, unless the Company purchase these Old Quay Works, they shall, before interfering in any way with the present cart road leading from Runcorn to the works, construct "and at all times maintain" a road in lieu of the present road, at least as convenient in all respects ;. and, further, before any interf rence takes place with the present supply of fresh water, the Canal Company shall pro- vide, and continue, free of cost, to Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele, such a supply of fresh water as will en- able that firm to carry on their business as effi- ciently as they could have done but for the execu- tion of the works of the Company. Another provision is that the Company, in constructingthe Canal, shall provide for the use of Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele, free of wharfage, a side basin or lay-bye, in connection with the canal, adjoining and along the front of the Old Quay Works. The basin is to have a depth of water of at least seven feet, and is to be of a size reasonably sufficient for the accommodation of the existing :mac of the works. In case, however, the C impany are served with a notice before commencing the canal in front of the Old Quay Works, requesting them to construct the side basin with a depth of not less than ten oe twelve feet, they shall do so, but they are not to be held liable for any damage to the works that may be occasioned by the deepening of the basin to the required extent. As a still further "protection" it is laid down that if Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele are hindered nr prevented from, or interrupted in. the efficient carrying on of the works, the Canal Company must either purchase the estate and in- terest of the firm, or make compensation to them for the loss and expense sustained. The priee Lobe paid for the works, or the compensation to be made, if not otherwise agreed upon, is to be decided by. arbitration. •

There is some probability that, over the part ot the canal which will lie more immediately north of Hal- ton Castle, there wilt be a couple of ferries one for vehicles andanother for foot passengers. ferries, of the ferries which have to he made to meet the require- ments of Sir Richard Brooke is to be situated at some point to be named by Sir Richard Brooke, lying between the commencement of what is known as the Ship Canal work No. 2, that is to say, a point a few hundred yards nearer Runcorn than Messrs. Wigg's works, and another point someth,ing like a mile and a half on the other or inland side of those works. This ferry is to be "suitable for all descrip- tions of vehicular traffic and for carrying fifteen ton loads." The Canal Company will also provide and maintain" free from all toll or charge for the use thereof by Sir Richard Brooke, and his tenants, agents, and workmen, and all other persona on his or their behalf, authorieed by him" a ferry over the , canal suitable for pedestrian, and alwayg available between sunrise and sunset. The site of this ferry, like that of the one previously mentioned, does not seem to have been definitely settled, but it is to be somewhere between the commencement of NA). 2 work and the fry which In the Wart will take the plitne of Bob's tumbridge near Moore. Should the Canal Company construct P turnbridge across the canal at or near Mem. Wigg'4 works, it is to be so constructed as to be suitable for all descrip- tions of vehicular traffic, and the company are to maintain it and to provide the necessary labour for its working by night and by day, and the passage of this turnbridge, too, is to be free from all toll and charge so far as Sir Richard Brooke, his tenants, agents, and workmen are concerned. In case this turnbridge is constructed and a right of access to it is obtained by Sir Richard Brooke, the Canal Company will be at liberty to discontinue the foot ferry previously referred to. div.head: NAVVIES' HUTS AT ACTON GRANGE.
div.p: THE NAVVIES' HUTS AT ACTON GRANGE.

At a meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, held on Tuesday, Mr. Farrington, the inspector', said, with regard to the Ship Canal, he had received a letter from Mr. Jos. R. Walker stating that he had twelve workmen's cottages ready for occupation and had got a well sunk for the water supply. He should be glad if the inspector could go over and arrange for a certificate of occupation at his earliest convenience. He (the in- spector) went over on the 2nd inst..and found thednits were situated at Acton Grange, near Mr. Bold's farm. The well was incomplete and he consequently declined to take a sample of the water. He saw Mr. Walker afterwards, and that gentleman asked him if he might not get the permission of the Mithority to the occupa- tion of the huts, the water to be used when it was fit. In fact he wished to have permission to occupy the huts and have the water tested afterwards.—The Chairman : We have never allowed that yet ?—Mr. Farrington said they had not. He had received atother letter from Mr. Walker stating that ten huts were ready for occupation near Moss-lane.—lt was decided that the authority could not give permission for the occupation of the huts until the water had been analysed, but in case of a favourable analysis before the next meeting of the Authority Mr. Farrington was authorised to allow occupation. ECCLES AND BARTON. At Lane-end, Eccles, a steam navvy has been got to work, and all is bustle and activity, lines of rails traver- ing the works in various directions. Two engines are engaged removing the wagons as they are filled, to form an embankment running for three or four hundred yards parallel with the river. Another steam navvy is shortly expected here. Large quantities of contractors' material continue to arrive by barges on the river. The majority of the men have found suitable lodgings at Eccles, Bar- ton, and Patrieroft. Not a few are married men, and have sent for their wives and children, in the meantime being on the look-out for suitable furnished apartments. Very few, except 'gangers" and some others, venture upon taking a home for themselves. At Barton the old corn mill is being dismantled, and a steam navvy has been got to work, at Peelgreen. As at Eccles much activity prevails. Wooden buildings are beimg rapidly erected, and offices, engine sheds, and workshops for blacksmiths and other workmen are now plentiful. Two additional locomotive engines have arrived on the works at Peelgreen, Barton for use on the Salteye cut- ting. A ballast line has been laid from Irlam statim to the river side. Large quantities of plant are in the course of unshipment for use by the contractor's men on this portion of the works. The works between the Eccles landing stage and Barton Locks have been barri- caded off, so as to prevent public admia. 4on, and people are now prohibited from walking along the towing path of the river, as ballast lines converge in every direction In the meadows adjoining the Irwell. There are now five ballast engines at work at Barton and Eccles.

div.head: VAR WAttilIXG OUTRAGE AT WARRINGTON. THE PRISONER DISCHARGED.
div.p: VAR WAttilIXG OUTRAGE AT WARRINGTON. THE PRISONER DISCHARGED.

At Warrington Borough Police Court i on Mon- day, Arthur Massey, a labourer, living at 55, Town Hill, was charged on remand With maliciously cut- ting and wounding William NV ails, in Crostleld-st., at about 9-15 on Tuesday evening, the 24th of April. , Mr. J. L. Whittle prosecuted, and Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the defendant.—Mr. Whittle, in ad- dressing the Bench, spoke of the serious nature of the outrage, and asked that, if the case could be brought home to the prisoner, it should be dealt with in such a manner as to prevent similar oc- currences.—William Walls the prosecator, said that he was a cdnfectioner, living in Atribur-st. About ten minutes past nine on the night qnestion he started from home to go 'to the Pt Office. He went down Crosfield-st., and when 1.00 yards down the street, he saw a tall man coming towards him, walking backwards, and aftef him a shorter man. The tall man he now knew to be Mr. Dobson; the other man he believed to be the prisoner. The shorter man called to the taller man to "stop," and the latter asked "What do you want?" The men were in the middle of the road. When he came up to the shorter man the latter called to him" stop," and walking up to him stabbed him through the ear into the neck. The man was striking at him again when he put up his left hand and caught the blow with one of his fingers. He gave the man no provOcation. Witness then ran away. The men fol- lowed him for about 20 yards mud called to him again to "stop." When near Sankey-st. he met the postman, who went with him to Dr. Williams. The prisoner was very like the man who stabbed him. He (the man) wore his hat at the back of his head; and the prisoner, when he first saw him in the Parade-room, was wearing his hat in a similar manner. The prisoner's voice was also like that of the man who stabbed him.—Cross-examined by Mr. Davies: He believed that the postman gave in- formation to the police. He had never before seen the man who assaulted him. When he was stabbed, Mr. Dobson was a few yards away, he could not say how far, as he had passed witness. He thought that Mr. Dobson was sufficiently near to see what took place. Ile did not know at first that he was stabbed, though he knew that he had been struck. He saw no instrument in the hand of the man who struck him. He saw no one in the street at the time except Mr. Dobson and the postman. He would not swear that prisoner was the man who stabbed him.—Dr. G. H. Williams, Sankey-st., said the prosecutor came to his surgery on the -night in question about half-past nine suffering from a wound which completely divided the cartilage of the left ear. There was a wound behind the ear about an inch and a half in length, and about half an inch in depth. There was also a wound on his left hand. Fortunately, the wound was ' not a dangerous one. The knife now produced might have caused it. —Joseph Dobson, mechanical draughtsman, 19, Froghall- lane, said he was going down Crosfield-st. opt the night in question about a quarter-past nine, in the direction of Sankey-st. When hg had got about half-way down the street a man of shott stature came up to him and demanded him to "Stop." He could not say the prisoner was the man, but he was like him. He saw his face, but not distinctly, as it was dark. The man was in a very excited state. He said to him " stand," " halt," "stop," and " passport "or "password." He had something in his hand which might have been a piece of Wood. He asked the man several times what he wanted but he made no reply except "stop," "stand." A young man passed him on the left side. There was no one else in the street at the time. .He backed from him towardsFroghall-lane. The short man said to the prosecutor "stand," and made a grab at him. Then the latter got clear and ran to- wards Sankey-st. The stranger then came up to him again and said "stand," "stop." Witness moved quick-

This committee reported that the Rev, G. F. Roberts and Mr. Greening had been re-appointed chairman and vice-chairman of the committee respectively, for the en- suing year. The doctor reported the general health of the children to be very good. Mr. Moseley reported that the boys and girls had passed a very fair examination. It was recommended that Mr. and Mrs. Green be appoin- ted tailor and IiOVA' industrial trainer, and foster mother of No. 1 home respectively, and that third class railway fares and necessary expenses be allowed the two sets of applicaitts. It was mentioned in the minutes that Har- riet Morris and Elizabeth G. Webbe, appeared before the committee as candidates for the post of schoolmistress, and that third class railway fare and necessary expenses were allowed.—The Caemaari moved, and Mr. GREENING seconded the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. BLAC/CHURST thought that the appointment of applicants for vacant offices should be made by the Board and not by the Com- mittees, and Mr. DARBYSHIR.E being of a similar opinion, moved that in all cases the committees should select two applicants to appear before the Board.—Mr. BLACK-HURST seconded the proposal.—Mr. ISHERWOOD moved, as an amendment, that Committees have power to recommend one or more applicants to the Board for appointment.— Mr. VOISEY seconded this amendment, which, on a divi- sion, was carried by 12 votes to four.—Tho minutes were then confirmed.

div.head: SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE.

This committee minutes stated that on the motion of Mr. Greening, seconded by Mr. Harrison, Mr. G. Black- hurst was re-appointed chairman of the committee for the ensuing year. Fees were allowed in 77 cases, 55 of which were old and 22 new cases.—On the motion Mr. BLACKRURST, seconded by Mr. GREENING, the minutes were confirmed. Tint ADVERTISING QUESTION. The CLERK said, he had received the following letter from the" Examiner" office:— . _ _

Dear Sir,—We shall feel obliged if you will allow us to draw the attention of your Board to the unfair position in which "The Warrington Examiner" has been recently placed with regard to the Board's advertisements. "The Examiner" nine years ago, and after haying been in ex- istence about ten years, was voluntarily adopted by your Board for a share of the Board's advertisements. We understand, however, that, in consequence of an applica- tion made by ayoupg contemporary for a share of the Board's advertising, it has been decided to exclude our newspapers from some of the advertisements we have been hitherto favoured with. We respectfully submit that this is scarcely fair. If the status of the "Exami- ner" was sufficiently good nine years ago to warrant your Board. in recognising its claims, we submit that nothing has since occurred to affect our position; and further, that the "Examiner" ought not in justice to be affected by any application made by a comparatively new paper. We therefore respectfully solicit your Board , to re-instate us in the position we have held so long as a recolhised medium of the Board's advertisements. Trust- ing you will lay this communication before your Board , at its next meeting, we remain, your obedient servants, JOHN WALKER & CO.—P.S. We may add that during the period which has elapsed since your Board adopted "The Examiner," its importance as an advertising medium has largely increased, as will be seen by reference to the piper as issued to-day. A second letter from the " Observer " Company, Limited, asking the Board "to reconsider the question of advertising," was also read.—Mr. BLACKHURST said he thought that the last time that the matter came before them the Board very'properly determined that each case of advertising that came before them should be decided on its merits. When an advertisement came before them, it would be time enough to consider whether it was worth while putting it into more than one paper or not. —Mr. JOLLEY did not think Mr. Blackhurst's view was the correct one at all. The proprietors of the newspapers were ratepayers, and it was for the Board to deal fairly with ratepayers in every way and shape. If there was- any advantage to be given he thought the Board ought to deal fairly all round. Mr. Blackhurst seemed to stick up very firmly for the neutral paper.—Mr. BLACK- UtIRSY : Nay, I am not a shareholder in it. (Laughter.)—Mr. JOLLEY said they eré —all 'de- cided on the point that the Board was not a political Board, and seeing that they represented all , sorts and conditions of men he was not satisfied with Mr. Blackhurst's suggestion that the Matter slicluld rest where it was. If they did advertise at all, let them ad- vertise in the three papers. That was the only . way in which they could meet the question, and it was'only a matter of a fe.vr shillings.—Mr. Ittercurrs said he thought the "Observer" was scarcely read at all in his district.—Mr. JOLLEY said that was became they were so benighted in Newton and not so well posted up as they ought to be. (Laughter.) Be, however, did not want to *3 personal. He thought if it were put to the Board they would find that there was a principle in- volved, and that they should deal equally with all their , local papers which Yore large ratepayers, and that there should not be an exclusion of either Liberal or Tory.— The CHAIRMAN said there was no resolutiml before the Board nor was it likely that there would be one. Those letters had, however, been sent to the Board, and it was I only right and fair that they should be laid before the ; Board. Re hoped that any gentleman who wished to say anything on the subject would express himself briefly , and avoid personalities. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. RATCIIFFE I thought they ought to advertise in papers which were read in other townships of the Union as well as in War- rington. As he had said before, they started that " Observer " in their district (Newton), but it was a per- fect failure. Some gentlemen seemed to have got the " Observer "on the brain, and he thought they must have got an interest in that paper. (Laughter.) Mr. DARBYSHIRE We had better keep to the point. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. VOISEY said it seemed to him to be not the time to enter into a discussion of that kind. At present there seemed to be a spirit of rivalry between those three papers. The necessary advertising had al- ready been done; they were not gqing to advertise afresh, and when the matter of advertising came up at some future time they could discuss it.—Mr. DAREYSHIRE hoped that course would be pursued. At the same time he should just like to state for the information of the Board that, so far as he couldascertain at the committee meeting, out of the thirteen applications they had for the office of schoolmistress none of them acknowledged hav- ing seen the advertisement in the local papers. That, he thought, showed that it was sometimes unnecessary to advertise in any of the local papers. All the thirteen ap- plicants acknowledged haying seen the advertisement in the "Local Government Chronicle." He should suggest that they advertise first in one local paper and then in another, but to put advertisements of such a character as they had a week or two ago in four or five papers would be simply a waste of money.—Mr. JOLLEY That is very sensible.—The Cireimniar thought they had better allow the matter to drop, and the matter dropped accordingly '

GUARDIANS AND THEIR QUALIFICATIONS. Mr. VOISEY said that he understood there was at the present time before Parliament. a Guardians of the Poor Qualification Bill, the intention of whichwas he understood to-dispen.se with thequalification of a £2O rateable value now necessa..ry for a member of a Board of Guardians. His own opinion was that it would be much better to preserve the qualification, for although he was not going to say that there were not people without the qualification who would make suitable Guardians, he would say that there was a much larger proportion who might be elected and be totally unfit. He also mentioned that there was a feeling on the part of some Board of Guardians to memo- rialise the House of Commons against the bill.—The CLERK having stated that there was such a bill as the one mentioned.—Mr. VOISEY said his• feeling was that it would be better to elevate the qualifications of Guar- dians than to make them lower.—Mr. BLACKHURST did not agree with Mr. Voisey, and remarked that he thought a qualification which did for the House of Commons would do for Boards of Guardians. He did notsee why they I should have any property qualification whatever for Boards of Guardians as there was as many intelligent men out- side the present qualification as inside it.—Mr. JOLLEY supported Mr. Voisey's remarks. He (Mr. Jolley) thought the higher tone, the more intelligence and edu- cation they could get, the better. • As for members of the House of Commons they were mere nothings com- pared with members of Boards of Guardians. (Laugh- ter.) He , thought the property qualification in nine cases out of ten got them men of higher standing than they should get if that qualification were removed.—The matter then dropped. The relief cases were then proceeded with.

div.head: POOH LAW CONFERENCE.
div.p: THE POOH LAW CONFERENCE.

The CHAMMAN mentioned that he and the vice-chair- man, Mr. Balharry, and the clerk, had attended in Man- chester the conference of the North-Western Poor Law district, and he gave a summary of the discussions at Conference. With regard to a discussion that had taken place as to the 4d per head per day to be allowed for in- door paupers under the new County Government Bill, he said his own opinion was that the time would come when all the Union relief would be indoor relief, but that sys- tem would not be adopted so long as the carrying of it .out would .act harshly on poor people. (Hear, hear.) He thought some means would be eventually adopted for bringing rich people more immediately into contact with poor people. He thought that some day a system of charitable relief would be organised of a sufficiently satis- factory kind that Unions might proceed to something like a confinement of their relief to what was given in the workhouse. At the present time, however, he would very much regret the confinement of relief to indoor re- lief, and until some such system as he had referred to was carried into effect he thought they would have to deal with each case of relief on its merits. (Hear, hear.)
Dressmakers can buy no better sewing cotton than B.tgley and Wright's, which for strength is unegualied.--„Advt.

He preferred to out any failure of the past Let them start this asseelA tion on better and firmer lines, and let the past fe;, them not to drop into the same failures in the fut He thought Mr. White took up a quest at the meeting at the Town Hall which affected tiwo I very vitally—the agricultural question. In to afternoon the service of sacred song " Theßiver Sur* was very nicely rendered by the choir and school dren, the solos being taken by Miss Stockley. div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATI7RDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess. AN INQUISITIVE BEGGAR.—Shery Johnson, a tramp, was charged with begging on School-brow on Friday after- noon. It was stated that the prisoner went to the back- door of a house on School-brow, and, finding no one in the kitchen, began to "rummage" in the cupboard. When arrested prisoner was wearing two suits of clothes, and carried an old pair of slippers to enable him to walk into houses without being heard. Prisoner was sent to gaol for seven days, with hard labour.—Samuel Green, a pudler, last from Prescot, for a similar offence in Cock- hedge-lane, was sent to prison for a like period. A TROUBLESOME CesuAr..—Patrick Monaghan a power- fully built inmate of the casual ward of the Workhouse, was sent to gaol for 14 days for refusing to perform the work set him that morning by the master. MoNray.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Alder- man Harrison, and Councillor Greening. RUNNING AWAY FROM THE WORKHOUSE. Catherine Taylor was charged withhaving, on Saturday, absconded from the Workhouse, taking with her clothing, the pro- perty of the Guardians. Prisoner escaped by climbing over the wall on Saturday morning, and surrendered her- self to the police on Monday morning. She was sent to prison for fourteen days, with hard labour. DRINK AND THEFT.— Margaret Donlan pleaded guilty to having, on the 30th ult., stolen a vest from the bed- room of Martin Denlan, of 7, Carlisle-st. She said that she must have been drunk, or she should not have com- mitted the offence.—She was fined lOs and costs, or, in default, seven days imprisonment with hard labour. DRUNKENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—John Burke, in Pilkington's-yard, on Saturday evening, fined 5s and costs; Edward O'Donlan, in Dallam-lane. on Saturday, fined ss, including costs; Michael Murphy. in Union-st., on Saturday, fined 5s and costs; Ellen Burke, in Dial-st., on the 27th ult., fined 5s and costs; Letitia Ellis, in Turner-st., on the 28th ult., fined 5s and costs; William Mahoney, in Buttermarket- st., on the 28th ult., fined ss, including costs; Thomas Parnell, in Bank-st., on the 28th ult., fined 5s and costs; Jane Hennessey, in Croppers-brow, on the 13th ult., fined 5s and costs; Joseph Jackson, in Bewsey-st., on the 30th ult.,,fined ss, in gludintcosts ; James Rowson, in Horsemarket-st., on the 30th ult., ordered to be bound over to be of good behaviour in his own recognisances, and to pay costs. DISTURBING THE PEACE. Mary Finn was charged with having disturbed the peace by fighting on Friars- green, on the 13th ult., and as ordered to pay the costs and be bound over to keep the peace for six months.— Richard Bramford, summoned for having committed a breach of the peace by assaulting a person in Bridge-st., was bound over in his own recognisances, and ordered to pay the costs. OBSTRUCTION —Piers Marsh, a sweep, was summoned for having caused an obstruction in Cairo-st. by deposit- ing a quantity of soot there.—He was fined ss, including costs.

FURIOUS RlDlNG.—George Shaw, for furiously riding a horse, to the danger of passengers, in Folly-lane, was ordered to pay the costs, 3s ed. CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—James Irelane was ordered to orfeit is for having allowed the chinfirney of his dwelling- house to be on fire.

CRUELTY.—SamueI Stringer was summoned for having ill-treated a horse, on the 28th ult., by working it whilst in an unfit-state. He was ordered to pay 3s 6d, the costs.—Alfred Atherton was summoned for having caused a mare to be worked whilst in an unfit condition, and James Newton was summoned for having worked it. The case was dismissed.

MARKET PILFERING .—Sarah Webster, a respectable- looking woman, was fined 10s and costs for having stolen a pair of child's boots, value 2s 11d, from a stall in the market belonging to Joseph Frisby. She said that she picked the boots up from the ground, and had no in- tention of committing a felony. TEksPORARY AIITHORITY.—Temporary authority to sell at the Red Lion, Winwick-road, was granted to John Shepherd. SLEEPING OUT.— William Arthur Quinn, a lad, was brought up on a charge of slveping out in a yard at Bridge-foot, on the same morning. As he has for genie time perted in leaving home and sleeping out, the magistrates ordered him to receive six strokes with the birch rod.

BEGGING.—For this offence James Dalton was sent to prison for fourteen days. ASSAULT ON A POLICEMAN.-- John Ward, for having been drunk and disorderly in Ship-yard on Saturday, and for having assaulted P.C. Smith, was fined 10g and costs, or fourteen days' imprisonment, with hard labour. SEnmus WIFE ASSAULT.—John McCoan was fined 10s and costs, or, in default, 14 days' imprisonment, for hav- ing, on the 30th inst., assaulted his wife, Mary McCoan (who appeared in court in a very weak state). Prisoner complained that his wife got drunk and neglected the 'children.

TugsnAY.--)3efore Councillor R. W. Francomb. A DESERTER.—Joseph Slater was charged by Sergeant Cheeny with being a deserter from Her Majesty's 20th Regiment of Fusiliers, stationed at Salford. Prisoner pleaded guilty, and was remanded t..) await military escort.
THURSDAY.—Before Major Litton Alderman Webster •

and Councilloni Greening and Platt. A RAILWAY STATION ANNOYANCII.—James Leslie and Robert Atherton were charged with having trespassed 9t Bank Quay railway station, after having been warned to leave. It waS stated that the defendants annoyed pas- sengers by importuning them for permission to carry luggage. Leslie, who had been convicted before, was fined lOs and costs; and Atherttha *as fined 5s and costs.

THEFT OF PIGEONS. - Humphrey Stout, file-cutter, Vere-st., was charged with having, on Monday, stolen seven pigeons, value Bs, from the Red Lion Inn, Win- wick-road. Richard Cooper, the occupier of the Red Lion, was on Monday leaving that house. In the after- noon he said that the pigeons were safe in the cote, but in the evening he missed them. Subsequently prisoner admitted having taken them, but said that he did so in in a drunken freak. He repeated that statement to the magistrates, and pleaded for leniency. He was fined lOs and costs, in all RI. us Od,

ALI.ECIN:D THEFT BY A TRlCK.—Elizabeth iJohnson, a young girl, was charged with haying stolen, by means of a trick, a white silk handkerchief, value is. from Mary Elizabeth McCormick. The case was dismissed. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and Dr. Gornall. BEGOll4o.—Patrick Glynn was charged with haying asked alms in Wilderspool-road on the previous after- noon. He was discharged on promising to leave the town.
• Eliza Ryder was summoned by Sarah Ann Gatley for having assaulted her on the .Bth of May. She was fined 5s and costs.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. J. Brundrit and Mr. H. Reynolds. CIIIMNIES ON FlRE.—Samuel Abrams, Speakman-st. and Mary Collier, grocer, Church-st., were each tined 3d and costs, 8s 6d. DRUNKENNESS.—ToIm Wenlock, Regent-st. • Jane Vere, rercival's-lane ; Edward West, a navvy, Norton; Roger Buckley, and Daniel Cavanagh were each fined in vary- ing amounts for being drunk and disorderly. Peter O'Niel, of Mersey-st., was ordered to pay 25s or go to gaol for 14 days for a similar offence. A NAME Wabrreo.—George Leathwood, farmer, of Hal- ton, was fined 5s and costa for allowing a eart,to be used on the highway withiaut having his name painted thereon.
WIDNES POLICE COURT: MoNosy.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr, John Brock.

DRUMEENNESS.—A fine of Ss and costs was imposed upon each of the following persons for drunkenness : Thomas Breen, 31, Eleanor-st. ; William Redman, Marsh- st. ; Eli Young, '2B, Gladstone-st. ; James Cosgrove, Walmsley-st. ; Patrick Burns, Catherine-st. ; Wm. Burns, Martin Mullaney, Elizabeth-st. ; and G.eorge Wareing, sainberry-road, St. Helens.

A DISHONEST POLE.—Annie Marcalis, a middle-aged Polish woman, of Cromwell-st., was brought up on re- mand charged with having stolen a silver spoon and a pair of socks, valued at 3s, the property /of Joseph Kaslusky, of 14, Water-et. The prisoner still declared her innocence, but as she had failed to bring the wit- nesses for which the case was adjourned, the prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

div.head: ?Letter to the attar.
div.p: ?Letter to the attar.

- _ THE WALKING DAY QUEStiON. Sir,—l much regret to notice that tliti bid bother is cropping up about the date of Walking Day. When last the subject agitated the public mind, and meeting were called and speeches delivered regarding it, I thought it had been settled once and for all. Now, within a few days of the time when most people were expecting this annual event to be celebrated, certain discontented people commence again to stir up mischief. They wish to re- open the question. For my own part I do not care what date is faxed, but I think it should be possible to fix on a date that could be annually adhered to without all this discussion and calling of public meetings. I see by the placards on the wall that a meeting is to be held to-night on the subject. Those who requisitioned the Mayor to call it might at least have had the grace to give the pub- lic a little more notice, and not let those people who wish Walking Day to be in Whit-week remain so long under the idea that this year there was to be no dispute on the matter.—Yours, &c., 0. P.

Warrington, May 11th, 1888. Sir,—The Warrington day school teachers seem to think themselves badly injured by Walking Day having been fixed permanently for the Friday in Whit-week. But is it not a pity that they are only now becoming conscious of the injury? When that day was perma- nently fixed some time ago, I believe that there was very little, if any, protest from that much-injured sec- tion of the community. I believe very few of them took the trouble to attend the meeting. As one of them was frank enough to admit on Monday night, "f only a third of number who now cry out aloud for a public meeting to redress the injury haa attended that meeting, as requested at the time, and expressed their views on the subject, they would easily have carried their points." I think that it iS a great shame that, when a number of people are either too careless or too indifferent a look after their own advantage at the proper time, they should upset the arrangements of everyone else. There was a cry also raised about the cold weather on account of the dear children's health." Now, sir, I appeal to everyone's personal observation—Has not the weather lately been warm enough for any fellow ? And I should like to ask—ls the dear children's health at the bottom of the agitation, or has the advantage of the school teachers anything to do with the question ?—Yours, Ac., PRUDENTIA.

div.head: MINE RENTS AND MINERAL ROYALTIES.
div.p: MINE RENTS AND MINERAL ROYALTIES.

Sir,—You will perhaps allow me to express a few opinions about Mr. C. M. Percy's pamphlet on "Mine Rents and Mineral Royalties," to which you have refer- red in a leader, and about which Mr. Percy writes in your List issue. Briefly, then, I should say that those who wish to know what mine rents and mineral royalties in England really are how and to what extent they are levied, and in what manner they operate upon industry, will be well repaid by a perusal of the pamphlet; but that those who expect to find an important question treated with clear and consistent reasoning, in its broad economic, and national aspects, will be sorely

disappointed. In his letter of last week, Mr. Percy thus summarises his pamphlet—" I have" he says, "said in my pam- phlet that the nation gave away all its minerals without knowing that any minerals were in existence. I have said that the amount already lost by the nation would about wipe off the National Debt; and that the annual amount the Nation is still losing is about £3.000,000 a year. Still lam no advocate for the Nation entering mto possession. I have said so in my pamphlet, and I say so here. I would not confiscate a single pound of coal or iron. But I would adopt such payments as have to be made so as not to hamper our National industries, and I would reduce the £8,000,000 we now pay per year, one fourth, or one half, or three fourths, or as much as might be found needful to enable us to compete oa some- thing like just terms with other mining and iron and sta.! nations; and whether our annual payments were £6,000,000 or £1,000,000 I would charge the sum with local rates."

Now, sir, I will venture to say that it would be ex- tremlly difficult to find anywhere else, in so short a pas- sage, such confused and self-contradictory argument, and such an absolute misconception of the real relations of the state to the owners of royalties as we have here. In one sentence Mr. Percy says he would not confiscate a single pound of coal or iron, and in the next he would re- duce the £5,000,000 now paid in royalties by one-fourth, one-half, or three-fourths, and that he would charge the remainder with local rates, which would probably sweep it away entirely. In other words, he tells us in a single breath, so to speak, that he would take nothing from royalty owners, and yet, that under certain circumstan- ces he would leave them nothing. Mr. Percy claims to be a "good robust Radical," but it seems to me that he shows a complete ignorance or misconception of Radical doctrine as to the relation of the state as a whole to its various parts and classes when he says that the " Nation gave away all its minerals," and upon the strength of this supposed ",giving away" adds that he is "no advocate for the Nation entering into possession." Now, sir, I contend that the State has never given anything away to the owners of mineral royalties, at least in that absolute way which Mr. Percy seems to suppose. It is true that in times past laws have been passed securing to certain people, under certain conditions, the ownership, and the advantages consequent en the ownership, of minerals, but no " good " Radical, and, indeed, en one who wishes for political advance- ment la the future would concede for a moment that this is a giving away of the minerals by the Nation. The late Professor W. Stanley Jevons was no "Extremist," yet in his singularly valuable book thi "The State in Relation to Labour" he enunciates in clear and vigorous language, opinions which are not new, which in fact i have been the texts of almost all reformers, but whiGh jt would ha wall ii:gothe "Badieall " I gently study and lay to heart. Law, u-hieh gives mineral owners their only title, is, as Mr. Tevohs says "hut a series of arbitrary rules accumulated of varied from century to century, and defining the terms on which people may best live in each others society. It is a system of adjustments and compromises founded upon experience and trial. It may be imagined that a person has an absolute right to his own property. Apart, however, frem the difficulty of defining what is his own property a cursory examination of the statute book would show that this absolute right has been invaded in every conceivable way." "It may be fearlessly said," continues Professor Jevon.s, "that no serial transforma- tion would be too great to be commended and attempted if only it could be clearly shown to lead to the greater happiness of the community. No scheme of Bellers, or Babeuf, or Robert Owen could be resisted if only their advocates could adduce scientific evidence of their prac- tibility and good tendency. No laws, no customs, no rights of property are so sacred that they may not be made away with if it can be clearly shown that they stand in the way of the greatest happiness, qa( populi ..ruprenia lex." This, sir. r venture to commend as the correct and best sla'ne for all "good robust Radicals" who wish to carry forward the standard of reform either in regard to royalties er anything else. The would-be reformer who adniits that minerals have been given away" by the nation, and that the resumption bi them by the State would be confiscatios, is in the Thwition of a soldier who goes into battle without a single weapon in his hand. This letter having already reached an inordinate length, I will, with your permission, again refer to this important subject of mineral royalties.—l am, sir, PHYSIOCRAT.

THE REV. PETER MACKENZIE AT WIDNES. ( The Rev. Peter Mackenzie preached in the Vic- toria-road Wesleyan Chapel on Thursday afternoon. In the evening he delivered his new lecture, sub ject, " Naaman, the Leper, or the advantages o disadvantage." There was a large congregation Mr. T. Sutton Timmis had been announced to pre- side, but owing to indisposition was unable to be present. With the letter apologising for non- attendance, however. Mr. Timmis enclosed a cheque. value .£lO. Mr. Anderton. of Nut Grove, was voted to the chair, and there were .also Oil the platform—The Revs. R. Burdoa and J. Bryant; Messrs. T. Robinson, S. Robinson, and R. Fogg. After the Chairman, had introduced the lecturer, the Rev. P. Mackenzie was received with applause. He said few portions of Scripture were more inter- esting than the history of Elisha. He proceeded to give an interesting account of the life of Naaman, and the wondrous miracle by which his care was wrought. He further showed the advantages aris- ing from the disadvantages of Naaman's affliction. The lecture • was full of racy anecdotes and trite sayings, and was much enjoyed.. Votes of thanks were accorded to Mr. Mackenzie at the close, on the motion of Mr. S. Robinson, seconded by Mr. T. Robinson. A similar compliment was also Raid to the Chairman, on the motion of Mr. Mackenzie.

ROYAL VISIT TO BLACKBURN.—The Prince and Prin- cess of Wales visited Blackburn, on Wednesday, for the purpose of laying the foundation-stone of a Te-hnical School, which is being erected at a cost of £25,000, as the town's memorial of the Jubilee of her Majesty's; reign. Their Royal Highnesses arrived at Cherry Tree Station, near Blackburn, from Glasgow, at half-past nine o'clock, where they were received by Lieutenant General FeildPn, M.P., to whose residence, Witton. Park, they were then driven. The Royal party, leaving Witton Park at half- past eleven o'clock, were met on the way to the town by the Mayor and numerous members of local authori- ties, a procession being then formed which passed through the principal streets to the site of the new school at Blakey Moor, where his Royal Highness re' ceived from the town clerk and the Mayor respectively an address of the Corporation and the honorary freedom of the borough. The Prince, having replied, laid the foundation-stone with the ordinary masonic ceremony. Their Royal Highnesses were afterwards entertained to luncheon at the Town Hall, and left at 3-25 for London by a London and North-Western special train. The town was gaily decorated, and the streets were thronged with spectators, from whom the distinguished visitors had everywhere a most enthusiastic reception.
