div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 12, 188 S.

the back of the wretch. She is coming to be a thorn in the side of my poor sister's children but be avenged I will. Wherever you live, I will follow, and woe be to the Manchester outcast. You think that I am quiet , about the will that was made, but I will put you in gaol for that deed yet. I thank God that there were two wit- nesses, and I will make you produce the will, or swear , that you ' committed perjury, you wicked, bad, . If you have acted in a right and straightfor- : ward manner come out and meet me in a court of jus- tice, you dastardly wretch. Warrington is up about. i you. People tell me about it, and I say Cross was shar- . per than you. His doom came quickly, but I hope yours , will linger. May you and the woman with the ugly i front takes the shivers at the alter, and never be warm , again until you are both dead. That lump on her shoul- ders is a complete ugly construction. You have four nice - looking children. Prize them. But i you are thinking of nothing but that one ' . bad wornan. No decent woman would for ; shame go up Allen-st. grinning on your arm. Your children are sorely left, with a father of your past. character and a woman to match. She knows ; all your past career, and thinks it bright. If you each take to the same way, which man ana wife ought, you ' are not fit to bring up the children of a respectable woman. This woman, whom nature has been so unkind to, is not a widow, and an old zbaid you abhor. As you . know they are too pure for you, so you set your face • against them' and go in for the only sort of characters , left. I shall be in Warrington in a week or two, to talk to the new neighbours."—ln the course of a short legal ' discussion that followed, it was stated that Mr. Cotton's first wife died in October last, that the letter given above was written on the 11th February following, and that on the 18th of. February Mr. Cotton was married to the prosecutrix. The marriage so soon after the decease of the first wife was understood to have caused the trouble. —Mr. Jenkins then plead a second letter, dated March Ist, 1888, in which the 'miter said :—"I want to know how it is that Herbert is going about in such a disgraceful condition. His mother left money enough to keep two women at your house. Surely thop two women cau look after Herbert and keep him tilly ; he never was , kept like that in his mother's time. He wants two new suits and an overcoat. He was sent back to school after 'the holiday's with his clothes shabby and thread- bare ; poor lad, he suffers more than all put together. for !•A wag kept from scbool and had to work at night during his mother's illness, as he ought not to have done. And then, after she died, he must go on cleaning the grate and run home from school early to fetch butter for tea. I have watched him go, and I know then he had no business to have to think of any- thing but his lessons: why did you not brave your troubles and surmount your difficulties as a man should have done; spend your spare time at home and not on a woman to let your money go down her throat. Oh, that throat! Yourtroubleshayeyet to commence; but Herbert's troubles hays been on for nine months, and there seems no turning for hinl. I Must tell you straight, that you can be compelled to dress your son suitable to your posi- tion and means, and Herbert can, if he sees there is noth- ing else for him, buy suitable clothing and have it piet down to you, and you will be made to pay. It is no use him going to see for a place as office boy in such attire. He gave you the money he earned. lie is not a bad boy, and I defy you or all the people who wish to say that he is bad. The odds have been against him. Why don't you, as a father, take him in hand now ; dress him suitably and do all in you power to get him work."— Mr. Davies said that the letters were only written in an- swer to others received by his client from Mr. Cotton. They had offered to aplogise,—Mr. Jenkins, having con- sulted with his clients expras' ed willingness to accept an apology from Miss Howtroft, to be published, on condition that Miss floweret% Pay the costs, and undertake that no tarther proceedings, should be taken in the matter. Finally dila course was agreed upon, the defendant con- senting to Apologise and nay MO to over all costs.—lt was Mentioned that a letter read at a previous hearing et the court, commencing "Old Devil,' had not, as was then alleged, been written by the defendant.

div.head: POOL HALL.
div.p: POOL HALL.
(From the " Manchester Guardian.")

The making of the Ship Canal will bring into view a number of interesting places scarcely known at present outside certain circles. Such a place is Pool Hall, a fine example of the houses of the gentry of about Henry the Eight's time, and spoken of by the "learned and elegant " Ormerod as one of the most venerable specimens of domestic architecture in the country. The mansion is within a stone-throw ot the Canal line (or, for the sake of the olden time, say a bowshot, though the arrow might pass over the works into the sea), and the harsh clatter of the steam digger echoes about the ancient walls. The Hall is some four miles up the river from Eastham Ferry, where the Canal goes into the estuary. A line of rails put down by the contractor connects the ferry with Ellesmere Port, and one way of reaching this beautiful old building is on the wing of one of the short, thick-set engines which skirr to and fro as head to a long tail of waggons. They have a curiously stunted look these engines, as if they had been put to work too soon and never had time to do more than bolt their coal. In their own world one would name them the Children of Gibeon. One little bit of sentiment clings to them. They bear names picked up on the scene of their first labours. The "Ellesmere "and the " Hootou" are among the new comers on this section, and by and by they will take these Canal names to other ' works, just as the " Monmouth " brings here memo- ries of the great Severn Tunnel enterprise. It I makes a short journey of the four miles, but we do not recommend the visitor to go per engine to Pcol Hall, even if there be no trouble in getting leave. Policemen on duty at the worka and other people who make frequent rounds may get into the trick of feeling comfortable on the sooty flanks of an engine, but a novice is likely to come down from his perch in a frame of mind ill suited for the res- pectful examination of a venerable building. In oar con case we took the risk of this for the sake of a ktheral vieW of the Work: The excavation for the Las goes titt at a rapid pace, and the whole area is now so broken up with working " faces," each with its lint,bf rails, that a through train has to pick its way giingerly through the iron network, with the assistance of signal boys at intersecting points. From the outside face of the locks there is now about a mile of continuous cutting, and to meet the advance from the Eastham side excavations are in progressopposite the ancient ' building we are about to visit. Between these two places the line of the Canal goes across a bit of the foreshore in front of Booston Wood, and a linp of posts out on the sand marks the course of an Inn- bankment it will be necessary to make against , the sea. When it reaches Pool Hall the line of the I Canal has again come inland, and the steam digger ' is now dealing here with the first of the red sand- stone, which at this point comes within fifteen feet of the surface,

Pool Hall loccupel in these later times by Mr. James Pickering, who farms the estate. The Pool Wll9 built the menOon IYM .s9n 9f a certain Sir William. who was High Sheriff of the county in Henry the Eighth's time. And the chronicler men- tions that this Thomas, whom he describes as " Esquyer," covenanted with a certain Sir Edwaid Fittone that his son and heir apparent should marry Sir Edward's daughter, and that the lady's jointure was settled at £lO per annum in conside- ration of a marriage portion paid to Mr. Pool of .C 246 ls 4d; a transaction which has about it a fine flavour of old times. A deed with regard to the manor is enrolled in the Cheshire Domesday, dated "the Thursday before the feast next after the re-. turn of Earl Randle from Jerusalem," Which event took place in 1220. One of the Pools (who were a Catholic family) married Matilda, daughter of Geoffrey, hereditary master cook of the neighbour- ing Abbot of St. Werburgh. To appreciate the fine dust-laden quality of these facts one must enter the embattled porch and climb up the solid blocks of oak which compose the stairs, and peep . out through the ancient ivy at the present day in the Vandal shape of the steam digger at work upon the Canal. Members of Mr. Pickering's household found the old rooms excellent ground for a hide- and-seek game. And if some of the floors were worm-eaten into holes through which one could drop, and there was a chance of meeting in the old chapel on the upper floor the ghost of a young lady without a head, a charm of uncertainty would enter into the game which would simply be priceless. The young lady without the head has not been seen for some time; how she came by her misfortune the chronicler says not. The Hall probably looks much prettier now than it did when the Pool of an "elder day," brought home the daughter of the Abbot's hereditary master cook. If time has worn a little the face of the walls, it has made upon them some delicious studies in yellows, reds, and greens. Of these our sketch can giveno hint, but readers will get from the pic- ture all that neeed be said about the general style of the building. A striking feature is, of course, the octagon turret. Some modern additions in brick have been made at the back. The upper part of the front is also of brick, later in date than the stone, but old enough to have acquired a beauti- ful colour which gives a warm feeling to the whole front. A considerable number of years ago some swords, pistols, and other implements of war were found in a pit near the Hall. They were much corroded, but their condition was good enough to show that they had been of the most costly anti delicate manufacture. The chronicler leans to the view that they were buried during the civil wars; perhaps the young lady who in a painfully literal sense lost her head could have set the question at rest.

FATAL MACHINERY ACCIDENT.—On Thursday morning, at the Acre Mill Cotton Weaving Shed, Haslingden, John Entwistle, 34, a weaver, met with a fatal accident. He was caught by a loom strap and carried round the shaft- ing several times until the strap broke and he fell to the floor. He died almost immediately. The deceased's head was badly injured, and his right arm broken.

div.head: MOORE.
div.p: MOORE.

There is not much to report in connection with the work in the neighbourhood of Moore this week, except it be to say that progress rapidly goes on. A portion of another steam digger has arrived, and the ponderous machine is in course of erection at Walton. At Acton Grange the steam navvy that has been at work there for some time is steadily effecting its object, and tearing up mass after mass of soil. The cutting that it has made is now very deep, is of great width, and extends for a con- siderable distance. From Acton Grange the navvy is persistently making a way towards Moore village, and on the ground ahead of it a large number of men con- tinue to be engaged in preparatory operations—remov- ing the surface earth being there the principal work. Pumping operations are also being carried on. Beyond Bob's Bridge the German navvy is having a great effect on the soil, and pumping operations are being carried on in this locality.

div.head: THELWALL.
div.p: THELWALL.

Great progress continues to be made by the two steam navvies, which are rapidly working towards each other, on the works between Morris Brook and the river at Thelwall. The cuttings are now both wide and deep, and the heaps of spoil very large and being continually added to by the loaded wagons, which are hauled up by small but übiquitous locomotives. A week ago we men- tioned that preparations were being made for erecting offices, &c., on the ground near Alderman Pickmete's late residence, and so energetically has the work there been carried:on, that not only has the framework of these structuresbeenerected, but some progress has beenmade with the wooden sides and roofs, and bricklayers are busily engaged in setting fireplaces. It is worth noting i , that n the course of excavation at Thelwall a , bed of peat was struck upon, and in this were found several large sized trunks of beech and oak. Water percolated through the peat, but notwithstanding their long immersion, probably of hundreds, and it may be of athousand years, the oak trunks, at all events, were in a fair state of preservation, but the beech, which is not of so tough and enduring fibre, was more or less- rotted by the moisture. When the peat was come upon ' one of the steam navvies beg on tAi eiok, and it was feared that it might dt appeat altogether. By some hours of hard work it was, however, secured from the threatened danger. Across the river from Thelwall a conspicuous obiect at present is a crane of unusual length which we understand, is to be used in connection with the work of excavation in the deeper parts of the new river bed bed past Wildegmve Farmhouse. LYMM.

Work is to some ext;iit--- a standstill at Statham owing to a hitch which has taken place in regard to the roadways leading across the course of the canal there. These roads are the only means of access to the land which lies between the canal and the Mersey. and be- fore they are demolished some settlement will have to be come to with regard to the land in question. The steam navvy which, as we mentioned last week, has been put up at Statham has not yet been got to work, but the parts of another of these mechanical monsters is now on the ground, and it is expected that once the difficultY referred to is swept away, the work- bf excavating will be set about with renewed vigour. On Raton Leys, which are across the river from Statham, a large chain pump is in operation, and the, soil there which was for- merly so damp as to stop progress, now seems to be thoroughly dry and workable. NEW BARNS.

A correspondent writes :—On going over the ground set apart for Spoil purposes at New Barns, the magni- tude Of the " tip " becomes more apparent. The south side is bounded by the Racecourse and Buffalo Bill's- road, opposite the end of which the contractor is erect- ing one of his numerous temporary wooden bridges to facilitate acru.as to the works from the Salford side, and he is commencing to lay in a new railway on the north or cemetery side, so as to increase the speed of his opera- tions in filling in the low-lying land. At the Manchester end of the canal proper, on the Barton section, neat the Sewage Works, men are busy stripping the sktrface soil, preparatory to the work of the steam naviies, one of which is already on the ground, and at this point alsu another temporary bridge is being constructed. AN OFFICIAL VISIT.

• ---- On Thursday a number of the directors of the Man- chester Ship Canal, including Sir Joseph C. Lee, Mr. Henry Boddingt,on, jun., Mr. W. H. Bailey, and others, accompanied by Mr. Leader Williams, engineer, Mr. Wal- ter L, Bourke, resident engineer of the Barton section, and J. H. Whitworth, secretary to the company, paid a visit to the works at Lane End, Eccles, and Barton. The different phases of the works were explained by Mr. Leader Williams and Mr. Bourke. The party afterwards proceeded in a barge to visit the works at Hollins Green, on the Cadishead and Irlam section of the undertaking. Satisfaction was expressed with the progress that was being made with the works.

div.head: ALLEGED LIBEL ON A WATt- RINGTON LADY.
div.p: THE ALLEGED LIBEL ON A WATt- RINGTON LADY.

At Warrington Borough Police Court, yesterday morning. Mary Jane llowcroft, confectioner, 10, Myrtle-st., Liverpool, was summoned to answer a charge of having, in February last, maliciously published a defamatory libel concerning Mrs. Eliza Cotton, wife of Mr. Samuel Cotton, engineer, Allen- at., Warrington. Mr. Jenkins appeared for the pro- secutrix, and Mr. P. Davies represented the defen- dant.—Mr. Jenkins having explained under what section the proceedings were taken, said that the I defendant was a sister of the late wife of Mr. Cot- ton, the husband of the prosecutrix, and that relit-- tionship was really at the bottom of the trouble. It had been found impovible to stop Miss Ilowcroft writing letters, and reeourse was now being had to that court to put a stop to a source of great annoy- ance. The letters in question were sent through the post to Mr. Cotton, who communicated their con- tents to his wife. This, he claimed, was libellone, and quoted a case in view of that contention. The letter referred to in the information was written in February, and was as follows :—" And so, Sam Cotton, you are to be married to that fashion of a woman from Church-st. Well, thank God. I never spoke to her style of creature and never shall ; the brassy madam; the impudent brazen face; is to be " steppy "to my sister's children! May she never live to see the day which is drawing so near, and you that is shunned by all: respectable women take I her on your arm through the market and everywhere, and even into house-visiting. The town may well cry shame of you. I was there on Wednesday, and if the respectable women:in Warrington had their way with the I pair of you, you would look worse maltreated than your face does at present. You are a town's talk. You have time for nothing, but—have I done my last, old fellow? No, indeed; when I see my dear sister's best mantles on

div.p: LYMM.

MIISIc.—On Saturday evening last the brass band of the Church of England Temperance Society, under the leadership of Mr. T. Gregson, gave a choice selection of music at Lymm Cross. VAGRANCY.—On Saturday afternoon James Hennesey was charged before Mr. T. P. Norris, at the Lymm Police Court, with begging at Lymm. Sent to Strange- ways for seven days.--Joseph Allen was charged with begging the same afternoon at Lymm. Seven days to Strangeways.--John Eccleston was charged with beg- ging at Higher-lane, at one p.m. on the 7th, and was let off on promising to leave Lyinm at once. H (Lymm) COMPANY 3RD VOLUNTEER B.C.R.—The above coMpany having assembled at the Drill Hall, on Sunday morning, proceeded to Lymm Church for Divine service, by way of Booth's Hill, F sde-brow, and Church Green. There was a very large congregation. The service was read by the curate, the Rev. E. W. Lomax the sermon being preached by the Rector. The route back was along the Dam Head and throygh Booth's-lane. Captain J. G. Jones commanded, together with Assistant-Surgeon Wil- liamson and Lieutenant Cookson. THE LATE REV. J. H. OUSTON.—It is stated that the members of the Congregational Church have under con- sideration the question of erecting* a marble tablet in their church to the memory of their late pastor, Mr. Ouston. A funeral sermon was preached in the New- road Congregational Church, Bury, on Sunday last, and at its close it was agreed to erect a tablet in their church to the memory of Mr. Ouston, who was ordained there in 1858. A vote of condolence has been forwarded through Mr. Dutton by the members of the Congrega- tional Church, to Mrs. Ouston and family, on the great and irreparable loss 'sustained in the death of Mr. Ouston.

A DISORDERLY ROUGH. - Michael Heavy, a strongly- built young man, was charged at the Sale Petty Sessions with doing wilful damage to the extent of 16s, to the windows of the Nag's Head public-house, Lymm, on the sth May, and also with assaulting Police-Constable Dut- ton at the same time and place. It appeared that the prisoner and some companions were drinking together in the public-house when a quarrel took place. The men were ejected, and the door fastened, whereupon the prisoner broke eight panes of glass, and challenged any- one in the place to fight him. • P.C. Dutton, being in- formed of what had occurred, attempted to arrest' the prisoner, but the man was so violent that the services of several men were required before he could be handcuffed Prisoner pleaded he was drunk at the time, and did not remember anything about it.—He was ordered to pay the amount of the damage to the windows, and for the assault on the constable he was fined 53 and costs. non. BY A NEIGHBOUR.-At the Sale Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr W. Armitage and other magis- trates, a middle-aged woman, named Mary Rooney, was charged with having stolen 3s from the house of James Nicholson, at Lymm, on the 13th ult.—lt appeared from the evidence that the wife of Nicholson and the prisoner were neighbours, and on the day in question Mrs Nichol- son went out, leaving her rent (3s) between the leaves of

the rent book on a dresser. Her two children were left in charge. During her absence the prisoner came in, and the children went out to play. The children, how- ever, who had seen what had passed through the win- dow of the house, followed her, and asked her for the money. She denied having taken it. Prisoner had had drink at the time. Information of the theft having been given to the police, prisoner was arrested, and had beet' a week in custody —The Magistrates' Clerk handed a letter to the Bench, and the Chairman after reading it said that a gentleman had written ttç request the Bench to impose a fine and he would pay it. Had it not been for this they would have sent the prisoner to gaol. The prisoner would be fined 5s and costs.

div.p: MARKETS.

LONDON PRODUCII, FRIDAY.—The sugar market is gene- rally quiet; beetroot 12s 100 May and 13s June. Coffee firm for most qualities. Tea quiet to-day. Rice dull and in- active. Cotton very quiet. Jute unchanged. Tallow Y.O , 36s on the spot. Rape oil, 229 70; linseed ditto, 18s tlid. Turpentine. 28s 6d to 28s 9d. Petroleum: American, Sid, and Russian 51d. Lwitaeoot, PRovistotts. FRIDAY.— For beef holders are firm, asking an advance. Pork remains steady at recent rates. For bacon the demand is quiet, but there is no disposition on the part of holders to press sales. With larger offerings in hams and shoulders, values tend slightly in favour of buyers. Cheese meets a moderate request at irregular prices. Butter. is quite nominal. Cable advices from America, received to- day, quote nomaterial change in the value of hogs, lard, tor bacon.

Twist cops are very firm, and in some instances early delivery is impracticable. Slairtings are dull, and very little inquiry is being made. ILLNESS OF CARDINAL HOWARD.—Tho recovery of Cardinal Howard being declared to be hopeless, the Pope has appointment Cardinal Monaco administrator of the diocese of _Frascati, of which Cardinal Howard was titular bishop. The English cardinal will also be re- placed as the Archpriest of Saint Peter's...

FATAL ICCIDYNT.AT • COLLIERY.—WhiIst a number of men were removing some smouldering cinders at Blun- dell's Colliery, Pemberton, on Wednesday, for the new railway works, a portion of the heap fell upon them. Three of the men had to be removed to the Wigan Infir- mary, and two of these—Dennis M‘Gmth and ,Tohn Melia died during the night from their burns.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

General Armstrong, C.8.A., a 'well-known officer of the Indian Army, died at Folkestone on Friday morn- ing. By command of the Queen the Prince of Wales held a levee at two o'clock on Friday, at St. James's Palace. There was .a good attendance

Mr. Shirlei Brooks, the editor of the "Sporting Times," died suddenly on Friday morning He was the eldest son of Shirley Brooks, the former editor of" Punch." The " Weekly Herald," a metropolitan Catholic journal, states that her Majesty's Government have agreed to found and endow an Irish Catholic Univer- sity.. _ _
Mr. Thomas E. Ellis, M.P., has propounded the outline of a scheme for the formation of a Welsh National Coun- cil, to which he would delegate the management of purely Welsh affairs.

The annual assembly of the Congregational Union, on Friday, carried, without discussion, a resolution protes- ting against the proposal of the 'Government to create a vested interest in the liquor licences. . .

Lord Salisbury's attack on% Lord Wolseley in the House of Lords on Friday has caused much sensation. and it is considered probable that Lord Wolseley will resign his post as Adjutant-General of the Forces. MEN-CV-WAR AGAIN IN COLLISION.—A Lloyd's Ports mouth telegram states that whilst her Majesty's brig Martin was going to her buoy on Friday she came into collision with the St. Vincent, damaging a boat and carrying away her own topgallant mast. MURWIR IN IRELAND.—At an inquest held at Fallagh- loon county Derry, on Friday, on the body of Francis Bradley, a verdict of wilful murder was returned against Patrick Bradley, who is in custody. There was over £lOO on the body. CAPTURE OF AN ALLEGED MOONLIGIITER.—OR Friday morning, John Guinea, an alleged Moonlighter, and one of a band who attacked and fired into the house of a far- mer named Curtin, in Kerry, last Sunday, was arrested when embarking on the steamship Egypt for New York, under an assumed name.

• DEA.= OF MR. JOHN HEYWOOD.—Mr. John Heywood, the well-known Lancashire publisher, died on Thursday night at his residence, Stretford, of angina pectoris. He was best known as a great publisher and bookseller, and as a publisher of scholastic books his name was known throughout Great Britain. He took no part in municipal or political life, but was a type of the successful self- wade man of business. He was fifty-five years old. AMALGAMATION OF SALFORD WITH MANCHESTER.—At the weekly meeting of the Salford Board of Guardians. on Friday, the Chairman said that if the rates of the two places were amalgamated, so far as the maintenance of .the poor was concerned, the balance would be in favour of Salford. Mr. J. G. Groves said the population of Sal- ford was rapidly increasing, and the rateable value was bound to increase, whereas in Manchester the population was decreasing, and probably its rateable value would decrease.—The subject then dropped. ALLIDED POISONING: COMMITTED FOR MDEDER.—At Worcester, on Friday afternoon, Mary Eleanor Powell, aged 36 years, widow of a publican, and James Henry Keatley, 32, hairdresser, were committed for trial on charge of wilfully murdering Henry Powell, husband of the first-named prisoner. The prosecution allege that the deceased, whose life was insured by Mrs. Powell for £2OO, died from narcotic poisoning. The case against the servant girl, named Humphries, who was charged with being concerned in the murder, was dismissed.

THE BROWILANDS POACHING AFFRAY.—At Altriire.haM, on Friday afternoon, Thomas Gayterja powerful-looking man, was charged with being concerned in the affray with poachers at Brooklands, in November last, when Sergeant Cooper and Constable Prod!!love were seriously injured. Prisoner was apprehended in Manchester on Thursday night. He had his head plastered, and had evidently sustained injuries in the scuffle. Prisoner denied the charge, and was remanded for the production of the boatman. It is stated that Gayer is a native of Runcorn. _ '

- MH:IOHW DILLON SENT TO PnisoN.2-The trial of Mr. I Dillon, M.P., for conspiracy, was resumed at Mellon Friday, before Messrs. Mayne and Hamilton. Sergeant Brownlee was cross-examined as to the placard conven- ing the Tullyallen moetingt, and Mr. Harrington then ad- dressed the court for the defendant. The Bench after- wards retired, and on returning, sentenced Mr. Dillon to six months' imprisonment without hard labour. The second case was then proceeded with, but Mr.. Har- rington had an altercation with the Bench, and retired from the court. After some discussion, the hearing of the second charge was adjourned, and Mr. Dillon having given notice of appeal against the sentence was liberated on bail. The appeal will be heard at Dundalk on June 12th.

div.head: ABOLITION OF SLAVERY IN BRAZIL.
div.p: ABOLITION OF SLAVERY IN BRAZIL.
RIO DE JANEIRO, TRURSDAY.----We iTRZiI7;II Chamber of Deputies has voted the immediate and unconditional abolition of slavery in Brazil. NEWFOUNDLAND AND THE FISHERIES BILL.

OTTAWA, TxunsnAv.—Sir Charles Tupper has received word that both the Newfoundland Houses of Parliament have passed the Fisheries Bill. RELAPSE OF THE EMPEROR OF BRAZIL. It WAS announced from Milan, on Friday morning, that the Emperor of Brazil has had a relapse, and that symptoms of neuralgic cerebral congestion have appeared. Dr. Charcot has been summoned from Paris, and Dr. Giovanni from Padua, to hold a consul- tation.

div.head: EMPEROR FREDERICK.
div.p: THE EMPEROR FREDERICK.

The following bulletin was issued on Friday morning: —The Emperor's condition during the last few days has been relatively good. The fever has been quite insigni- ficant, and his Majesty's sleep, although occasionally bro ken, has, nevertheless, been of a refreshing character. The illustrious patient's strength has again improved.
MINING DISASTER IN IrRUSSIA.-18 KILLED,
MANY INJURED.

A telegram from Stassfurth, in the Prussian province of Saxony, states that there was a tremendous fall of rock in a mine at that place on Wednesday. A large number of miners were buried, 18 being killed, and many others seriously injured.
LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS

The House met atfour o'cl*k. - OUR MILITARY SYSTEM: ATTACK ON LORD WOLSLEY. —Viscount HARDING& called the attention of the Duke of Cambridge to an article in the "Daily Telegraph" that morning on "England in Danger," and to statements Said to have been contributed by the highest military anthorities. He asked the Duke whether he was the ‘authority referred to. The Duke of Cambridge emphati- %ally denied having supplied any information to the vier of the highly sensational article. The whole question of our military system was, he knew, occupy ing the attention of the Government, and doubtless the result would be satisfactory to the country.—The Mar- quis of SALISBURY said that the Government were fully alive to the question, but entered a most emphatic pro- test against the recent statement made by Lord Wolse- ley in after-dinner, panic-creating speech. If Lord Wolseley thought it his duty to make such statements, he should do so in the House where he could be an- swered.

div.head: HOLISE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOLISE OF COMMONS.
_ Speaker took the chair at ten minutes past three The ty o'clock.

THE CART AND WHEEL DUTIES. In reply to Major Rasch, the CHANCELLOR of the Examonan stated that if farmers' locomotives were used on the public roads they would be liable to the cart and wheel duties. CREMATION.—In answer to Mr. James Ellis, Mr. RIT- CHIE said he had no intention of conferring upon the new District Councils the right of cremation. THE ALLEGED NEW CATnottc Commas .—Mr W. H. SMITH said there was no truth in the statement that her Majesty's Government have decided to found or endow a Catholic college in Ireland. (Hear, hear.) There have been no negociations which could reasonably give rise to such a report. (Cheers). NAVAL STATION..—Sir J. FERGUSON, replying to Mr. Conybeare, said it was intended to give up the Island of Ascension as a naval station.

NEW MEMBERS.—Mr. BILADLAtOH moved, as an amendment to going into Committee of Supply, a reso- lution providing that when a new member presented himself at the Bar, the Speaker should, unless the House otherwise ordered, call him to the table for the purpose of taking his seat.—Sir H. James, Lord R. Churchill. and the Attorney-General, spoke on the motion for going into Supply.—The motion was negatived by 153 votes to 147.—0 n Mr. Bradlaugh's resolution being put as the main question, Sir H. JAMES moved the omission of the words "unless the House otherwise resol*ed" from the resolution. He did not think it was intended to autho- rise the House to interfere to prevent a duly elected mem- ber from taking his seat.—Lord R. Cacao:nu, said the amendment showed the awkward position the House had got into. The Government had knocked down their own motion for going into Supply. He considered the resolu- tion altogether unnecessary.—Mr. W. H. SMITH said the Government thought the resolution wholly unnecessary, but they were willing to,aceept it in the way proposed, because they thought it perfectly innocuous. He, how- ever, Bllfmested the matter should be postponed till the Speaker was in chair.—Mr. JOJIN MORLEY said the Attorney-General in his former observations said he was prepared to assent to the resolution. Yet he hadivoted against it.—Mr. BRADLAUGH pointed out that the words it was now proposed to strike out were not his, and he accused the First Lord of the Treasury of wilfully break- ing an engagement he had entered into last night.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL said it was only dn the introduction of the words "unless the House should other- wise resolve" that he assented to the amendment.— As it was now proposed to strike out those words, he should oppose the resolution.—Mr. LABOUCHERE wished to know what course the government intended to adopt in the matter.—Mr. Sxrra said if the words were allowed to remain, the government would assent to the resolution; if they ere struck out the governmerts would oppose it. Mr. T. HEALY pointed out that they had got muddled, and here they had the First Lord of the Treasury contra- dicting the Attorney-General (Laughter.) The propo- sal to omit the words from the resolution was carried !without a. division.—Mr. W. SMITH said, as the words I had been struck outhe would now oppose the resolution,

It having been proposed that all towns of 50.000 Inhabitants and upwards should be made Counties of themselves, and thus possess the many advantages which the Bill would con- fer upon them in that position. A POLL will be taken of the number of persons in the Borough on the night of Sunday, the Thirteenth May, 1888, in order to ascer- tain the exact population, and with the object of securing the best possible position under the above Bill. Papers will be delivered on Saturday next, in which occu- piers are requested to insert the number of persons who on the night of Sunday, the Thirteenth May, sleep in their house, including In such number every Man. Woman, and Child. The papers will be collected on Monday, the Fourteenth May, 1888. WM. HY. BROOK, Town Clerk.
